Text description provided by the architects. The idea of renovating a mid-terrace home—tucked between a small street and an alley—changed radically when the opportunity arose to purchase the adjacent plot, a long, narrow strip measuring 25 meters long by just 2.5 meters wide, built edge to edge. This allowed for the creation of large openings onto the new courtyard, and the project transformed into an exploration of all possible ways to bring light into the homes: sliding windows flush with the wall exterior, vertical and horizontal pivoting panels, arched French doors, circular skylights, guillotine windows, and liftable panes.

#8938. A New Study Reveals 3 Migraine Triggers That Might Be Making Your Headaches Worse—See Them Here

Temperatures are starting to rise, with some parts of the US facing a record-setting early heat wave this week. But while you’re probably focused on staying cool, there’s one more thing that should be on your radar: a higher-than-usual risk of migraine headaches.

That’s the major takeaway from new research published in the journal Neurology: The study uncovered three lesser-known factors that can trigger migraine—and these triggers can crop up even more in the late spring and summer.

If you’re one of the 12% of Americans who deals with these headaches, this is information to keep in your back pocket. Here’s what the study found, plus how doctors who treat patients with migraine recommend protecting yourself.

For the study, researchers followed 7,032 people living in Israel for about a decade who suffered from migraines. During the study period, researchers looked at participants’ daily exposure to air pollution, along with tracking weather conditions. They also looked at how often and when people visited the hospital or their primary care doctor with a migraine. That data was compared to the levels of pollution and weather conditions on that particular day, along with seven days before that.

During the study period, 2,215 people (or 32%) had at least one visit to the hospital or a clinic with a migraine. The researchers also found that 47% of participants in the study bought triptan medications at one point or another—fast-acting prescription medications that are designed to stop a migraine—with most using at least two tablets a month.

Ultimately, the researchers discovered a link between three weather-related factors and migraine: air pollution, temperature (including UV exposure), and humidity. First, they found a correlation between higher levels of air pollution and the most number of visits to a hospital or clinic for a migraine. They also found that the day with the least visits to the hospital or clinic also had lower-than-average pollution levels. People with short-term exposure to high levels of nitrogen dioxide (a common pollutant from traffic exhaust) were 41% more likely to go to the hospital or clinic for migraine than people who weren’t exposed to high levels of the gas.

The study also showed that people who were exposed to high levels of UV rays from the sun on a given day were 23% more likely to visit a healthcare provider for migraine symptoms than those who weren’t. High temperatures and low humidity appear to be linked to more migraine headaches, likely because they amplify the effect of nitrogen dioxide, the researchers said.

With climate change intensifying how often we deal with heat waves and pollution, it’s important to consider these risk factors when it comes to migraine, the researchers wrote.

It’s important to note that the study didn’t prove that air pollution, heat, and lower humidity levels cause migraines—it just found a link between them. But doctors say there’s likely something here.

Air pollution can spark neuroinflammation (the immune system’s inflammatory response in the brain and spinal cord), which is a risk factor for migraine, Sana Ghafoor, MD, neurologist at Tufts Medical Center, tells SELF. This may cause a release of pain chemicals like calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and substance P that can lead to a migraine, Dr. Ghafoor says.

Air pollution may be particularly problematic for people with allergies who also struggle with migraines, Clifford Segil, DO, a neurologist at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, California, tells SELF. The body may see air pollution as an allergen and mount an immune response, which can spark a migraine in people who are sensitive to this trigger, he explains.

Then, there’s the fact that heat can impact blood vessels and nerves. “When people heat up, nerves and blood vessels in tight locations can become irritated, as the diameter of a blood vessel or nerves increases with heat,” Dr. Segil says. That, too, can trigger a migraine. You’re also more susceptible to getting dehydrated when it’s hot out, Dr. Ghafoor says: “If you're overheated and dehydrated, those can also trigger migraines.”

Dr. Segil points out that high humidity common in the spring and summer (and not just that related to air pollution) can trigger migraines too. High humidity causes you to sweat and lose water, which can decrease the amount of blood in your blood vessels (if you don’t replace it), Dr. Segil says. “This decreases the diameter of blood vessels and can cause headaches, just like an increased blood vessel diameter,” he says.

Dr. Ghafoor says she often sees more patients have migraine headaches when high humidity strikes. “Even with small [atmospheric] pressure changes, it can activate nerve endings and sinuses, which can lead to the release of pain chemicals,” she says.

These are some of the most common migraine triggers, according to the US National Library of Medicine:

These foods and ingredients can also trigger migraines, per the US National Library of Medicine:

Migraine triggers are personal, making it important to do what you can to figure out yours and then try to avoid them as best as possible. (Dr. Ghafoor recommends keeping a headache diary to try to narrow things down.) But factors like air pollution, heat, and humidity can be tough to avoid.

If levels of air pollution are high in your area, Dr. Segil recommends wearing a face mask like an N95 when you need to be outdoors. Keeping your windows shut and running an air purifier can also help tamp down on pollution indoors. If you’d like, you can track pollution levels throughout the day and try to stay inside during peak times, Dr. Ghafoor says.

When heat and humidity strikes, Dr. Ghafoor recommends doing what you can to stay well hydrated. “Make sure that it’s not just water, but electrolytes too,” she says. “All of that is a very important part of lifestyle management for patients who have migraine.”

Ultimately, doing your best to try to figure out your triggers (and avoid them) can go a long way toward helping to keep you more comfortable on a regular basis. “Knowing and identifying migraine triggers is very important,” Dr. Ghafoor says. “It’s empowering the patient to understand their disease.”

#8935. After Losing My Son, I Didn't Want to Be ‘Strong’

During my pregnancy with my son Milan, I remember sitting with a pain that didn’t feel normal. It was sharp, persistent, and unsettling in a way I couldn’t ignore. As a former labor and delivery nurse, I understood the risks in a way many patients do not. I knew what to watch for. I knew my history. I knew when something felt wrong. Yet when I raised concerns, they were not met with the urgency they deserved.

At the time of my pregnancy with Milan, I had already experienced a high-risk pregnancy and an emergency C-section during a previous pregnancy. I knew that the vertical incision on my uterus could put a future pregnancy at risk. I spoke up. I asked questions. I paid attention to my body. Still, when I experienced a uterine rupture, I was navigating a system that did not respond with the level of care and urgency that the moment required.

If someone with years of labor and delivery experience can recognize the signs, advocate for herself, and still be failed, what happens to the women with less information, fewer resources, or less confidence that they will be heard?

Conversations during Black Maternal Health Week often center around one urgent truth: Black women are still far more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes in this country than white women. This is not an assumption. It is a proven fact, and it should stop all of us in our tracks. It also does not only impact one socioeconomic group. It affects everyone, including some of the most visible and resourced women in the world.

As the founder of Mielle, my mission is to empower women, especially Black women, to express their authentic selves. At its core, that mission is about care, agency, and visibility, which is why conversations like this matter. It’s about showing up for every part of Black women’s experience. We need to talk more candidly about what happens to Black women who survive the trauma of miscarriage or stillbirth, and the prolonged mental health challenges that can follow, including postpartum depression.

Black women are expected to remain “strong” while navigating medical emergencies. We’re dismissed, told to wait, to calm down, and to trust a system that has not always earned that trust. We survive experiences that change our families and us forever. And then, too often, we are expected to do something just as impossible: keep going as if survival is the end of the story. It is not.

That is why Black Maternal Health Week cannot be about mortality alone. It must also be about what it means to live after trauma, preventable harm, and loss that reshapes your life.

The data make clear that this crisis is ongoing. Black women are about three times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes than white women, and more than 80% of those deaths are considered preventable. Black infants also die at more than twice the rate of white infants. These are not random gaps. They reflect a healthcare system and a culture that too often normalizes Black women’s pain instead of responding to it.

Research shows that one in five women, or about 20%, report mistreatment during maternity care, but for Black women, that figure climbs to nearly 30%, reflecting more frequent experiences of bias, disrespect, and lack of autonomy in clinical settings. Nearly half of women say they have held back from asking questions or sharing concerns. In one of the most vulnerable moments of a person’s life, too many are already calculating whether speaking up will make things worse.

In my own life, grief did not arrive quietly. It entered my marriage, my motherhood, my body, my faith, and eventually my work. In my book, The Glory In Your Story, I write about how grief does not follow a timeline. It becomes part of who you are, and healing begins not by outrunning it, but by acknowledging it.

That matters because so many Black women are praised for being strong when what we actually need is space to be human. After losing Milan, I returned to work. I kept moving. I built Mielle. From the outside, it can look like a story of resilience. And in many ways, it is. But we have to be honest about the lessons we take from stories like mine.

The lesson should not be that Black women are uniquely equipped to carry devastating grief and still perform at a high level. It should not be that our resilience makes systemic failures acceptable. And it should not be that we have to turn survival into something productive just to make our pain legible.

Too often, we celebrate the comeback without sitting long enough with the conditions that made it necessary.

Faith carried me. Purpose helped me rebuild. But none of that changes the reality that more listening, better care, stronger hospital systems, and greater urgency might have changed my story. If we are serious about maternal health, we have to be just as serious about saying that clearly.

Black Maternal Health Week gives us an opportunity to think more broadly about what justice looks like. It looks like hospitals are equipped for emergencies. It looks like providers who listen to Black women the first time, without requiring patients to fight to be believed. It looks like support for families after loss–not just during a crisis. And it looks like making space for grief without expecting Black women to turn it into inspiration before we are ready.

It’s time that we honor not only the women we have lost, but also the women still here carrying what the system could not or would not hold for them. Survival is not the finish line. Being heard, protected, and cared for should be.

#8933. Jan Frodeno and Flora Duffy on Olympic Gold vs. Ironman Paydays

This roundtable conversation, facilitated by Triathlete contributor Jordan Blanco, explores the push and pull professional triathletes feel when it comes to deciding whether to pursue the Olympics or other race series for financial gain.

We are two years out from the Los Angeles Olympics, and short-course triathletes are approaching a decision that is both deeply personal and increasingly difficult to justify on a spreadsheet.

That tension was clearly on display at the recent Ironman World Championship in Kona, Hawaii. Taylor Knibb added an Ironman world title to her palmares, even as the American is collecting Olympic qualifying points in the hope of racing a third Olympics on home soil in Los Angeles. Vincent Luis, a three-time Olympian and two-time short-course world champion, won Kona on his debut, having spent much of his career chasing Olympic success before making a late transition to long-course racing.

Others also offered different perspectives. Marten Van Riel described having been stuck in the Olympic pipeline for a long time before finally getting the opportunity to race in Kona. Ironman Hawaii third-place finisher and Olympic silver medalist from Paris 2024, Julie Derron, has not ruled out a return to short-course racing and a place on the Swiss Olympic team in 2028.

Their experiences reflect the choices of a growing number of professional triathletes. An Olympic campaign can consume an athlete’s schedule for years. Qualification requires global travel, points chasing, federation politics, and enough patience to build multiple seasons around a race that offers only three medals and no conventional prize purse. At the same time, T100 and the Ironman Pro Series circuit offer credible alternatives: more races, more ways to earn significant sums of money, and for some athletes, a clearer pathway to build a career in professional triathlon.

Yet reducing the choice to money misses much of what gives the Olympics their power. Jan Frodeno and Flora Duffy built two of the most decorated careers in triathlon, moving between the Olympic and long-course worlds in very different ways. Frodeno’s victory at the 2008 Beijing Games was the first race he had ever won. He later became a multiple Ironman and Ironman 70.3 world champion but remained known far beyond triathlon first as an Olympic champion. Duffy competed at five Games, won gold in Tokyo, and became a national figure in Bermuda. Even after exploring longer-distance racing, the Olympics remained her north star.

Their experiences also complicate the idea that athletes must choose between Olympic meaning and financial reward. Both describe the Olympic title as commercially valuable, although not in the form of race-day prize money. For Duffy, contracts tied to success in Tokyo and the new sponsors she signed afterward made Olympic gold financially lucrative. For Frodeno, being an Olympic Champion is a credential that continues to open doors almost two decades later.

But neither describes gold as an uncomplicated ending. Frodeno found himself struggling for direction after reaching the apparent summit of the sport in his first victory. Duffy returned for another quad because the possibility of repeating victory remained more compelling than a run at Kona.

Triathlete spoke with Frodeno and Duffy separately, then brought their answers together. The conversations have been condensed and edited for clarity.

Jan Frodeno: I come from not just a non-sporting but almost anti-sporting family. My parents had nothing to do with sports, and the only time sport was really valued was when the Olympics were on television. I remember being at my grandparents’ house during the 1988 Olympics. For two and a half weeks, the television was on nonstop, and the athletes who came home were cherished as heroes.

That planted a seed somewhere deep in my subconscious. I was always active and always needed an outlet, but sport wasn’t appreciated in my family at that time. The Olympics gave me a horizon – hope that I could change my stars. It was such an audacious goal that nobody really understood what it meant or could tell me it was completely crazy. It seemed like a parallel world where different people lived.

[The Olympics] gave me meaning and hope for close to two decades, until I actually got there. Triathlon wasn’t even in the Olympics in 1988. Later I met Conrad Stoltz, who went to Sydney for South Africa, and he was my first real Olympic contact. He was just a regular guy who happened to be better at triathlon than other people. Seeing that made the Olympics accessible. It made me realize I wanted to pursue that dream.

Flora Duffy: The Olympics were always the ultimate goal. They were what I dreamed of doing. I saw the Games as the pinnacle of sport when I was growing up. Every four years, I would sit down and watch, and the Olympics would take over.

Sydney was the first Games I clearly remember watching. There was something special about it. The event is iconic, everybody knows about it and it has such a rich history. Maybe part of it is that it happens only every four years. There is scarcity value. The buildup starts years in advance – just as we’re already talking about Los Angeles now.

Duffy: My position is probably different from that of many athletes because I come from such a small place. Bermuda sends an extremely small team to the Olympics: 10 athletes would be a lot. In Tokyo, there were only two of us.

Tyler Butterfield was a few years older than me and raced in Athens. He was the first Bermudian Olympian I could really relate to. He did triathlon, I did triathlon, and he was competing at the Olympic Games. Suddenly I could think, “Maybe I can do that too.” He had also competed at the Junior World Championships and won a medal before I did. Those moments made the pathway feel real.

I later saw what an Olympic medal could do for a small country, and I got to live the biggest version of that by winning gold in Tokyo. It meant so much. It united the island and became this deep, meaningful moment that transcended swim, bike, and run. There are now landmarks in Bermuda associated with me: the track at the national stadium, a pool at my high school, a road, murals. That shows how powerful the Olympics can be.

Frodeno: You go to the Olympics as a national athlete and contribute to your country’s medal table, but you also walk away with the honor yourself. [Being an Olympic champion] is forever, and it doesn’t really matter where you are from. It is the one title that sticks outside the triathlon bubble.

Hawaii is the Wimbledon of our sport. We care very deeply about it, and it is extremely meaningful to me. But when I make a public appearance, I am still introduced as the Olympic champion. That title shines beyond any individual sport.

There is also the experience of going as part of a national team. Triathlon is such an individual sport, but at the Olympics you live with athletes from completely different sports and share the experience with them. One of my roommates in Beijing was Moritz Fürste, the captain of the German hockey team. I won my medal a few days before the hockey team won theirs, and it was wild.

Frodeno: You get one shot every four years. A world championship happens every year – and that is not to take anything away from a world championship – but having one chance in four years exponentially increases the potential for error. Most athletes might get one or two Olympic opportunities in a career. A few get three. Flora went five times, which is crazy.

That scarcity gives it something special. It reaches beyond the sport itself. The title of Olympic champion stays with you in a way that almost nothing does.

Duffy: There are only three medals. If you finish fourth, fifth or sixth, there is no prize money. You leave empty-handed after dedicating the previous four years – or more – to that one event.

At the same time, that uncertainty is part of what makes sport beautiful. You never know what is going to happen on the day. That is why athletes train and pursue the goal. They build their whole careers around chasing that one opportunity.

Duffy: For most of my career, racing short course was quite lucrative. I loved the fast, dynamic style of racing, and I had enough success early on to stay committed to it. Each Olympic build was different, and I was a different athlete in every cycle, so I wasn’t looking around and asking what else I could do in triathlon.

Now there are many more opportunities. Athletes are trying to decide whether to race short-course, T100, or the Ironman Pro Series while also attempting to qualify for the Olympics. The danger is they spread themselves too thin.

Are you pursuing the Olympics because that is your dream and your ultimate goal? Or do you want to focus on T100 and the Ironman Pro Series because you want to make money? For some athletes, that is the goal. They are not interested in the Olympics, and there is nothing wrong with that.

The other side is that short-course athletes may receive federation funding, health insurance, and travel support. They might not be earning a huge amount, but they have enough security to pursue the goal without relying entirely on sponsors or race results. The calculation is more complicated than looking only at prize purses.

Frodeno: I don’t know that I would have chosen differently. Don’t get me wrong: I am definitely economically motivated. But there were lucrative races in my era too. Hy-Vee put enormous money on the line, and I never really chased it.

I think it is fantastic that athletes now have so many possibilities. But more choice can also make the decision harder. Going through a federation can be frustrating and grating because volunteers are sometimes making the decisions that affect your professional career. It can look easier to get a pro license and pursue immediate prize money.

Still, if the Olympics are what genuinely pull you, that experience is not something you can recreate later. It is not something you can read about in a blog after the fact.

Duffy: Standing on an Olympic podium with a medal around your neck is priceless, but it can also lead to more sponsorship and exposure. My situation was unique because my contracts were geared toward Tokyo and winning there. For me, it was a very lucrative day. I also signed new sponsors afterward because I was the Olympic champion.

That success carried into the next cycle. A lot of my sponsors were geared toward Paris and short-course racing, so they were happy that I remained on that path. There was also all this momentum around returning to the Olympics as the defending champion, particularly as someone from a small island.

Frodeno: It changed my circumstances, but the lasting commercial value was not simply cashing in on the medal or earning a certain amount in sponsorship. That fades relatively quickly. The unique thing about being an Olympic champion is that it is a door opener.

That is still valued commercially now, 18 years later. I don’t walk around with my medal. It is more something that people say about you than something you need to say about yourself. But the title carries.

Frodeno: What many people don’t realize is that the Olympics were the first race I ever won. I had never won a World Cup. I went from never having tasted victory to reaching the apparent end state of the game on my first win.

That was wonderful, but it was also the pinnacle. Any World Cup afterward could not compare to three helicopters overhead, the media coverage, and the scale of the Olympics. It also threw me into some of the darkest times of my life because I struggled to find meaning afterward. It was seven years before I won my first world title, at the 2015 70.3 World Championship, and during that period I wondered whether I was a one-hit wonder.

I had thought winning gold would mean arriving at all my dreams. It took me from a miserable little apartment to a wonderful loft, a fancy car, and flying business class. But I didn’t see the writing on the wall soon enough that what I actually loved about triathlon was triathlon itself and the training. It was – and still is – just a love for the sport.

A few weeks before Beijing, I remember completing a brutal session in the rain and telling myself, “If you get through this, you never have to go this hard again.” In hindsight, that was strange, because hard training was what I chose to keep doing for nearly two more decades.

Duffy: Tokyo was hugely meaningful for me, my team and my country. Going into Paris, the intrigue was whether I could do it again. Could I win another medal? Could I defend the title and become a two-time Olympic champion?

The Olympics had always been my ultimate goal. Even late in my career, I never developed the dream of going to Kona and winning. I thought that bug would catch me but it never did.

Now that I am retired, if I ask myself whether I wish I had a proper shot at Kona or a better build into Paris, my regret is that I did not have a better build into Paris. I don’t regret not racing Kona. That says a lot about where the Olympics sat for me.

Frodeno: I went to two Olympics, but I did not have the guts to recognize that my Olympic ambition and campaign were effectively done by 2012. I loved the experience, but I probably should have gone a different way after Beijing. As John Mayer sings in Gravity, “Twice as much is not twice as good.”

It is difficult to give generic advice because everybody comes from a different place. The thing I did well was to listen to my gut. My mother wanted me to study because she was looking after my best interests, but I knew I had to go all in. At the time, almost nobody was making money in Olympic-distance triathlon, but I followed what I enjoyed most and found a way to build a career around it.

Duffy: For many, the Olympic pathway comes first, and then, assuming they remain healthy, they move to middle- or long-distance racing later. They have their Olympic experience, whether it was good, disappointing or successful, and then they begin the second part of their career.

My path was different because the Olympic goal continued to excite me. The possibility of returning for Paris meant more to me than moving fully into long-course racing. That will not be true for every athlete, and it should not be.

This is a hard lifestyle. What is going to get you out of bed to train for several hours a day and deal with injuries? The answer is different for everybody. For me, it was the Olympics.

Duffy: Athletes often go into the Olympics with slightly unrealistic expectations. On one hand, that is good. You have to dream and believe. But if you are not realistic, you can come out the other side deeply disappointed.

Everything is heightened at the Olympics: the pressure, expectations and noise. The buildup is stressful. There is team selection, chasing points around the world, dealing with injuries and trying to arrive at the last minute in the right shape. It is extremely difficult, but it is also extremely rewarding.

Unrealistic expectations can take some of the joy out of racing at an iconic venue and representing your country. I was guilty of that in Paris. It was my fifth and final Olympics, and I already had a gold medal. The result was not going to make or break my career. But I finished fifth and was extremely disappointed, and that disappointment took away some of the joy of being at the Games and watching athletes from around the world.

It is difficult to balance expectations with appreciating the moment. Athletes should dream big, but they should also understand how hard it is to perform on that one day.

Frodeno: Nowadays, the decision is probably harder because there is so much choice. The one thing I did well was listen to my gut instinct. If the Olympics really get to you – particularly with a home Games in Los Angeles – riding through the streets of LA with tens of thousands, hopefully hundreds of thousands of people cheering is priceless. It is not an economic choice. It is about living life to the fullest.

Experiencing the Olympics through your national team and alongside athletes from other sports is a unique construct. It brings a core group of people together in a way that money cannot buy.

#8930. Obstructive Sleep Apnea Impacts Women Differently.

There are at least a dozen reasons why women may wake up with a headache, jitter with anxiety, or struggle to keep their eyes open at work, no matter how well they think they slept: menstruation, menopause, motherhood—the list truly goes on. But these symptoms, as vague as they are, could actually stem from a health condition that’s historically been deemed a “male disease”: obstructive sleep apnea, or OSA.

If you immediately pictured an older man snoozing on a couch and snoring like a lawn mower, you’re not alone. It wasn’t until the ’90s that researchers first recognized that OSA, which causes you to repeatedly stop breathing while asleep, often presents differently in women than it does in men. For starters women with the condition may not even snore.

There’s still much to discover about the biology underlying these distinctions, but research suggests that hormonal fluctuations throughout life, differences in upper airway anatomy, and even social stigmas about how women should sleep are likely at play.

“The disease itself was defined in men,” explains Jennifer Martin, PhD, a behavioral sleep medicine specialist and professor at Florida International University’s Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine in Miami. “The way men and women breathe when they’re asleep is not the same, and our definition of the disease doesn’t account for that.”

Although obstructive sleep apnea appears to be less common and typically milder in women (at least before menopause), studies suggest that the consequences of the disease, if left untreated, can be similar, if not worse, for us, making it vital to learn the signs and seek help. Here’s what we know about obstructive sleep apnea and its impact on women. Plus, experts explain how to advocate for the best care if you think you may have the condition.

Sleep apnea is one of several conditions that fall under the sleep-disordered breathing umbrella. The most common type is OSA, which happens when your upper airway repeatedly collapses during sleep, making it harder for air to reach your lungs, says Anita Valanju Shelgikar, MD, a sleep medicine physician with University of Michigan Health and president of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

The textbook symptoms of this condition—which, for the record, were determined based on studies mostly involving men—include loud snoring and dramatic gasps for air as a person tries to continue breathing while asleep. But this often isn’t the case for women, Dr. Shelgikar tells SELF. Instead, women with OSA are more likely to have nightmares, wake up multiple times a night, have trouble staying asleep, and deal with insomnia, which then causes symptoms like daytime fatigue, morning headaches, and mood swings. Women also have more hypopneas (shallow breaths with less oxygen flow), whereas men tend toward apneas (complete pauses in breathing).

Some experts speculate that it’s possible snoring isn’t commonly reported among women with this disorder because they’re embarrassed to talk about it, given society expects them to sleep like Disney princesses. But a growing body of research suggests that biology may better explain this and other sex-related differences in symptoms. For example, compared with men, women have smaller, more stable airways that are less likely to collapse (and in turn vibrate, making you snore) during sleep. Women also tend to have less fat around their necks, and before menopause they seemingly benefit from the protective effects of estrogen and progesterone, which interact with the respiratory system in a way that aids breathing.

All things considered, it makes sense why more men than women in the US have this condition, making up about 59% and 41% of obstructive sleep apnea patients, respectively. However, once women go through menopause, which causes their estrogen and progesterone levels to drop, the rate of OSA and the severity of symptoms in this group increases dramatically, Dr. Martin says. Studies have found that anywhere from 47% to 67% of postmenopausal women have obstructive sleep apnea, which is about the same as men in this age range (50 and older). The number of women who actually get diagnosed with the condition is a different story, though—more on that shortly.

Regardless of age, however, women still deal with more sleep apnea–related symptoms than men, Dr. Martin adds, even if they have a less severe form of the condition. This is likely because women have more “subtle breathing disturbances” during sleep that hurt the overall quality of their rest compared with men, Dr. Martin says.

Because women often don’t experience “classic” OSA symptoms, they end up being misdiagnosed or dismissed. “When [men] walk into a physician’s office and say they’re sleepy and they snore, they get a diagnostic test right away,” Dr. Martin says. “When a woman walks in and says, ‘I don’t sleep well, and I’m very fatigued during the day,’ they don’t often get referred” for screening. In fact, research suggests that men are nine times more likely to be referred for diagnostic testing than women.

Women with OSA commonly have their symptoms misattributed to conditions like depression, anxiety, insomnia, and menopause or even medication side effects, says Dr. Shelgikar, who is also a neurology professor at the University of Michigan Medical School. Not to mention women can have these other conditions as well, which might make their sleep apnea not only harder to detect but also worsen it. Take the double whammy that is insomnia and OSA: Having both of these disorders at the same time is more common among women than men, Dr. Martin says, and in some cases they may be given a sleep aid (such as diphenhydramine or a benzodiazepine) that can further relax their throat muscles, exacerbating their sleep apnea and leaving them even more oxygen-deprived.

And it doesn’t help that, as we talked about earlier, the diagnostic criteria for OSA are largely based on how the condition presents in men. “When we diagnose sleep apnea, we require one of two things to happen: A breathing interruption has to be associated either with a drop in oxygen levels or a brief awakening from sleep,” Dr. Martin says. “Women don’t have those very deep drops in oxygen levels that men do. So that means that the way we define the disease itself kind of biases us towards diagnosing it more in men than women.” What’s more, Medicare, which the vast majority of Americans ages 65 and older rely on for health insurance, only recognizes a sleep apnea diagnosis if a person has those steep drops in oxygen, Dr. Martin says. Those typical mid-slumber wake-ups don’t count on their own. So even “the criteria that Medicare forces people to use to define sleep apnea is very male-centric,” she adds.

Home sleep apnea tests, which are becoming increasingly common as a cheaper alternative to the gold standard in-lab exams, are also more prone to miss the condition in women. Because women tend to have fewer and milder events than men, these at-home tests may not be able to diagnose sleep apnea as accurately in this population, Dr. Martin says. They can be even more inaccurate in women with insomnia. These individuals “may not get enough sleep to get an accurate diagnosis,” she says, “so if they wear [the monitor] for six hours, but they’re only sleeping for four of them, it may look like they have less sleep apnea than they really do.”

That’s all to say that sleep apnea is likely much more common among women than the available data suggests, experts tell SELF. And that reality reveals a sobering point: A lot of women with this condition probably aren’t receiving the care they need, a delay that can, for some people, snowball into an avalanche of additional yet preventable health issues.

If left untreated, sleep apnea can have downstream effects on your health, particularly your heart, says Atul Malhotra, MD, research chief of pulmonary, critical care, and sleep medicine at UC San Diego Health. Every time you stop breathing, your body responds to the lack of oxygen by releasing the stress hormone adrenaline to jolt you awake so you take a breath. This happens really quickly; you are typically up for just a few seconds and probably won’t even remember it the next morning.

Over time this constant stress strains your cardiovascular system, Dr. Malhotra says, which may increase your risk for high blood pressure, heart attack, stroke, irregular heartbeat, and heart failure. Although the evidence is mixed, some research suggests that it’s more common for women with severe sleep apnea to experience cardiovascular complications than it is for men. Studies also show that women tend to have more health conditions upon diagnosis than men do, including thyroid disease, asthma, and depression. This raises the classic “chicken or the egg” question, but either way treating OSA can only help.

Because obstructive sleep apnea leads to low-quality shut-eye, it is also associated with memory and cognition issues and poor daytime alertness, which can boost the likelihood of car and workplace accidents (for certain high-risk jobs like those in the transportation and construction industries), Dr. Shelgikar says. Perhaps less discussed is how untreated sleep apnea affects our ability to care for ourselves and maintain relationships. “We don’t do a good job thinking about sleep apnea as a potential cause of mental health symptoms,” Dr. Martin says. In fact, research shows that managing OSA could actually help some people dealing with anxiety and depression improve their symptoms.

As researchers continue searching for answers, Dr. Martin points to a silver lining: There’s good evidence to suggest that women “benefit at least as much as men, if not more” from sleep apnea treatment, which is why it’s important to know what to look out for.

Although you’re quite literally working against decades of medical bias, it’s still possible to receive a sleep apnea diagnosis if you’re equipped with the right intel.

#8928. Can Swapping Out Your Plasma Slow the Aging Process?

Discovering the fountain of youth is an age-old pursuit (pun not intended). One of the latest clock-reversing experiments causing a buzz is a technique called therapeutic plasma exchange, a procedure that filters and replaces the liquid portion of your blood. A 2025 study in Aging Cell suggests the technique could lower biological age by two and a half years.

But before you start googling “plasma clinics near me,” it’s important to look past the headlines to what the study’s saying, and what it means—and doesn’t mean—about new plasma as an anti-aging elixir.

Plasma is more than just the liquid that surrounds the red and white blood cells in your bloodstream. Although it’s mostly water, it’s also rich in proteins, metabolites, hormones, and inflammatory signals—molecules that reflect and influence what’s happening across your organ systems, Andrea Maier, MD, PhD, geriatrician and board member of the Academy for Health and Lifespan Research, tells SELF.

“It’s a transport system like DHL, a vehicle to bring things from your brain to your muscles, from kidney to lungs, and so on. So it’s fluid with lots of information,” she says.

This makes it a smart focal point for longevity studies because it can capture a wide-angle view of your body’s internal state, also sometimes called your “biological age.” By measuring changes in the levels of thousands of circulating proteins in your plasma, you can get some sense of how well you’re functioning.

What that means is you may be 40, but your biology acts more like that of a 30-year-old—or a 50-year-old. It’s not a fixed or precise measurement, but it’s helpful health information, Keenan Walker, PhD, senior investigator at the National Institute on Aging, tells SELF.

“There’s no one biological age, but people try to estimate it,” he says. “And what studies have found is that people whose biological age is older than their chronological age are at greater risk for chronic conditions, diseases, and mortality.”

About 15 years ago, researchers started exploring the connection between plasma and the aging process. This led to experiments using a process called parabiosis, a surgical technique that links together the circulatory systems of two different organisms. In studies, researchers would stitch together the systems of old mice and young mice, with the hypothesis that if you circulated younger plasma in an older organism, the older organism’s body would reap the benefits.

And the studies did show that. Older mice who received the plasma of younger mice had more resilience to tissue and organ stress. This led to the development of using plasma exchange as a way to treat certain autoimmune diseases, neurological disorders, and blood cancers.

“So everything really came out of that question: Is there something in our circulation we could get rid of or infuse into it to be able to live longer?” says Dr. Maier. But there’s not a definitive answer to that question—yet.

In the Aging Cell study, researchers enrolled 42 people and exchanged their plasma with purified albumin (a blood protein) and saline. Some participants also got a type of immune therapy called IVIG added in. Researchers measured changes in their bodies with advanced lab tests that track aging at the molecular level.

At first glance, the results look significant: Some people in the study reduced their biological age by roughly 2.5 years. But Dr. Maier points out that this data comes from the middle of the study, not the end.

“If you are digging a little bit deeper, this ‘2.5 years younger’ is comparing people at midterm to the baseline, not at the end of the study and the baseline. At the end, the effect was nearly gone,” she says.

Part of the reason for this, says Dr. Maier, is you overwhelm your body when you take all its plasma out and reintroduce different plasma. The influx of young cells can produce a shift in your biological age, but then your body starts experiencing stress as it adapts to this major change, and your biomarkers swing back to what they were before. In other words, you may get some rejuvenation in the short-term, but it’s temporary.

Another noteworthy detail about the study was the health of the participants, says Dr. Walker. “Those who were less healthy saw a stronger intervention effect,” he says. “So I think it'll be important to find out for whom this works.”

As a concept, both Drs. Maier and Walker see some promise in blood-based interventions for improving overall health but hope to see a more personalized approach rather than a generalized non-specific plasma filtering process.

“I would call this a phase 1 study,” says Dr. Maier. “We’ve basically learned that we can safely do it, and now we have to see it in much bigger studies and look at the long-term effect. It’s not a crazy idea. It’s absolutely grounded in lots of evidence, but not for everybody. It needs to be more precise. The future is great in our field, and this is the first tiny step, but we should absolutely not implement it now in clinical practice because it is so rough on the body. I love innovation, and I love this study, but I think the future will give something else.”

#8926. The Work of Keeping a Public Building Public: The Drill Hall in Johannesburg

What happens to a building after the architecture is finished? For buildings intended to serve the public, their continued life depends on more than the physical conditions of their construction. It involves the activities that take place within them, the relationships they allow to develop, the people who occupy and shape them, and the institutional structures responsible for their upkeep. Yet these conditions are not always secured through the act of building itself. They are continually negotiated, often through forms of work that remain outside the conventional understanding of architectural practice.

The Drill Hall in central Johannesburg offers a way of examining this unfinished work. Its history is marked by changes in use, occupation and institutional responsibility, but also by repeated attempts to imagine what the building could offer the city.

#8925. Spring Allergies Can Cause Headaches. Here’s How to Deal

A stuffy nose and itchy, watery eyes are spring-allergy cornerstones—but they’re not the only symptoms that herald a pollen influx for some people. You might not immediately suspect a pulsing headache is due to allergies, but experts say it’s a common occurrence.

In fact, the same immune response that fills your nose with snot or leaves you sneezing up a storm can make your head throb. That’s especially true “if you have multiple seasonal allergies, for instance to grass and tree pollen; live near farms; or spend a lot of time outside during allergy season, being bombarded by pollen,” Beth Oller, MD, a family medicine physician in Stockton, Kansas, tells SELF. Keep reading to learn why allergies can spark headaches, plus how to tell if your head pain is allergy-related and find relief.

If you have spring allergies and breathe in pollen, “your immune system perceives it as a foreign invader,” Dr. Oller says, and releases a bunch of inflammatory chemicals like histamine. The resulting inflammation triggers swelling in your nasal cavities, which are connected to your sinuses, Rekha Raveendran, MD, allergist and immunologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, tells SELF. The sinuses extend behind the cheekbones, eyes, and bridge of the nose, and up into the forehead—so when they get puffy, you can wind up with a sensation of facial pressure and also headache, she explains.

At the same time, experiencing the effects of spring allergies may spark migraine attacks in those with migraine. The surge of inflammation and congestion can irritate a nearby nerve that plays a role in migraine, and allergy-driven fatigue and insomnia can be migraine triggers in and of themselves. Research suggests that among people with migraine, those who also have allergies tend to have worse, more frequent attacks than those who don’t.

An allergy headache typically feels like a dull throbbing in your temples, cheeks, or forehead, and makes your face feel heavy. It comes along with congestion, Dr. Oller says, and lying down or tilting your head can increase the pressure. (FYI: This is the same kind of pain as you’d get with a sinus headache, which is caused by a viral or bacterial infection in your sinuses—both lead to mucus buildup and swelling within the sinuses.)

By contrast, migraine attacks (whether or not they’re precipitated by allergies) trigger intense pain on one side of the head. They often come along with nausea, and sensitivity to light and sound, which you would not typically find with allergy headaches, Dr. Raveendran says. Meanwhile, tension headaches tend to feel more like a band squeezing around the head, and cluster headaches spark a surge of pain in or around one eye.

If you get walloped with allergy headaches each year, Dr. Oller suggests starting on an oral antihistamine medication right about now. Pollen counts are rising, and antihistamines take a week or two of daily use to kick in, she explains. The non-drowsy options work best for daytime—think: cetirizine (Zyrtec), levocetirizine (Xyzal), loratadine (Claritin), or fexofenadine (Allegra). You can use the sleepiness-inducing diphenhydramine (Benadryl) at night, but just know that you shouldn’t make a habit of relying on it as a sleep aid.

Both doctors suggest pairing oral allergy meds with a nasal corticosteroid spray like fluticasone (Flonase) or triamcinolone (Nasocort). “They hit those mucus membranes and help decrease inflammation in that region,” Dr. Oller says. It’s best to take both drugs daily throughout allergy season, she adds, not just when you think you need them. (If your headaches are barely alleviated, or the pollen counts in your area are sky-high, you may also be able to safely increase your dose of these allergy meds to boost their efficacy.)

The less pollen that enters your airspace, the fewer symptoms you’ll experience. But you don’t have to stay cooped up to cut your exposure. Keeping your windows closed, using a high-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filter in your HVAC system (or a portable air purifier that has one), and vacuuming often can make a difference, according to Dr. Oller.

Whenever you do spend ample time outside, Dr. Oller says to rinse off once you get home. This way, you’re not inhaling pollen any longer than you have to. While you’re at it, “shower your sinuses too,” Dr. Oller adds, with a nasal saline spray or Neti Pot. This helps clear some mucus to release pressure and offer temporary relief, Dr. Raveendran says.

If the congestion is making it feel like your face is chock-full of mucus, you might be tempted to reach for an OTC oral decongestant. But take note: While pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) can be helpful, it’s not recommended to use it more than a few days in a row, and isn’t a good choice if you have high blood pressure, Dr. Raveendran says. It’s a stimulant that can make some people feel jittery, or cause a fast heart rate or insomnia.

Nasal decongestants, which include phenylephrine- or oxymetazoline-based sprays (like Afrin and Vicks Sinex), can open up your nose fast but should only be used for three days at a time max, Dr. Raveendran adds. “There’s a risk of rebound congestion that leads to overall worsening of symptoms and addiction to the nasal decongestants,” she says.

Sometimes you just need in-the-moment relief for the head pain. In that case, you can pop an OTC pain reliever like ibuprofen (Advil), naproxen (Aleve), or acetaminophen (Tylenol), Dr. Oller says. The former two may be better at resolving allergy headaches because they combat inflammation. But it’s not advised to take these non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for more than 10 days straight (unless your doctor tells you otherwise) because of potential effects on your stomach and kidneys. Tylenol, by contrast, is generally safer to take long-term, though shouldn’t be combined with alcohol due to the risk for liver damage.

If you find that your allergy headaches have you reaching for pain relievers more than a few days in a row, check in with your primary care doctor or allergist. They may recommend a more intensive treatment, like prescription steroids, or suggest seeing an ear, nose, and throat doctor or neurologist, in case something else might be behind your head pain.

## The Moment You Recline Into ANA "The Room" The flight attendant slides your suite door closed. You're somewhere over the Pacific, 35,000 feet above the ocean, enclosed in what ANA calls "The Room" — a fully private, floor-to-ceiling enclosed business class suite on a Boeing 777-300ER. The seat converts to a fully flat 78-inch bed. There's direct aisle access. The service is famously meticulous. And you're flying from New York to Tokyo in a product that rivals first class on most other carriers. This is not a fantasy. This is what 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles buys you on ANA's JFK → NRT route. ### The Math That Should Stop You Cold A one-way business class ticket on ANA between New York and Tokyo typically retails for **$6,000 to $12,000 in cash**. That's not a typo. Premium cabin trans-Pacific fares are genuinely that expensive, which is precisely why the ChooseFI community treats travel rewards as a core pillar of the FI lifestyle — you're unlocking experiences that would otherwise require years of extra saving. At 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles for that same seat, your points are delivering **6.7 to 13.3 cents per point (CPP)** in value. To put that in context: most points are considered "good" redemptions at 1.5–2 CPP. This redemption is 4 to 9 times that benchmark. This is what a true sweet spot looks like. ### Why the Gap Exists Virgin Atlantic prices its ANA partner awards using a **fixed award chart** — a relic of the old loyalty program era when airlines published static pricing tables rather than dynamic, revenue-based pricing. ANA's own Mileage Club program charges 75,000–90,000 miles for the same route. Virgin Atlantic's chart prices it at 90,000, but — and here's the critical part — **with zero fuel surcharges on partner-operated flights**. What you see is what you pay. The result is one of the most compelling premium cabin redemptions in all of loyalty programs. The ChooseFI community's founding principle is that every dollar has a job. When 90,000 transferable points can do the job of $12,000 in cash, that's not just travel rewards — that's an asymmetric opportunity you'd be leaving on the table.

One of the highest cents-per-mile redemptions in all of travel rewards

Here's the aha moment: Virgin Atlantic is selling you access to ANA's inventory at a price ANA itself doesn't offer domestically in the same way. That's the inefficiency. And it's hiding in plain sight.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club maintains a fixed award chart for partner flights. This is increasingly rare in a world where airlines have moved to dynamic, revenue-linked pricing. Because the chart is fixed, Virgin Atlantic charges 90,000 miles for ANA business class between North America and Japan — regardless of whether that seat would cost $6,000 or $12,000 in cash on the day you're flying.

When cash prices spike (holiday season, cherry blossom season, Golden Week), your points cost stays the same. That's not the case when you book directly through ANA Mileage Club, where pricing can vary, or through programs that have adopted dynamic pricing altogether.

This detail alone makes or breaks the redemption. Virgin Atlantic levies high fuel surcharges on its own metal (Virgin-operated flights). Book a Virgin Atlantic-operated long-haul in business class and you might pay $500–$800 in fees on top of your miles.

But when you book partner-operated flights through Virgin Atlantic — specifically ANA — those surcharges drop to zero. You pay government taxes only, typically $50–$100 on a trans-Pacific itinerary. That's it. No fuel surcharge games.

This redemption is accessible because Virgin Atlantic Flying Club accepts transfers from the two most popular transferable points currencies in the ChooseFI ecosystem:

All transfers are instant. This matters because ANA business class availability on partner programs is scarce, and when you find a seat, you need to move fast. You cannot afford to wait 3–5 days for points to post.

Here's a non-obvious but critical piece of tradecraft: you do not search for ANA award availability on Virgin Atlantic's website. Virgin Atlantic's search engine is limited for partner award space. Instead, you search on United.com, because United and ANA are both Star Alliance members and United shows ANA partner award availability accurately in its search results.

Find the space on United.com, confirm the flight numbers and dates, then call or use the online booking tool at flyingclub.virginatlantic.com to complete the booking.

Virgin Atlantic miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. This means as long as you earn or redeem even one mile every three years, your balance stays alive. Keep that in mind as you accumulate — a small card transaction through the program every couple of years is all it takes to protect a hard-earned balance.

You need 90,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles for a one-way business class ticket. Before anything else, confirm you have this balance — or the equivalent — in Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Citi ThankYou Points, or Bilt Rewards. Do NOT transfer points until you have confirmed award space. Points transferred cannot be retrieved.

Go to united.com and use the award search tool. United is a Star Alliance partner with ANA, which means their search engine surfaces ANA partner award inventory accurately.

Note the exact flight numbers, dates, and departure times. You'll need these when booking through Virgin Atlantic.

Key timing: ANA releases partner award space 331 days in advance. Set a calendar reminder and search the moment the window opens for your target travel dates. The best availability — especially on flagship routes like JFK–NRT — goes fast.

Once you have candidate flights from United.com, go to flyingclub.virginatlantic.com and attempt to search the same flights. Availability is sometimes different between partner search engines, so confirm that Virgin Atlantic can see and price the space before you transfer anything.

With miles now in your Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account, complete the booking at flyingclub.virginatlantic.com. Use the flight numbers you identified in Step 2. You should see $0 in fuel surcharges — only government taxes (typically $50–$100 for trans-Pacific routing).

If you can't find JFK–NRT availability, try these alternatives:

Airlines partner with each other through alliances and bilateral agreements, allowing their frequent flyer programs to book seats on each other's flights. The pricing inefficiency occurs when Partner A prices Partner B's premium cabin at a different rate than Partner B charges through its own program. Virgin Atlantic maintains a fixed partner award chart that prices ANA business class at 90,000 miles regardless of demand or seasonality. ANA's own dynamic pricing can push award costs significantly higher during peak periods. This arbitrage between partner pricing and the operating airline's own program is the foundation of most airline travel rewards sweet spots.

This redemption is rated year-round, but ANA's award space to Japan tightens dramatically during cherry blossom season (late March–April), Golden Week (late April–early May), and December holidays. For the best combination of availability and experience, consider September–November or January–February travel.

The most efficient path to 90,000 Virgin Atlantic miles is through Chase Ultimate Rewards (Chase Sapphire Preferred earns 3x on dining and travel; Chase Sapphire Reserve earns 3x on travel and dining) or Amex Membership Rewards (Amex Platinum earns 5x on flights booked directly with airlines). Both transfer 1:1 to Virgin Atlantic instantly.

This redemption is built for the couple or solo traveler who has been building a transferable points balance and is ready to make Japan the centerpiece of a bucket-list trip. If you've been diligently earning Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards and you want to experience what a truly premium long-haul flight feels like — without paying $8,000–$12,000 out of pocket — this is your redemption.

It's particularly well-suited to the FI-minded traveler who values experience over stuff. You're not flying business class because you can't manage without it. You're flying it because 90,000 points delivering $8,000–$12,000 in value is one of the most efficient uses of a points balance available anywhere in loyalty programs today.

For the ChooseFI traveler who has optimized their earning strategy and is ready to deploy a meaningful points balance on a once-in-a-decade trip, this is one of the most compelling redemptions on the board.

## Why This Redemption Is Rated Moderate This isn't a beginner redemption, but it's absolutely within reach for someone who understands the basics of transferable points programs. Here's what makes it moderate rather than easy — and how to handle each challenge. ### Challenge 1: Finding Available Award Space ANA business class partner award seats are genuinely scarce. ANA doesn't release large blocks of partner availability, and what they do release on prime routes like JFK–NRT goes quickly. This is the single biggest obstacle. **The fix:** Search at exactly 331 days out, use United.com for the most accurate availability search, and have flexibility in your travel dates by at least one week in either direction. ### Challenge 2: The Multi-Program Booking Process You're searching on one airline's website (United), transferring points from a bank program (Chase/Amex) to a third airline's loyalty program (Virgin Atlantic), and then booking through that third airline's portal. It's a three-step process across three platforms. **The fix:** Follow the step-by-step process above methodically. Don't rush. Confirm availability before touching your points. ### Challenge 3: Points Accumulation 90,000 miles is a meaningful balance — but it's achievable. Chase Sapphire Reserve's welcome bonus alone can get you most of the way there. This earns a 4 out of 5 on the "Easy to Earn" scale for good reason. ### The Bottom Line If you've successfully transferred points and booked an award before, you can do this. The learning curve is real but short. The reward — flying ANA "The Room" over the Pacific for $60 in fees — makes every minute of research worthwhile.

#8921. The Latest and Greatest Sunglasses for Triathletes, Tested in Training and Racing

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Sunglasses and triathletes go hand in hand. With not one but two sports calling for a good pair, and after so much time spent nitpicking over the perfect goggles, we can’t settle for less when it comes to shading our eyes through the bulk of our training and racing.

It’s not just about UV protection and keeping bugs and debris out, because, let’s be honest: style matters, too. And today’s saturated performance sunglasses market offers a nearly unlimited selection of styles, with many pairs more high-tech and often higher-priced than ever before.

We wanted to get a clearer, less-tinted picture of the triathlon-worthy sunglasses landscape in 2026, so we combed the internet to see what was on the cutting edge and spent the summer testing a wide range of pairs while running and cycling across different terrains and climates.

Along the way, we explored the latest tech, picked out standout features, and figured out what felt worth the money – and what wasn’t quite there yet. From light-shifting photochromic lenses and video-recording AI smart glasses to everyday pairs that won’t break the bank, here’s our roundup of the best sunglasses for triathletes in 2026.

In the Pacific Northwest where I live, it can be raining one minute and sunny the next. A ride might take you from wide-open roads into dense, dark forests, sometimes around a single corner. For that reason, I’ve found light-shifting lenses incredibly useful. But even if you don’t live where I do, these glasses are practical in plenty of other changing light conditions, such as an early-morning long ride that starts before the sun comes up and ends well into the day.

One of the biggest drawbacks of traditional photochromic sunglasses is that the lenses don’t always adjust as quickly as the light changes. Their tint range also has limits, and they don’t always get as clear or as dark as you’d like. Most rely on UV light to darken, which means they may not respond as you’d expect behind a UV-blocking windshield in your car or when you’re testing them by a window before heading outside.

That’s a perfect segue into where we’ll start, as the first pair on our list looks to address these issues by taking a different approach: tint you control with a swipe.

One of the most intriguing pairs on this entire list comes from a new brand called Povec. Rather than waiting for the lenses to react to changing light, these glasses allow you to swipe an interface on the temple to change the tint in about a second.

Sure enough, I was surprised by just how quickly, and how dramatically, the tint changed. It started shifting as soon as we swiped the temple, so naturally, we spent the next several days playing with it back and forth. The electrochromic tech, as it’s called, worked so well that the glasses quickly became a showpiece for impressing friends.

These glasses ironically shone in dimmer conditions, especially when we went off-road or deep into the forests and needed to change the tint quickly. When mountain biking, being able to change the tint almost immediately as we rounded a corner into a dense forest descent felt invaluable.

At the same time, we were slightly less impressed with the optical quality in harsher light. There are subtle but apparent reflections, and the clarity is just a little off. It’s nothing dramatic, but it is noticeable, especially compared with the crystal-clear optics of some other glasses on this list.

Our favorite everyday pair of photochromic sunglasses, especially for spring and fall days in the PNW forests, was the SunGod Velans 2.

This ultralight pair offered some of the best optical clarity, field of view, and comfort of any glasses on this list, even before the added bonus of photochromic lenses. They shifted from light to dark quickly enough for our normal riding, although they couldn’t match the on-demand tint changes of the Povecs.

SunGod has become increasingly visible in triathlon thanks to athletes such as Hayden Wilde and Chelsea Sodaro donning them, but also because of a few appealing extras not often found elsewhere in the market. An array of customization options, an emphasis on durability, repairability, and recycled packaging, and a lifetime guarantee that includes repairs for accidental breakage make the higher price easier to digest. Furthermore, features such as replacement lenses and screwless hinges make the price more logical and suggest this pair will likely last you for the long term rather than just a couple of seasons.

Tifosi consistently makes it into our roundups for offering quality sunglasses at some of the best prices, and its light-shifting options are no exception.

We tried the Rail XC with Clarion Blue “Fototec” lenses, which offer a stated light-transmission range of 12% to 46%.

Compared with the SunGods, these felt like only a small step down in optical quality and fit during our testing. We did notice more glare from sunlight at certain angles and slightly more fogging during humid runs. At 31 grams, they were also a little heavier.

But beyond that, there’s little else to nitpick. They’re comfortable, clear, and transition smoothly and quickly, with nose pads and temple tips that adjust on the fly, offering plenty of room to dial in comfort.

Perhaps the most controversial pair on this list, these smart glasses have divided opinions about where this technology belongs in triathlon. From Ironman banning their use at its events to T100 welcoming them through a partnership, it’s a hot topic.

After training and racing in them twice, my own mixed opinion comes down to something simpler: I thoroughly enjoy wearing them and appreciate their practicality, but I’m still struggling with the bulky styling of the Vanguard. Enough so that I often intentionally leave them behind so I’m not the guy with the video sunglasses when running or cycling with friends.

That functionality, on the other hand, is hard to argue with. Being able to capture hands-free video and photos, listen to music, take phone calls, and ask Meta questions — among many other features — makes these glasses useful in ways a regular pair simply can’t match.

The Oakley Prizm lenses offered the clarity we expected, although the bulkier frame slightly restricted the field of view. Even after keeping them in their case and using only a microfiber cloth to clean them, I also noticed tiny scratches under close inspection after a few months of use. They weren’t noticeable while wearing the glasses, but they were there.

At 66 grams, you’ll notice the weight, too. If you have one of the lightweight alternatives on this list sitting next to them, you might think twice before grabbing these for an everyday session.

Where these really earned their place is in documenting your triathlon experiences. At SOS Triathlon and Escape from Alcatraz, capturing moments before, during, and after the race felt almost effortless. I could quickly tell Meta to take a photo or record a video, then download the footage to my phone through the app afterward, and I was set. Compared with previously having to bring GoPros, set up shots, and worry about batteries and SD cards, it makes it all too easy.

On the way to the SOS check-in tent, I even asked Meta to help me remember the different stages of this unique multi-stage race (read more about the SOS here).

Like it or not, smart glasses are likely to become an increasingly familiar sight around triathletes. After using them, I can understand the appeal.

Read a full Oakley Meta Vanguard review here.

The award for the most pleasantly surprising sunglasses on this entire list goes to this Oakley Meta rival, which packed in enough features to put the Vanguard on the ropes.

I’ll admit I went into testing the Rover sunglasses with the preconceived notion that these wouldn’t compete with the powerhouse name above. But I was taken aback by both the quality and functionality.

The first things I noticed were the weight, more than 10 grams lighter than the Vanguard, and the lenses. I hadn’t expected optics this good from a brand I had never heard of.

Then it only got better. The Rovers offer both landscape and portrait recording, plus a tiltable camera that helps you adjust the shot. The video resolution was also better than I expected at 3K and 60 fps – all capabilities the Vanguard doesn’t offer.

One of the standout features was the intercom function, which lets the glasses act like a walkie-talkie with fellow cyclists using the BleeqUp app. Being able to talk to each other more easily is something I’ve always wanted on small group rides, and hearing everyone clearly through the sunglasses themselves takes away the hassle of phone calls or dealing with headphones.

They’re marketed as AI sunglasses, with tools for quickly editing captured footage and adding ride-data overlays. If you’re feeling extra AI-adventurous, you can also generate a third-person view of your ride using mapping data and an uploaded photo of yourself and your bike. The results were interesting, to say the least.

Where the Rovers fell slightly behind the Vanguards was in the polish. The interface, AI assistant, and connectivity didn’t feel as refined as Meta’s. The feedback sounds weren’t as distinct, and connecting the glasses could be a little confusing, with frequent requests to reconnect to their Wi-Fi.

The Vanguard also comes with a charging case, which simplifies things, while the Rover uses a magnetic USB charger. Finally, having to say “Hey Bleeker” to activate the assistant just felt super weird.

One final gripe: The temples could rub against the lenses when folded, which felt like a small but frustrating design oversight.

In contrast to the pleasant surprise of the BleeqUp Rovers, these heads-up display sunglasses fell well short of my expectations.

I was excited to see whether technology similar to what we’ve enjoyed in Form’s smart swim goggles could bring the same benefit to running and cycling. Unfortunately, I was disappointed from the moment I unboxed them.

The idea is great, but the execution wasn’t there. The fit was the least comfortable of any glasses on this list, sitting unusually high on my face, and the secondary inner lens that houses the HUD projection compromised the view.

The bright green data displayed on the inner lenses is intended to keep cyclists from having to look down at their bike computer so they can focus on what’s ahead. In practice, however, I found the view even more distracting, sometimes struggling to adjust my focus from what I was reading on the glasses back to the road.

It was less of an issue while running, and thankfully, you can adjust the brightness and make some changes to the display position to keep the data less intrusive, but that was little consolation.

The app also felt unfinished, and we experienced several issues trying to connect our devices. Top it off with the worst-sounding built-in speakers and most robotic voice assistants I’ve heard in a while, and I’ll sadly be leaving HUD glasses out of my periphery for a while.

If I had the budget and could choose just one everyday pair to wear everyday or bring on a trip, like our recent all-in Ironman World Championship coverage, I’d choose the Oslo 2.0.

The blend of aesthetics, lens quality, and fit is hard to beat. Grippy temple tips and a very grippy nosepiece (which comes in various sizes) help it transition easily from casual use to training. Although it doesn’t look like it’s meant for running, it performs as well as a pair designed specifically for the sport.

For cycling, though, I prefer a little more lens coverage. That’s where I’d reach for Roka’s San Remo Air, which offers a similarly understated cafe style, but with more coverage and a vented lens for hot days.

Both were pairs I could happily wear all day, and all night if I had to. They also had some of the fewest fogging issues while running in the heat and humidity of a Washington summer and felt among the most premium of the bunch — from the finish of the frames to the cases they came in.

Our favorite mid-priced everyday pair was the Adidas Kaphiros, which came surprisingly close to the Rokas in overall performance. It also became the pair my wife consistently stole – sorry, “borrowed” – before we headed out for a ride together.

These are truly glasses you forget you’re wearing. They almost feel like they float above your ears. If pressure around your ears is something that regularly bothers you — as it has for me in the past — this is the pair I’d recommend.

The lenses offer generous coverage for cycling protection, and the optical quality impressed me. Small openings in the temples let air through while riding, although the glasses tended to fog during hot, humid runs — likely due to the size of the lenses.

Tifosi makes this list for a second time, beating out plenty of other running and cycling sunglasses as our favorite budget everyday pair.

The Vogel XC is lightweight, has proved durable enough to survive a couple of seasons with me, and offers a rimless, vented design that’s hard to beat at this price.

The lens tint we tested hit a useful middle ground for the varied conditions we wore it in. And the size and shape don’t scream “I’m a triathlete” every time you wear them out in public.
