#8854. Inside Sullivan Middaugh’s Balancing Act Between Off-Road Dominance and LA 2028

There are few races Sullivan Middaugh would like to target more than next year’s XTERRA World Championship in New Mexico. However, if everything goes to plan, there’s only a slim chance he’ll be on the start line to defend his title.

That’s because Middaugh is part of an exciting crop of American men trying to help the Project Podium program live up to its name at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. And with an increasingly crowded triathlon calendar, the timing doesn’t quite work.

The challenge is that the 2027 XTERRA World Championship weekend in Ruidoso falls between the World Triathlon Championship Finals in Hamburg, Germany, and another top-level race in Weihai, China. Both are part of the rebranded T50 Championship series.

Not only could these events prove critical in helping the U.S. secure three men’s spots for Los Angeles – the host nation is already guaranteed two – but Hamburg could also present an opportunity for Middaugh to stake his claim to one of those places.

He can’t afford to let up. It’s still early in the Olympic qualification cycle, but the U.S. currently has eight men in the top 50 of the Olympic rankings, more than any other nation, with Middaugh the fourth-ranked American at 31st overall.

But while the focus will understandably shift toward the work of coach Parker Spencer’s Project Podium squad, which splits its time between Tempe, Arizona, in the winter and Park City, Utah, in the summer, XTERRA will never be entirely out of mind.

After all, it’s the discipline that put the Middaugh family on the triathlon map, and never more so than earlier this month, when Sullivan claimed his first full-distance XTERRA world title, younger brother Porter finished seventh, and father Josiah, at 48 years young, placed sixth.

Three members of the same family, spanning two generations, finishing in the top seven of a World Championship race is a remarkable feat, with few obvious parallels across elite sport.

The achievement was even more special because it had been 11 years since an American man last won the event. That was Josiah, in 2015. Before him, you have to go back another 15 years to Michael Tobin’s victory in 2000.

“No, I haven’t heard anything quite like that,” Sullivan confirms. “And especially having my dad in the race is pretty incredible!”

More than the result itself, it’s the opportunity to continue racing alongside his father that Sullivan appreciates.

“Following in his footsteps is pretty awesome,” he continues. “Every year he says he’s gonna retire, but I don’t know. It’s been pretty awesome to be able to continue to train and race with him. I grew up just following him on the XTERRA circuit and going to races and watching him. I never really thought we’d be racing together.”

Sullivan’s success also made up for his defeat by Reed Legg at the North American Championship earlier this year. Legg’s victory interrupted a Middaugh dynasty that has seen Josiah win 15 U.S. elite national titles and Sullivan dominate the more recent championship era.

And it was made all the sweeter by the XTERRA World Championship’s return to the U.S. after four years in Italy.

“I put it on my calendar and kept it in mind all year,” Sullivan says. “It was a race at altitude, which I grew up at, and so I felt like it was a good opportunity. Grindstone Lake, where we swam, is at 7,000 feet and the course got up to maybe a little bit over 8,000 feet. But at home in Colorado, my house is at like 7,500 feet, and you can only really go up from there. So, the six or seven weeks leading in, I went home and trained with dad because I knew it would be a big advantage if I could be fully acclimatized.”

While Porter, who also trains with Project Podium, finished seventh, Sullivan believes his younger brother might have mounted a stronger challenge had he not been racing at the Under-23 World Championship in Spain.

Sullivan skipped that race to sharpen his mountain biking skills, although it didn’t prevent an early spill on the bike.

“Yeah, I overcooked the corners a little bit on the first couple of turns in the single track section,” he explains. “It wasn’t a bad spill out, but I kinda had to slam on the brake, go off the trail, tip over and get up quick. My bike computer fell off, which wasn’t a big deal, and maybe a blessing in disguise to not worry about power and just focus on effort.”

Sullivan had an almost four-minute lead heading onto the run and extended his advantage with the day’s fastest 10K split, but at no point did he feel comfortable.

“I didn’t really get any splits and thought that no lead was safe on the run. I just tried to give it full gas, focusing on pushing the climbs and rolling the downhills because I knew they’d be coming.”

Among the athletes trying to hunt him down were two very familiar faces – Porter and Josiah – and there was a brief moment of family camaraderie as their paths crossed on the course.

“I just focus on myself for the most part, but it reminds you that they’re also out there battling. I saw them running together, so that was pretty cool because I knew they’d be pushing each other. We were all pumped, gave each other a high five, and that was pretty much it.”

There were plenty more high fives and hugs at the finish, where Sullivan’s mom, sister, and grandparents were also in attendance.

While this was Sullivan’s first full-distance XTERRA world title, he had previously won the Short Track World Championship in Molveno, Italy, in 2024.

In recent years, short-track racing has typically taken place a couple of days before or the day after the main event, although it wasn’t on the schedule in Ruidoso.

“It’s like a three or four-minute swim, maybe a 15-minute bike and a seven-minute run,” Sullivan says, with distances depending on the course layout. “It’s all under 30 minutes for the most part, so more intense and a little bit different, and you can’t make as many mistakes. I think it suits me because I’ve spent a lot of time training for sprint distance draft-legal triathlons. I really enjoy it.”

While XTERRA might be seen as a distraction from road triathlon, Sullivan believes it complements his efforts elsewhere.

“It helps me with my skills for the draft-legal stuff as well. I look to people like Flora Duffy and Hayden Wilde who were able to do well at both, and think they’re an example for me.”

For the next 18 months, the priority will be collecting Olympic qualification points, with the window having opened in May.

Sullivan has already recorded top-10 finishes at World Triathlon Cups in Huatulco, Mexico; Edmonton, Canada; Rio de Janeiro, Brazil; and Asunción, Paraguay. He also competed at the Americas Triathlon Championships in Antofagasta, Chile, finishing 11th. He now heads to Chile for two more World Cup races, in San Pedro de la Paz and Iquique.

While USA Triathlon hasn’t officially released its selection policy for Los Angeles, Sullivan expects the Olympic test event in July 2027 and the World Championship Finals in Hamburg to be key races. He anticipates that a top-eight finish, combined with being the leading American, could be enough to meet the automatic selection criteria.

But first, he needs to secure starts at the biggest races. “Spots keep flipping, so it’s gonna be pretty tough,” he adds. “I’ve been mostly focusing on the World Cup level, which is the step below the World Championship Series, but as my swim develops, I’ll try and focus more on the World Championship Series because that’s the level you need to be at in the Olympics.”

The higher the level, the more critical the swim becomes. “If you’re the best swimmer, you can be in the race up until the run, but if you don’t have a good swim, you may never even be in the race,” he explains. “The swim sets you up for a good day to get in the right bike group, but you also need to be able to run well off a hard bike. That’s something XTERRA helps me with.”

Sullivan admits that bridging the gap in the swim is his biggest immediate challenge, but he also knows he’ll need a blistering run to compete at the very top.

“Especially with Alex Yee and Hayden Wilde, it is just getting faster and faster,” he says. “You need to be an elite runner if you want to be on the podium, and that means hitting sub-14 minutes sometimes in the 5K and sub-29 minutes occasionally on the 10K. Right now, I’m in the low 14s and around 30, maybe a little under depending on the course.”

If he can get there, it will be with the help of Project Podium. Established in 2018, Project Podium is funded by USA Triathlon, corporate sponsors, and private donors, including longtime benefactors Dr. Bill Warren and his wife Lynne. Based at Arizona State University, the program provides promising American male triathletes with coaching, scholarships, and financial support as they pursue Olympic ambitions.

Sullivan, who graduated with a degree in biomedical sciences in August, has enormous respect for coach Spencer, who he says also understands his passion for the trails and why XTERRA should remain part of his program.

“I love mountain biking, and so it’s good for me to be able to kinda go in and out, but I think that as the Olympics get closer I’ll have to take a slight step away from XTERRA, but we’ll see.”

Finally, if Sullivan’s Olympic dream does come to fruition, could there be more than one Middaugh on the U.S. team?

“That’s definitely a big ask, but would be amazing. I don’t know if it’s on the cards for ’28, but maybe for ’32 it could be more plausible. I think we both have the ability to get to that level if we stick with it, and when I see Porter in the race, we don’t really need to say anything. We just understand what we need to do.”

A timeshare is a shared ownership or usage right in a vacation property. You pay an upfront purchase price — typically $20,000 to $40,000 — plus annual maintenance fees that currently average $1,120 per year and increase 3-5% annually. In exchange, you get the right to use a resort unit for a specific period each year, usually one week.

The timeshare industry generates over $10 billion in annual sales, and roughly 9.9 million U.S. households own at least one timeshare. But ownership satisfaction varies dramatically, and the financial reality rarely matches the sales presentation delivered during high-pressure resort tours.

Deeded (Fixed Week): You own a fractional interest in a specific unit during a specific week each year. This is actual real property — you receive a deed, it's recorded with the county, and you can theoretically sell, rent, or bequeath it. The problem: the secondary market for these deeds values most of them at near zero.

Right-to-Use (Leased): You purchase the right to use a property for a set number of years (typically 20-40 years) but don't own real estate. At the end of the term, your usage right expires with nothing to show for it. This is common with newer resort brands.

Points-Based Systems: Instead of a fixed week at a fixed resort, you purchase an annual allotment of points that can be redeemed at various properties within a resort network. Flexibility is the selling point, but availability at popular destinations during peak seasons is often limited — and points can inflate over time, requiring more points for the same week.

Timeshare companies spend an average of $4,000 in marketing costs per sale — and much of that goes toward the high-pressure sales presentations that are a signature of the industry. These presentations use urgency tactics ("this price is only available today"), comparison anchoring (showing the cost per vacation day), and emotional triggers ("don't you want the best for your family?"). The FI community's rule: never make a five-figure financial decision on the same day you learn about it. Walk away, run the numbers at home, and compare alternatives. The offer will still be available tomorrow — despite what the salesperson claims.

Timeshare sales presentations focus on the purchase price and the "cost per vacation night." What they don't emphasize is the total lifetime cost, which includes mandatory annual fees that increase every year, special assessments for major repairs, exchange fees if you want to trade your week, and the opportunity cost of that capital.

Let's run the real numbers on a typical timeshare over 20 years:

At $4,204 per week over 20 years — without accounting for the opportunity cost of the capital — you can book luxury vacation rentals in most destinations for less money with zero long-term commitment.

This is the most important financial fact about timeshares: they have almost no resale value. The American Resort Development Association (ARDA) — the timeshare industry's own trade group — acknowledges that resale prices are a fraction of the original purchase price. In practice, most timeshares on the secondary market are listed for $1 or even offered for free, because the buyer inherits the mandatory annual maintenance fees.

Websites like RedWeek, TUG (Timeshare Users Group), and eBay are filled with timeshare listings at $0-$1. Owners often can't give them away because the ongoing fee obligation makes them a liability, not an asset. This is the fundamental difference between a timeshare and a real investment: real investments appreciate or generate income. Timeshares depreciate to zero and generate mandatory ongoing costs.

If you already own a timeshare and want out, here are your realistic options:

Rescission Period: Most states give you 3-15 days after purchase to cancel without penalty. This is your best exit — if you're within this window, cancel immediately in writing via certified mail.

Sell on the Resale Market: List on TUG (Timeshare Users Group), RedWeek, or eBay. Set your expectations: you'll likely sell for $0-$1, and the "sale" is really about transferring the maintenance fee obligation to a willing buyer.

Contact the Resort's Deed-Back Program: Some major resort chains (Wyndham, Marriott, Hilton) offer deed-back or surrender programs where you can return the timeshare to the resort. Eligibility varies and there may be fees, but this is a legitimate exit path.

Timeshare Exit Companies: Proceed with Extreme Caution. The timeshare exit industry is plagued with scams. Legitimate exit attorneys exist, but many "exit companies" charge $3,000-$10,000 upfront and deliver nothing. The FTC and state attorneys general have pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Before hiring anyone, check their BBB rating, look for complaints with your state attorney general, and never pay the full fee upfront.

The FI community has consistently found that travel rewards credit cards, vacation rental platforms, and strategic booking provide better vacation value than timeshare ownership:

Here's the number that should end the timeshare debate for any FI-focused person: the average timeshare's annual maintenance fee ($1,120) invested in index funds at a 10% average return grows to $72,000+ in 20 years and $203,000+ in 30 years. Add the opportunity cost of the $24,140 purchase price invested instead, and the 30-year FI impact exceeds $440,000. That's nearly half a million dollars diverted from your FI number for one week of vacation per year at a resort you didn't choose.

Travel well, spend less, keep your FI timeline intact.

Choose a card that matches your spending patterns and offers flexible points or transferable miles. Sign-up bonuses alone often cover 1-2 free flights or hotel stays in the first year.

Pro tip: Pay the balance in full every month. Travel rewards only work financially if you never carry a balance and pay interest.

Instead of paying $1,120/year in mandatory timeshare fees, deposit that same amount monthly ($93/month) into a high-yield savings account earmarked for travel. You'll have $1,120+ per year to spend on any vacation, anywhere.

Research destinations on Airbnb, VRBO, and Booking.com. Booking 3-6 months ahead gets the best selection. Compare total costs including cleaning fees and service charges to timeshare equivalent costs.

Shifting your vacation by 2-4 weeks outside peak season saves 30-50% on flights and accommodation. Shoulder season often has better weather than peak season with fewer crowds.

If you were considering a $24,000 timeshare purchase, invest that money instead. At 10% average returns, $24,000 grows to $62,000 in 10 years and $161,000 in 20 years — all while you vacation on your own terms.

Pro tip: Set up automatic monthly investments for the amount you would have spent on timeshare financing payments.

A timeshare's purchase price ($24,140) plus 30 years of maintenance fees ($1,120/year growing at 3.5%) totals over $83,000 in direct costs. Invested in index funds at 10% average returns instead, that same money grows to over $440,000. That's the true cost of a timeshare — not the sticker price, but nearly half a million dollars of lost wealth-building potential over a career.

No. A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan, not an investment. Timeshares depreciate to near-zero resale value, generate mandatory ongoing costs that increase annually, and cannot produce income for the owner in most cases. The timeshare industry itself has moved away from calling them investments because of regulatory scrutiny.

The average annual maintenance fee is $1,120, according to ARDA (the industry trade group). Fees increase an average of 3-5% per year and are mandatory — you must pay them whether or not you use your timeshare. Some resort areas (Hawaii, ski towns) charge $1,500-$2,500+ per year. Special assessments for major repairs can add $1,000-$5,000 in any given year.

Technically yes, but practically it's very difficult. The secondary market is flooded with inventory at $0-$1 prices because most owners are trying to escape their maintenance fee obligations. Resale companies that promise to sell your timeshare for thousands of dollars are almost always scams. The most realistic options are deed-back to the resort, transfer to a willing buyer at $0-$1, or working with a licensed timeshare exit attorney.

The resort will send your account to collections, report the delinquency to credit bureaus (damaging your credit score), and potentially pursue legal action. For deeded timeshares, the resort can foreclose on the property. Maintenance fee obligations are contractual and legally enforceable — you cannot simply walk away without consequences.

Some are, many are not. The FTC has pursued multiple timeshare exit companies for fraud. Red flags include: demanding full payment ($3,000-$10,000) upfront, guaranteeing results, using high-pressure sales tactics similar to timeshare presentations, and lack of BBB accreditation. If you need exit help, consult a licensed real estate attorney in the state where the timeshare is located.

In very narrow circumstances: if you genuinely vacation at the same resort every year, the annual cost (maintenance fees amortized with purchase price) is lower than booking that same unit independently, and you purchased on the resale market for $0-$1 (avoiding the $24,000+ retail markup). Even then, you're locked into one destination with escalating fees. For most people, the flexibility and cost advantage of alternatives makes timeshares a poor choice.

A timeshare is a prepaid vacation plan with a near-zero resale value, mandatory escalating fees, and an extremely difficult exit process. The average timeshare costs over $84,000 across 20 years of ownership — and that money invested instead could grow to over $440,000 in 30 years. Modern alternatives like travel rewards cards, vacation rentals, and strategic off-peak booking deliver comparable or better vacation experiences with zero long-term commitment. If you're building toward financial independence, a timeshare is one of the most damaging financial products you can buy. If you already own one, explore deed-back programs or resale as your fastest path out.

#8852. The 2026 New York City Marathon Was the Largest Marathon in History

More than 61,000 runners—from ages 18 to 90—crossed the finish line on Sunday.

One of the world's biggest marathons keeps getting bigger. On Sunday, November 1, the 2026 New York City Marathon officially cemented its place in the history books as the largest marathon of all time, surpassing the 2026 London Marathon, which had 59,830 finishers.

According to results released Monday by New York Road Runners (NYRR), 61,146 runners crossed the iconic finish line in Central Park (61,529 started the event). That total blasts past last year’s NYC tally of 59,226 finishers—which followed 2024’s record-breaking field of 55,646—marking the third consecutive year the five-borough race has raised the bar worldwide for mass participation.

This year’s record served as a nice topper for a historic run as it coincided with the 50th anniversary of the five-borough course. When organizers first took the race out of Central Park and onto the streets of Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx, and Manhattan in 1976, the event was a bold urban experiment. Five decades later, it is an epicenter of the global running community, with waves of marathoners streaming from the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge from 8 a.m. until well after dark.

While tens of thousands of age-groupers, charity runners, and first-timers chased personal glory, the pro fields delivered plenty of fireworks at the front of the pack:

There were plenty of other milestones as well.

Kevin Donahue is a freelance journalist who has worked in news and service journalism for organizations that include Men's Health, Philadelphia public media station WHYY, and The Philadelphia Inquirer.

#8851. A 24-Year-Old Runner Died After a Medical Emergency in the Final Miles of the NYC Marathon

Rachel Apa was running her first marathon to raise money for Parkinson's research in memory of her grandfather.

Rachel Apa was nearing the end of her first New York City Marathon when she collapsed in Central Park on Sunday, November 1. The 24-year-old had spent months putting in the work needed to conquer 26.2 miles, but never made it across the finish line. Instead, she was taken to Mount Sinai Medical Center, where she died later that night.

Apa, a Bucknell University alum who lived in central Pennsylvania, came to New York to run with Parkinson's Foundation Champions, raising money in memory of her grandfather, who died from the disease in 2022.

According to reporting from The New York Times, the medical emergency happened around 1:30 p.m. close to Mile 24, around 85th Street, right as runners enter the final stretch through Central Park. Several spectators rushed to help and began performing CPR. New York Road Runners medical staff arrived shortly after, and tried to resuscitate her with a defibrillator before paramedics took her to the hospital.

Her parents had been keeping up with Rachel throughout the race as she made her way through the five boroughs, though from different locations. Michelle Apa, her mother, was in New York and watched Rachel run through Queens at Mile 14, while Steve Apa, her father, was back home in Lewisberry, Pennsylvania, following her progress through the marathon's tracking app.

Steve had been texting his daughter throughout the day. According to messages he shared with the Times, Rachel sent an "Ow" text at Mile 18, followed by a double "Ow ow" at Mile 19. She kept moving through the course, although her dad received no replies after that. As she reached Mile 23 on the app, Steve sent another message: "Final stretch." Rachel never responded.

Michelle eventually made her way to Central Park, reportedly arriving just as the ambulance carrying her daughter was leaving, per the Times. Doctors spent hours trying to save Rachel. Steve told the newspaper she was pronounced dead around 9:40 p.m.

"It's unfathomable," he told the newspaper. "Perfect health, perfect shape, 24 years old."

Steve told the Times that his daughter died from rhabdomyolysis, which occurs when damaged muscle tissue breaks down and releases substances into the bloodstream. The condition can cause serious kidney damage and, according to the Cleveland Clinic, can be triggered by extreme physical exertion.

An official cause of death had not been established as of Tuesday, November 3, with CBS New York reporting that the city's medical examiner was still investigating.

Sunday marked the marathon's first runner death following a medical incident since 2024, according to NYRR. The organization released a statement Monday:

"We are deeply saddened by the death of one of our runners following yesterday's race. Our thoughts and sincere sympathies are with the runner's family, friends, and the entire running community."

Before the marathon, Apa explained her decision to run on her fundraising page, sharing how much her grandfather influenced her love of sports and why supporting the Parkinson's Foundation mattered to her.

"He taught me to stay active, push my limits, and embrace challenges, shaping my love for sports and movement," she wrote.

Apa explained that watching him lose his mobility after his Parkinson's diagnosis had made her want to help others facing the disease. She wanted to use her first marathon to help others affected by it, raising money and awareness in the process “for research, better care, and a cure.”

As of 5 p.m. ET Tuesday, the page had exceeded her $4,000 goal, and reflected more than $28,000 in donations.

Sean Abrams was the Senior Editor, Growth and Engagement at Men’s Health. He’s a former hip hop dancer who likes long walks on the beach and large glasses of tequila. You can find his previous work at Maxim, Elite Daily, and AskMen.

#8850. The 7 Best Jogging Strollers for Every Active Parent

These strollers combine comfort, convenience, and style. They’re perfect for moms and dads trying to get a workout in.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Getting out for a run as a parent of a little one is made infinitely easier with a great jogging stroller. As a running mom, I spent countless hours behind my kids, and now my nieces and nephews lacing up and getting behind a stroller for my own mental and physical health and giving my siblings a much-needed respite (I even bring back treats).

I’ve since made running my job, and have had the opportunity to test dozens of running strollers over the years, and let me tell you, they are not all the same. The range of quality and ride between them can be pretty bananas, and as someone who tends toward higher mileage, it took me a long time to find one that I loved.

Thankfully, jogging strollers have evolved a lot since my first runs with my baby over a decade ago, and now there is a great jogging stroller for everyone no matter your height, running style, surfaces you run on, or miles you’ll be logging. There are strollers that work as both running and everyday strollers, luxury running strollers, multisport strollers that can hit the snow, be towed by a bicycle, or pushed on your own steam, and there are high-tech jogging strollers ready to rack up at the races.

Every year, I dedicate hundreds of hours to testing jogging strollers. I run with kids aged roughly 7 months to 3 years on tracks, pavement, highly groomed trails, boardwalks, and even those charming New York sidewalks. Each stroller clocks at least 40 miles under my watch through all sorts of conditions—rain, snow, sunshine, you name it, we’re out there. Snack testing is a must for cleanability checks, naturally.

Storage? I’ve crammed everything imaginable into the baskets on these. Brakes get a relentless workout. I've folded, unfolded, and hauled these things all over the tri-state area. Airports? Been there, done that (huge mistake, by the way). Here’s my travel tip: check it in a stroller travel bag and thank me later.

Beyond the specs, it’s about the feel. How easy is it to push and steer, even one-handed? And since my nieces and nephews are my precious cargo, their comfort is paramount. We log countless miles, and I see firsthand how happy they are (or aren’t) in each stroller. Some provide a dream ride, others unleash their inner tiny terrors. Basically, I get the real 411 on what works and what doesn't.

Thule makes some of the best tech and outdoor gear on the market, and this stroller is a shining example of the brand. It’s somehow both rugged and elegant, providing the runner with easy, light-touch steering and braking. I was a huge fan of the two previous iterations of this stroller, but this version has surpassed my expectations. I always had issues with the length and size of the canopy, and the tilted position of the seat. But this version sits more upright and has a more generous canopy than its predecessors, making it more comfortable for your little one.

The pneumatic tires are fab and give the stroller a lot of give to glide over difficult terrain like boardwalks, bumpy tracks, and even some trails. I took this beast out on the jankiest boardwalk in all of the land—Rockaway Beach in Queens, New York, and not only did my little nephew fall asleep and stay asleep (and secure) in the stroller even as I almost tripped a dozen times, he fell asleep so deeply that he actually transferred from the stroller to the car seat without a stir.

The storage basket is a decent size, but I do wish it was mesh material, which sand and other dirt could fall through. Also, given that it’s a solid fabric and not mesh, I’d expect it to have a larger weight limit. As it is, 15 pounds is all you can carry beneath. That being said, there are tons of accessories, including handle bags that increase storage capacity and convenience.

I love the twisting hand brake on the Thule. It is a less-abrupt stop than a traditional hand brake, giving you more control. The foot brake is easily operated as well, though disengaging the brakes should not be done in sandals or bare feet.

As for the car seat attachment and available bassinet, both are great, but they do come at an extra price, and the Thule UG3 is bulky for every day. However, it’s such a nice ride, and since the front wheel locks in place and unlocks for easy turning, it is usable as an everyday stroller.

Finding any stroller for under $200 is a feat, especially right now. For families on a budget, the Baby Trend Expedition Jogger is a fantastic option that doesn’t skimp on features. Surprisingly, it includes multiple parent and child drink trays, an accessory often sold separately with more expensive models, adding a bit of convenience. (However, when running, skip the hard cups for the toddlers for safety.)

For the price, the ride is smooth and capable of handling casual jogs and everyday outings. However, it’s worth noting that the overall build quality and components feel a bit flimsier compared to higher-end strollers. The fabrics are a bit scratchier, and the frame and accessories are just not the same.

That said, it’s still a solid stroller with a lot of potential for families. It’s probably not going to withstand the same high mileage or rigorous use as its pricier counterparts, but it’s ideal for those with less intense running routines. Also, it’s specifically designed to be compatible with Baby Trend infant car seats, which is something to keep in mind when considering your overall travel system.

So you don’t want to store a stroller for every occasion? I get it. I live in Brooklyn and understand the limits of small spaces. Enter the solution to your problems: The Guava Roam is a fabulous compact everyday and jogging stroller known for its easy maneuverability and relatively compact fold. It features broad car seat compatibility via its adapters for various brands including Graco, Nuna, UppaBaby, Cybex, Chicco, and Britax. It has one of the smallest footprints both folded and unfolded, and while it’s a bit on the heavy side at 28.5 pounds, the way it folds makes it easy to lug around and stash in your trunk.

But the diminutive size and convenience aren’t the only things that make this an outstanding option for families and runners. My favorite bit about this stroller is the fact that you can lock and unlock the front wheel via a control at the handlebar. It’s genius. I have no earthly clue why more stroller companies aren’t doing this.

I’m also a huge fan of the independent suspension on this stroller that settles and levels as you hit large divots, giving the passenger a smooth, easy ride.

The seat on this stroller is our 3-year-old tester’s favorite, with the five-point harness that’s “not pinchy” and the seat “nice on your booty.” I like the accessory kit near the adjustable handlebar that fits your drink, your phone, your wallet, and at least four mini bags of gummy Nerd clusters (my running fuel of choice).

The stroller isn’t perfect, but it’s so good, you can almost overlook the shallow undercarriage basket and the fact it’s lacking a hand brake. Ideally, I’d love for this stroller to also have pneumatic tires for longer runs and better shock absorption, but the whole thing is just so convenient, its positives easily outweigh its negatives.

I’ve hauled about a gajillion strollers in and out of car trunks, and I know which ones claim to be compact when folded, and which really are. The Cybex Avi Spin is actually a compact jogging stroller. It has a unique way of folding that allows you to either do a basic, one-handed compact fold, or go all the way, and remove the tires first, and then fold it into something that’s around backpack-sized.

The ride is lovely for the jogger, with an adjustable handlebar (it requires two hands to adjust), soft, moisture-wicking grip, and lockable front wheel with an easy deceleration hand brake. It coasts over ruts and bumps really well, but it’s by no means going to hit any trails and remain stable. Jogging strollers aren’t really built for that, by and large.

It cleans up beautifully as well, with removable, machine-washable fabrics, including the UPF 50+-rated canopy. Just pretreat the fabric, wash on gentle, and lay flat to dry.

I do have one gripe, though, and it’s not nothing. The ergonomic, nearly lie-flat seat is fantastic for naps, and the no-rethread, easy-to-adjust harness is great, but younger passengers will lose most of the view if they’re reclined even a little purely because of positioning. This is common on many strollers, but for some reason, is more pronounced on this model. Our tester cared not at all, though, as he was busy looking straight out at the flock of American oystercatchers gathered on the boardwalk at the beach in Queens, New York, where I tested this stroller. My suggestion? Find a running area with dopey looking birds and kids are thrilled. Egrets are also a favorite, I’ve found.

I am a massive fan of this double stroller—Bob gets it right with this one. It’s largely one of the easiest to assemble and to fold, whether or not you take off the wheels. It’s a joy to push, even if you have two large toddlers in the seats. The tires are my favorite of any standard jogging stroller on this list. They are the best aligned, and the adjustable front wheel means you never have to worry if it comes out of alignment, as you can just fix it in a few tweaks.

But oh, how I could write sonnets about the storage. You know what you need a ton of when you’re pushing two kids for a two-plus hour run? Everything. Diapers, wipes, snacks, drinks, extra clothing, sunscreen, snacks for yourself, a few bottles of water, and more. And with the giant storage basket and all the storage cubbies on this beauty, you’ve got the space to hold them. The only thing it doesn’t store is extra patience for when they start fighting at mile 10 and you have 3.1 more miles on your run.

I have run over 200 miles with this stroller, and though I have had to replace the inner tube in the front tire, the stroller is still in great shape. The combination mesh and sealed poly storage basket underneath has seen some things in its life, and it still comes out clean and doesn’t smell, which is a huge accomplishment considering all it has been through.

While lugging it around folded isn't the easiest task, the Bob Revolution 3.0 Duallie’s exceptional performance and ample storage more than compensate. Overall, this double stroller is a top pick for parents who love to run and need the capacity for two little ones. It’s a durable, comfortable, and thoughtfully designed stroller that will make countless runs a joy for both you and your children.

I had heaps of fun testing this stroller out, and recently, I even got on a bicycle (not my thing!) and tried it out in tow mode. This stroller is a beast and, truly, it is only for the most sporting amongst us. If you’re a serious outdoor fanatic, you’ve met your match. It’s designed like a bike trailer, but thanks to its multiple bases/setups, it works as a stroller, a jogging stroller, a bike trailer, and even a stroller on skis for snowshoeing and fun in the sand.

This is technically the double version, but I think it’s worth it to get the wider Chariot Cross 2 over the single version, as it feels a bit more stable than the single, and gives your child some extra space. The seats inside are roomy, and I had no complaints from the Peanut Section about the straps or cushion levels, no matter if the kids were being towed, pushed, or shoved over ice and snow.

Switching the kits out could be simpler, but it’s not especially difficult. I managed to do it pretty easily, and I have a partially paralyzed left hand. Putting it together initially is honestly a bigger pain. It’s easy to clean, though, with removable pads. The materials can take a serious amount of scrubbing and hosing off without showing any wear, which is good considering how filthy a stroller like this could become.

I love the oversized storage bag that affixes to the back. It’s simple to use and clean, and deep enough to fit way more than you’d expect. It’s a slick feature that puts this stroller in a category of its own.

As for the ride, it’s as smooth as it can be over the snow, sand, and ice. This stroller is a bit heavy for an all-out run, but great for jogging slow, easy miles. As a regular stroller, it’s great for myriad applications, but my favorite way to use it is when you’re in a buggy area, as it’s completely enclosed. As a bike trailer, it shines, holding its ground and keeping everything steady. For serious outdoor enthusiasts seeking a versatile and durable multisport option, the Thule Chariot Cross 2 is a top-tier choice that's built to handle almost any adventure.

I’ve pushed the Veer Switch&Jog over 25 miles on all kinds of terrain, and it did well on almost everything. I struggled to push it on mud and sand, but that’s true of just about any stroller. The second I find one that doesn’t? You’ll be the first to know.

My favorite thing about this baby is that you’re able to switch out the jump seat back and forth. Additional pieces are available. The cooler is great, and the booster seat takes about two seconds to set up at a restaurant, which freaking rocks when you think about how dirty restaurant high chairs can get.

During the testing we had a projectile vomit situation. Totally my fault. I overfed the small human treats before the run. My bad, I know better. I took it straight to a self-serve car wash and sprayed absolute crap out of it with the a high-pressure wand. After a little scrubbing, it was totally fine, and the smell came out too (thank god, because it was dairy). I do wish the fabric was machine washable, but it’s attached so firmly to the frame that I get why it’s not.

On runs, it’s stable, and the telescoping handle and handbrake are both easy to use. The front wheel locks for straightaways and unlocks when you’re just wandering around the city.

Folding it is kind of a pain in the you-know-what, not gonna lie. But it’s a convertible tank of a stroller, and it’s very hard to beat at this price.

Given that jogging strollers can be a significant investment, it's crucial to select one that aligns with your needs. To ensure you choose the right stroller, consider these key specifications:

These specs directly relate to your running style. Serious runners will prioritize performance features like wheel type and suspension, while casual joggers might focus on convenience features like car seat compatibility and ease of folding.

To be included on this list, every jogging stroller must meet certain criteria. Key features of a good jogging stroller include a lockable front wheel for safe straightaways at a running pace, excellent build quality for durability, a large canopy for sun protection, and built-in safety features such as a wrist strap, sweat-resistant handlebar grips, and a secure harness system.

And, not for nothing, but they need to feel good when you run behind them. I can’t tell you how many clunkers I’ve tested that made my runs a chore. They need to provide both the runner and the passenger with a comfortable experience. If you’re kicking the storage basket or your hands feel like they’ve become permanently glued to the handlebar, you’re not going to want to use that stroller.

As avid runners who have embraced parenthood, we understand the unique demands placed on jogging strollers. We know that these aren't just tools for transporting children; they are crucial pieces of equipment that must perform flawlessly whether you're engaged in rigorous training for your next marathon or simply navigating the everyday errands with your little one in tow.

For years, the Runner's World team has been committed to guiding runners toward the gear that allows them to achieve peak performance and enjoy their passion for running to the max. This deep-seated expertise extends into our in-depth evaluations of running gear, and jogging strollers are no exception. Our primary objective is to thoroughly test and identify the options available on the market, and to provide informed and reliable recommendations for runners of all experience levels.

When is it safe to run with your child in the stroller?

The general rule recommended by pediatricians is to wait until the baby is at least 6 months old, and has good head, trunk, and neck control. AKA, they can sit unassisted for long periods of time.

What is the best way to clean a jogging stroller?

Honestly, some of these strollers allow you to remove many of the fabrics and wash them in the machine, but for a jogger, it’s kind of a pain. I suggest taking off the canopy, tilting the whole thing upside down and shaking it out before using a damp cloth and wiping it down, and allowing it to air dry. If it’s really gross, hose the thing down, but take off the harness first, as soaking it can reduce its efficacy.

What Should You Avoid in a jogging stroller?

You should be holding your child’s hard sippy cups and snacks and save those for walking breaks. Jogging can jostle, and I’ve seen some pretty gnarly dental injuries on kids who had plastic sippy cup incidents from jogging strollers.

Generally not. Even if they fall within the parameters set by Disney of 31- by 52 inches, I’ve heard of many of them (apart from the Guava) getting rejected at the gates.

For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and currently studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. Passionate about women’s health and neurodivergent inclusion, she advocates for closing research gaps and helping others—especially AudHD people—find joy in running and fitness.

#8849. Essential Yoga Poses That Deliver Serious Knee Strengthening

The thing about practicing yoga for knee strengthening is you typically don’t know you need to do it until there’s an issue. YouTube yoga teacher Yoga With Kassandra takes you through a routine designed to emphasize the muscles that support knee strength and explains how to modify the poses to suit your needs.

Whether you’re wanting to build knee strength to enhance your everyday functionality or you’re recovery from a knee injury and finally at the point where you can practice yoga, you need strengthening exercises that support all the muscles that support and stabilize your knees. Basically, you want to work on the hip adductors, the quads, the glutes, the hamstrings.

The following poses literally work all of the muscles that contribute to knee stability. You’ll also get to play around a little with some dynamic movement and try some balancing exercises that help you understand how to properly engage the muscles that support the knee. Then you can take that awareness into other yoga poses as well as your everyday movements.

Regularly practicing this yoga for knee strength routine will help anyone build knee strength. I know from personal experience just how frustrating a knee injury can be, so if that applies to you, know that the more you dedicate time towards rehabilitating yourself, and the more diligent you are with your practices, the more likely you’ll feel a difference in your ease of movement. And remember that rest is equally as important as stretching and strengthening.

You will need a block or a block-like item for several of these poses. If you experience pain in any of the poses, slowly come out and skip ahead to the next pose. Always consult with your physician or physical therapist prior to introducing new exercises.

Start lying on your back and bring your feet about hip-distance apart and your heels pretty close toward your glutes. Place the block directly in between the inner thighs and squeeze the block as much as you possibly can. Then push down into all four corners of both feet and slowly lift first the pelvis off the mat, then the lower back, and then the mid back in Bridge Pose. The higher you lift, the harder it becomes to squeeze your block, but keep squeezing it anyway. This helps train your inner thighs, or adductor muscles, to contract. Building inner thigh power can also help you become better at balancing poses.

Take about 3 breaths here, pushing down through your big toes. Then exhale and slowly roll down, inch by inch. Move your block to the side.

From lying on your back, lift your right leg toward the sky and straighten it without locking your knee or hyperextending it. Interlace your fingers behind your right hamstrings. Instead of making this a passive stretch, push your leg against your palms as much as you can, and feel your arms resist. Keep pushing, pushing, pushing with your hamstrings. This should be challenging. You’ll also get a little arm workout. Try to keep your lower back neutral and close to the mat. Continue for a few more breaths.

You might find that your leg starts coming a little closer toward your chest, and that’s fine, but don’t force the stretch. Then release and switch legs.

Re-extend your right leg and bring your hands behind the back of your calf muscles. If that means you need to bend a little in your knee, that’s perfectly fine. If you can’t reach that far, bring your hands to the hamstrings again, but shift them closer to the knee, which creates a different sensation. Same thing, you want to push against your hands and resist. Then repeat on the other side.

This is not a yoga pose, but it’s absolutely amazing for your adductors. Grab your block and place it between your inner thighs again. Instead of keeping your heels close to you as in Bridge, walk your feet out so it feels almost as if your legs are almost straight and there’s about 6 inches between the mat and the backs of your knees.

Flex your feet, push your heels down into the mat, and see if you can squeeze your block and lift your hips off the mat. They’re only going to lift about an inch or so and that’s fine. This is an intense pose. You’re gonna feel it in your legs pretty much right away. If you don’t feel it, it’s because your knees are too bent and you need to straighten them a little more. Squeeze your block, push down into your heels, and try to drag your heels toward your shoulders. Hold here for a few more breaths. Then lower and move your block off to the side.

Come into Downward-Facing Dog. Normally I would suggest some Cat and Cow stretches before going into Down Dog, but if you’re recovering from knee issues you might not be able to apply bring your knees to the mat because of the pressure, so consider those stretches optional or take a seated version of them. You’re pushing into the heels here to stretch your hamstrings, lengthen your arms, and lengthen your spine.

Reach your right leg toward the sky in Three-Legged Dog, then step forward toward the top of the mat. Push down into your feet and come up into High Lunge. You want your feet hip-distance apart for stability. It’s find to bend your back knee if that feels more doable. It’s important that your front knee is going in the same direction as your toes and is stacked over your ankle. You don’t want the knee to be swaying to one side or jutting forward in front of your toes.

Bring your hands to your heart and keep your right knee bent and focus on its stability as you tilt your chest forward into a variation of Warrior 3. Keep the knee of your supporting leg bent as you reach your left leg back and find your balance.

As you inhale, push your right leg straight, and then exhale gently as you bend your right knee again. Think of this as almost like a one-legged squat. So inhale, straighten the leg. Exhale, bend the knee.

Continue for several breaths. Keep your right knee pointing straight over the second and third toes. Last one, inhale to straighten and hold here.

From Warrior 3, reach your left leg straight toward the ceiling and bring your chest toward your right thigh in Standing Splits. You might want to bring your block underneath your hands or fingertips.

Then exhale, bend both knees as much as you can, and see if you can bring your knees together to touch, so you’re in a little ball with your left foot hovering above the mat.

Then inhale, open back up into Standing Splits. Look at your right knee and make certain it’s not shifting to the right or the left. Do that once more.

Bend both knees and bring your left foot to the mat with your big toes together and your heels slightly apart in Chair Pose. If this creates tension in your lower back, you can keep your feet hip-distance apart. Rock your weight back into your heels and keep your tailbone reaching back and your thighs hugging the midline as if you were still squeezing that block. Stay here or reach your arms alongside your head.

Lean more weight onto your right leg, and see if you can pick up your left foot and step it back into your High Lunge. Then very carefully pivot the back foot almost parallel to the short side of the mat, keeping your shin and your knee facing the same direction, in Warrior 2. Your right knee is still bending. Squeezing the glutes helps press that right knee open as it points forward. Reach your arms straight out from your shoulders.

To work on strengthening, inhale as you straighten the front leg and bring your hands together in front of you, and then exhale back into Warrior 2 and reach your arms. Repeat several times. The goal is not to rush this but to do it with control. You want to really feel that knee tracking directly over the second and third toes and not wobbling.

Straighten your right leg, being careful not to lock or hyperextend your knees. Then shift forward into Triangle Pose and reach your left arm upward. Draw your left shoulder slightly back as you open across the chest.

From Triangle, look down at the floor and circle your hands to the mat. Step to Downward-Facing Dog.

Repeat these poses on your left side, starting with High Lunge and continuing to Dynamic Warrior 3, Standing Splits, Chair Pose, Dynamic Warrior 2, Triangle, and Down Dog.

From Down Dog, walk your feet to the top of the mat. Bend your knees a little, grab your block, and come all the way to standing. Come into Mountain Pose with the block in between your thighs, just as you did in Bridge Pose. Squeeze the block and hug in toward the midline. You can feel the adductors engage. Plant down firmly through all four corners of both feet.

As you inhale, stand a little taller. As you exhale, continue to squeeze your block as you lower yourself into Chair Pose. Repeat this movement about 5 times, moving slowly and steadily, continuing to squeeze the block. You might need to adjust your block a little.

Slowly fold forward in Standing Forward Bend. If you need to bend your knees, that’s perfectly fine. Even in this fold, can you squeeze your block? Then bend your knees a little more and release your block.

Slowly roll all the way up to standing. Notice how you feel as you attempt the pose, because if you’re still injured, the shape might not be accessible to you, and it’s fine to skip it. Lean onto your right foot, bend your left knee, and catch hold of the inner edge of your left foot behind you with your left hand. Keep your left hip and knee drawing inward toward the midline. So imagine you’re still squeezing your block in between your thighs. That is really important.

Reach your right arm forward. Instead of dipping the chest down and thinking of lifting the leg up, focus on pushing your foot into your palm. You’re not going super far forward in your Dancer Pose. You’re not working on flexibility, you’re working on strength, although you might feel an intense stretch along the front of your lifted quads.

To help with balance, you can always practice within arm’s reach of a chair or a wall so that you can reach out if needed for extra steadiness.

Then release and repeat on your other leg, foot into the right hand.

Make your way onto your belly on the mat. The shape of this pose is very similar to Dancer, so if this isn’t working for you, work on Locust Pose. If you want to do Bow Pose, bend your knees and see if you can catch hold of your feet and imagine you still have the block in between the inner upper thighs. Squeeze in and start to push the feet against your hands.

If you’re not doing Bow Pose, then bring your arms alongside your body, palms facing the mat, and slowly lift your feet and legs and chest off the mat Focus your gaze forward and down to keep the back of your neck long. Hold here or slowly release and then lift several times.

Flip over onto your back. Grab your block, lift your hips, slide your block underneath your pelvis, and just let yourself settle here. Slow down your breath and start to unwind.

When you’re ready, press into your feet, lift your pelvis, and move your block to the side before lowering yourself down. Maybe you draw your knees toward your belly and bring your arms underneath your calves and stay still or rock a little side to side.

Extend your arms and legs, close your eyes, and notice how you feel now as opposed to when you first started this practice. Let yourself settle into this space.

When you’re ready, begin to lengthen your breath and wiggle your fingers and toes. You can reach your arms up overhead, take a big stretch, and roll onto one side. Come up to take a seat, sitting up tall, maybe closing your eyes for a moment.

Thank you so much for doing this knee-strengthening sequence with me. I hope that it gave you some ideas as to how you can strengthen your knees.

#8848. Here’s How to Train From Now Through the New Year to Maintain Your Hard-Earned Marathon Fitness

A run coach and an exercise physiologist break down the weekly mileage and workouts you need to preserve your speed, strength, and endurance.

You’ve spent months training for your fall marathon, so the thought of losing that hard-earned fitness after race day probably stings. But at the same time, you can’t simply continue logging miles and workouts like you’re in race mode. Trying to stay razor-sharp year-round can lead to injury and burnout; your body needs rest after training for peak fitness.

So, instead, put your marathon fitness on ice. Freeze the adaptations you’ve gained and the endurance you’ve built. Then, you can pick up where you left off on, say, January 1, or whenever it’s time to lock back in for a spring marathon.

If you train right in the weeks between now and the new year, you won’t feel like you’re rebuilding fitness from scratch. Instead, you’ll preserve the key aerobic, muscular, and endurance adaptations you’ve worked so hard to develop.

To do that, we explain the minimum miles you need for maintenance and how speed, strength, and cross-training keep you in prime condition. Expect to return to race training feeling well-rested, confident, and ready to tackle another marathon cycle this spring.

In the first two weeks immediately following your marathon, you’ll want to focus more on rest and easy time-based jogging. Once you’ve recovered, however, you can return to tracking your miles more closely.

The bare minimum mileage you’ll need to maintain will vary from runner to runner, Heather Milton, CSCS, lead exercise physiologist at Primary MD and cofounder of Master My Run, tells Runner’s World. Much of it depends on how many miles you regularly put in over the weeks of your marathon training cycle.

“Science does not give us an exact number of what percentage of your marathon volume to decrease to that still allows you to maintain the same amount of aerobic fitness,” Milton explains. From her coaching experience, however, she’s found this number is likely around 50 percent of a runner’s typical weekly mileage.

David Hall, an RRCA- and USATF-certified run coach and founder of Running Coach CT, agrees. When planning his athletes’ schedules for the off-season, he looks at their typical running volume during marathon training and reduces their weekly mileage to no less than half. Every fourth week, however, mileage can drop to as low as 20 percent of their average to help facilitate recovery.

“A runner who was running 60 miles per week during their marathon build could definitely cut that in half,” Milton says. Or, take a runner who averaged around 40 miles per week. This individual could reduce their weekly mileage to 20, add in some cross-training, and expect to maintain much of their progress.

In fact, Milton adds, every runner can benefit from incorporating more of those cross-training sessions in the off-season. “Other forms of exercise can decrease the repetitiveness of the running motion and help you develop more well-rounded fitness, so I do prefer more variety from cross-training in the down-season,” she explains.

At the same time, Milton wants people to do the exercise they enjoy and, of course, runners love running. “I have to be reasonable about what a runner is willing to do and what keeps them healthy while they’re doing it,” she says. If you want to keep running four days per week in the off-season, that’s still workable—with one important caveat: You need to prioritize strength training.

When you’re in the thick of marathon training, running is your main focus. So while you’re still doing strength work during this time, it mostly helps maintain the strength you already have, rather than increase it, Milton explains. The off-season provides an ideal time to really build up and strengthen your muscle mass and bone health as much as possible.

Each week, Milton says to aim for two to three resistance training sessions that focus on heavier weights with a low to moderate number of reps. (You can do more than three weekly sessions as long as you’re not working the same muscle groups two days in a row.) This sets you up for a stronger return to your spring training cycle because it helps improve running economy, your overall neuromuscular health, and your fast-twitch muscle fibers, which help power you through fast bursts of running or hill climbing.

“Plus, when you start training for your next marathon, you’ll be in a stronger position to increase your running volume again because you’ve strengthened all of the areas of your body that were impacted by your previous race, which can help prevent injuries,” Milton adds.

During the off-season, you certainly don’t need to run every day to maintain your fitness. In fact, you can preserve key fitness markers—such as your VO2 max—with as little as three workouts per week.

“The goal is to maintain at least three to four aerobic days per week to maintain your fitness level,” says Milton. You can opt to run as little as once per week, as long as you continue to cross-train on the remaining days, she adds.

Aim for 30 to 60 minutes of whichever aerobic exercise you most enjoy—hit the gym for the elliptical or indoor pool, or get outside for skiing and cycling.

Similarly, the number of running days per week for Hall’s athletes varies, but many have success with three because it allows more time for strength and flexibility work. He also adds a second rest day to the schedules of his runners who typically train six days per week during a marathon block. But in both cases, consistency is crucial—you don’t want to go a week without doing anything. “Do something every other day at a minimum to stay active,” Hall says.

One of your runs each week should be a bit longer than the others, but it doesn’t need to match the lengths of your true marathon long runs. Milton typically recommends a long run between five and 13 miles, depending on the individual’s training volume.

If you don’t want to worry about tracking mileage in the off-season, that’s fine, too. Running for time instead of miles provides the same endurance benefits, Hall says. Around four weeks postmarathon, his athletes will typically start with one-hour long runs. “Then, they’ll go up to 75 minutes, then to 90 minutes, and then maybe up to an hour and 45,” he explains.

Over several weeks, this gradual progression sets his runners up with a solid base to build from when they start their spring marathon training. “But don’t push the pace,” he emphasizes. “These are easy, conversational efforts.”

Whether you run for time or miles, make sure you’re not increasing either too quickly. “Keep the same rules in mind as when you’re building mileage in marathon training,” Milton says. “Aim to increase by no more than 10 percent each week.” Recent research suggests that, to reduce injury risk, you can apply this rule to the distance of any single run, as well.

What does this look like in practice? Let’s say a runner is doing five aerobic sessions per week, which includes about 20 miles of running. Two are cross-training days and the remaining three are running days. They might choose to run three to five miles one day, five to seven miles another day, and then five to 13 miles for their long run. You also don’t need to increase distance as quickly as you would in marathon training, Milton explains.

Over three weeks, she says a runner might balance their mileage as follows:

Week 1: 4 miles, 6 miles, 10 milesWeek 2: 5 miles, 6 miles, 9 milesWeek 3: 3 miles, 7 miles, 11 miles

In the four weeks immediately following your marathon, don’t worry about fast workouts or hitting paces, says Hall. During those first two weeks postrace, he advises his athletes to go for 20- to 30-minute daily walks. In the third and fourth weeks, he reintroduces easy running and a touch of speed.

“The general rule I apply is: no hard running for the number of days that’s equal to the number of miles in the race. So for a marathon, we’re talking about 30 days of walking and conversational effort running—maybe dipping into tempo pace a bit—but certainly nothing above lactate threshold.”

After that time, Hall says runners can start to add back intensity. In fact, he encourages it, suggesting you incorporate either a 20-minute run at threshold pace or an interval session for the same amount of time. He also recommends alternating one mile at your threshold pace, followed by one minute of easy jogging or brisk walking, until you reach 20 minutes.

“Training at lactate threshold pace can make conversational effort feel easier and can help you run faster while still remaining mostly in an aerobic zone,” Hall explains. In other words, your body adapts so running at any pace starts to feel like it requires less work.

Another way to get in some speed during the winter season? Sign up for a holiday race like a Turkey Trot or Jingle Bell Jog, he says. “It can get boring if all you do is train. Racing a 5K keeps the interest alive and lets you put in a hard effort.” Keep in mind, though, you did just run a marathon, so you don’t need to race all out or cross the finish line with a PR.

According to both Hall and Milton, the golden rule that will help you maintain your hard-earned gains is consistency. Once you’ve recovered physically and mentally from 26.2, get back into a routine that keeps you moving. “Doing something is always better than doing nothing,” Hall says—because you can lose 8 percent of your VO2 max in four to six weeks if you pull the plug on activity completely.

Similarly, you’ll want to avoid “stop-and-go” training. “If you’re running two to four days per week, keep running two to four days per week, every week—within reason, because life gets in the way sometimes,” Milton says. But running 30 miles one week, doing nothing for three weeks, and then trying to get back into it can lead to a real struggle, she adds.

As long as you do your best to stay consistent—and don’t stress when the holidays, travel, or other engagements inevitably interfere—you’ll find your fitness quite close to where you left it after your fall marathon. All that’s left for you to do? Thaw it out with a fresh marathon training cycle this spring.

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#8847. What Happens When Grief Derails Your Triathlon Training

Rachel Olson wins 2026 Ironman 70.3 São Paulo after struggling to train through the grief of losing her mother in November 2024. (Photo: Romulo Cruz/Ironman)

In late September, Rachel Olson crossed the finish line first at Ironman 70.3 São Paulo, nearly 10 minutes ahead of her nearest competitor. The race, by her own admission, was “not spectacular” for the longtime pro triathlete. But the support that followed was. The crowd embraced her, and athletes and fans who had followed her story cheered a little louder, as though they knew what it took just to get her to the start line.

Because in the months after her mother Janis died in November 2024 of liver disease, Olson could barely bring herself to work out. She did not want to disappear from triathlon. But she’d go to the pool and just sit on the edge and cry. She’d hop on her bike and feel a sudden urge to turn around. Running, always an easy way to manage big emotions, became a chore.

Then her body began to rebel: digestive issues, mysterious inflammation, bone-deep exhaustion, muscles that wouldn’t recover.

“My body was basically screaming at me that something was wrong, like it was constantly fighting something,” said Olson, 35, who lives in Boulder with her fiancé, fellow pro triathlete Andre Lopes. “Your mind is telling you to process, and your body is telling you to slow down.”

For endurance athletes, the instinct after a loss is often to train through the emotional pain. The adage goes that exercise helps with grief: Get outside, move your body, clear your head. Sometimes it does. But for Olson and many others, the very thing that once gave life structure can become one more demand on a body and mind already stretched thin.

“Grief doesn’t just live in the mind. It’s in the chest, in the restlessness, in this low-grade energy that has nowhere obvious to go,” said Kenza Haddock, president and co-founder of Oceanic Counseling Group in Murrells Inlet, South Carolina. “Endurance sport can tip from processing grief into outrunning it, using exhaustion to stay ahead of the feeling rather than move through it. It can just leave you more numb.”

Plenty of endurance athletes have turned grief into a mission. In August 2026, Matthew Hollingham, a 25-year-old doctoral student at Penn State, created an “Arctic Circle to Africa” triathlon in memory of his late fiancée Lovisa Arnesson-Cronhamre, who was killed in a hit-and-run while jogging on campus. Over 61 days and 3,545 miles, he swam in a lake above the Arctic Circle, ran a marathon a day for 37 days, and cycled just over 110 miles a day for 23. He raised more than $40,000 for two charities and kept her memory present.

Others have taken similar routes; at the 2026 London Marathon, Laura Coleman-Day, a 33-year-old mother from Lincolnshire in the U.K., went viral for changing into her wedding dress and running the final miles in it as a dedication to her late husband, Xander.

This kind of public mission can be cathartic, says Hilary Bucell, a psychotherapist and lecturer at Columbia University.

“Engaging in something like triathlon can become a ritualized space where the recognition of the loss is welcomed and at the same time, the sport’s necessity for present moment awareness also helps athletes acknowledge new life experiences continuing now beyond the loss,” she said.

Of course, racing to honor a loved one doesn’t erase grief — it just gives you a place to put it. It can also offer a healthy distraction from the deep ache of a devastating loss.

Some aren’t able to navigate their grief in such a public and profound way. There are those like Olson whose grief hits the body hard enough to derail training. In 2023, Gustav Iden, the 2022 Ironman World Champion, ended his season early to heal and regroup after the death of his mother, revealing “it was very emotional, and it was hard to find joy in training after that.” (He returned to racing about a year later.)

As one of her mother’s main caretakers, Olson spent two years before her death flying to her hometown in Texas for doctor’s appointments. Triathlon took a backseat: She parted ways with her coach and scaled back her training. Even when she did have time to work out, anxiety followed.

“I would think, ‘Am I going to be out on a bike ride and get a phone call saying she’s in the hospital? Are things going to go downhill?’”

After Janis died, that anxiety turned physical. Olson was never diagnosed with one specific issue, but testing showed elevated inflammation markers and low ferritin, requiring an iron infusion.

“Ultimately, I think my body was responding to trauma. It felt like I had an illness,” she said. “Trying to perform in a body that felt completely foreign to me was incredibly difficult. I didn’t understand why my body wasn’t doing what it had done before.”

Research suggests that grief can affect the body as well as the mind. The National Institutes of Health (NIH) lists impaired immune response and increased mortality from heart disease, especially in older, widowed patients, among the physical complications. The effects may vary, as not everyone experiences the same physical response.

Part of the explanation may lie in how the brain processes the loss of a loved one through interconnected systems involved in emotion, threat detection, and the regulation of stress hormones. Grief can flood the body with inflammatory signals. and increase cortisol, the steroid hormone produced by the adrenal glands that regulates the body’s response to stress.

“Grief is a neurological event that impacts your ability to learn and remember things, attend to things, and impacts your mood,” said Wilfred van Gorp, a Manhattan-based board-certified neuropsychologist. “Losing someone keeps your amygdala on high alert and elevates cortisol. It impacts you in your body as well as your mind.”

Grief and stress can also disrupt communication between the brain and the gut, which may contribute to everything from irritable bowel syndrome to acid reflux to ulcers, according to research.

For Olson, whose stomach swelled within days of her mother’s death, that brain-gut link was obvious.

“Only two days after [she passed], I woke up, and my stomach was distended about five inches. And then I kind of exploded in inflammation weight,” she shared. “Trying to get that down is not an easy process.”

Still, Olson pushed on. She’d qualified for her first Ironman World Championship slated for about 10 months after Janis died. She wanted to race there to honor her mom. She also didn’t want to lose her identity as a triathlete. Her training “wasn’t even close” to peak levels. In Kona, her stomach rebelled on the bike. After vomiting for three hours, she pulled out soon after starting the run.

“I held onto triathlon so tightly even though my body wasn’t ready. My mind wasn’t ready,” Olson said. “I kept pushing because I wanted it so badly. I attached too much weight to needing training [and racing] to go well and needing something in my life to be OK. Looking back, I realize I didn’t have to be OK.”

After Kona, Olson took a break. She focused on her other jobs as a triathlon coach and as a sales rep, and on envisioning what her wedding to Lopes could look like without her mom.

“I decided I wasn’t going to think about triathlon for a couple of weeks,” she shared. “If I still wanted it afterward, great. If I didn’t, that was OK, too.”

Spoiler: She still loved it. With the fog lifted, Olson saw a different future in the sport, starting with a new coach, Kasper Pedersen, who could build a sustainable load and understand her fragile state.

“I looked for a coach who understands that life happens,” said Olson. “Kasper is great at helping me push my boundaries, but he also knows that I may need to go at my own pace.”

They’re keeping her training volume relatively low as she re-establishes a baseline and repairs her frayed central nervous system.

“I really wanted to make my body and mind think, ‘This is fun. This is helping us,’ rather than setting off alarm bells every time I went out,” Olson shared. “There are still days where I have to take some time off. … Grief really is a roller coaster. But overall, we’ve done a really good job of figuring out what is working.”

Talking about it helps, too, though it doesn’t come easily. Olson describes her grief as a “cloud over her personal life,” and opening up about it has cost her: One friend drifted away, unable to understand what she was going through. Olson wonders if she was simply too much to handle. Still, she finds solace in speaking out, and in being a voice for others who may be grieving alone.

“As athletes, we want to put difficult things in the back of our minds and keep going,” she said. “But I’m glad I can be a voice for other people who are going through the same so they feel less alone than they think they are.”

If her recent win in Brazil is any sign, Olson is rounding a bend toward healing, with an approach to triathlon (and life) that’s less about control and more about leaning into the process, however unpredictable and messy it may be.

“I feel like I’m a different person than I was before [my mom died]. It will always feel like a part of me has been ripped away. But I also know that there’s literally no pain that hurts as bad as what I went through,” she said. “So I’ll keep telling myself, ‘Yes, I can do this thing.’”
