#8836. These Alignment Tips Are the Key to Balancing in Half Moon Pose

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva by Laura Harold)

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about how to do Half Moon Pose first appeared in the January-February 2003 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Every yoga pose is but a wrapper for its unique internal gift. Ardha Chandrasana (Half Moon Pose) gives you the license to fly. With only one hand and one foot touching the ground, the rest of your body is free to soar. Your body stretches from head to heel, creating a sense of wide-dancing euphoria. Your heart center opens, expanding to embrace all the world. Among the standing poses, Ardha Chandrasana offers unique access to this vast, unbridled freedom of the heart.

Yet to achieve this unbounded freedom, we must first ground ourselves in a myriad of details. I am frequently asked, “Why are there so many details to attend to in each pose? Why should I make a conscious effort to straighten my legs, rotate my hips, or lift the inner arches of my feet in Ardha Chandrasana? Why not just switch off my brain, relax, and feel?”

I have found that attending to detail actually deepens the ability to feel, rather than hindering it, and makes it possible to receive the inner gifts of yoga. Though details can sometimes be overwhelming, attention to them refines your evolution and gives you great fulfillment and joy.

On the most basic level, details protect you during your practice. On another level, details ensure that you receive the benefits of the pose; detailed instructions help you bring the specific energetic gift of the pose into yourself. For energy to flow correctly, precise alignment is required. Without alignment, energy drains away and the pose collapses.

Of course, refinements can be carried too far, and you can become so focused on details that you lose sight of the large energy flows that circulate through the whole body. The general rule is that you need enough detail so that there will be no injury to the body *and* so that the pose serves its unique function. A useful approach, especially at first, is to work on just one or two details each time you practice the pose, gradually adding more subtle details after you attain the basics of the physical alignment. Trying to do subtle inner work before becoming physically aligned will lead to a collapse in the posture and a sense of frustration.

Details have more profound purposes as well. When you work on generalities, your mind is dull. When you start to focus on detail—in Ardha Chandrasana or in any pose—your awareness is refined. And awareness is the essence of yoga. Through the attention to detail in your practice, through the cultivation of refinement, and through the constant and ever more careful attention to your existence, you will slowly become aware of the soft, inner voice that will guide you to your spirit and to your fulfillment.

Supta Padangusthasana II (Reclining Hand-to-Big-Toe Pose, side variation) prepares you for Ardha Chandrasana, since it contains all the major movements of Ardha Chandrasana but does not require you to bear weight or to balance. Working on this pose will prevent strain in the buttock muscles as you later try to hold the leg up in Ardha Chandrasana.

To do Supta Padangusthasana II, lie on your back with both legs straight. Bend your right leg and catch your right big toe with the first two fingers of your right hand. (Use a belt around the instep of the foot if you cannot reach your toe.) Exhaling, slowly straighten your right leg completely, fully contracting the thigh muscles of both legs. You should maintain this quadriceps contraction throughout the pose. On your next exhalation, press your right sitting bone away from your head and bring your right leg out to the right side and down toward the ground; if possible, rest the outer right ankle on the floor.

Rather than letting your left hip rise, work to make both iliac crests (front hip bones) equidistant from the floor. This will create flexibility in the adductors and release tense muscles in the front of your pelvis so that when you do Ardha Chandrasana, the pelvis will rest evenly on the head of the standing-leg femur (thighbone). Press your left thigh into the floor. Placing your left hand on your left frontal pelvis, pull it to the left to help open it (Figure 1). Stay for three to nine deep breaths. Exhaling, bring your right leg up so that your arm is once again perpendicular to the floor. Release your right foot, bringing it back down beside the left. Repeat on the other side.

Yoga practitioners move into Ardha Chandrasana from Trikonasana (Figure 2) because the pelvis and the front-leg thighbone are in similar positions in both poses. If you can maintain their placement as you move into Ardha Chandrasana, the pose becomes much easier.

In Trikonasana, take a deep inhalation and visualize your body moving to the next step. Slowly bend your right knee, keeping the right hip externally rotated. Reach forward with your right hand and place the fingertips on the floor about one-and-a-half feet in front of your right foot and slightly to the little toe side (Figure 3). On an exhalation, shift more weight onto your right hand, lifting the left leg toward the ceiling until it becomes parallel to the floor. If you cannot lift your left leg directly from Trikonasana, slide your left foot closer to your right before coming up. Keep your left hand stable and reaching up toward the ceiling throughout your transition. This will greatly improve your balance.

As you move into Ardha Chandrasana, spread the toes and toe mounds of both feet as far apart as you can. This will energize your feet, bring vitality to your brain, and stabilize your movement. Straighten the right leg, powerfully rotating your hip externally so that the right kneecap continues to face your right toes. Even after your right knee is completely straight, continue to rotate the right hip externally. This is the most important action for maintaining safety in the pose, since it protects your inner knee ligaments, a place where many people have searing pain from hyperextension. This rotation also places the head of your femur accurately into joint so that when you lift the left side of your pelvis, you will place your weight evenly on the right hip joint.

Once in Ardha Chandrasana, distribute your weight evenly between the inner and outer foot of your supporting leg. You will notice that your weight tends to drop to your outer foot. To counteract this, consciously press the big toe mound and the inner heel into the floor while lifting your arch. This action will improve your sense of balance because your foot is the foundation of your pose; its lateral stability will determine the stability of your knee and hip.

If your right knee has rotated internally and you find it difficult to rotate it externally, bend your knee a bit. This action will release your hip and make rotation easier. If your standing-leg knee hyperextends, press the calf muscle forward toward your shin, microbend your knee, and press the top of your thigh (the upper quadriceps) back toward your hamstrings. Maintaining both these movements realigns your leg and prevents your knee joint from locking and distorting.

Now lift your left ilium (hip bone) toward the ceiling. Be careful not to press it back, for this will jam your sacroiliac joints and may eventually cause a compression injury. Another point of caution: Lifting your left ilium will tend to make your right leg rotate internally, and this must be resisted to prevent the damage to your inner knee ligaments. Your right leg’s external rotation must always take priority over the lift of your left ilium. When you do become able to lift your left ilium while maintaining the right hip’s external rotation, you will find that the weight of your body will rest on the center of the hip joint, thereby relieving tension in the outer muscles of your right leg, where many beginners get cramps. For additional stability of your right hip, hug your right outer thigh toward your inner thigh before lifting the left ilium.

The outer right ankle bone, the outer right knee, and the greater trochanter of the right leg (the bony knob at the top outer edge of the thigh) should be in one straight line perpendicular to the floor. If your standing leg is leaning toward your head, there will be compression in the rear of that hip joint and excessive weight in the hand and head. Alternately, if your standing leg is leaning toward your back leg, there will be compression in the front of your standing-leg hip joint and your back leg will then feel sluggish and heavy.

Your standing leg should also be perpendicular when viewed from the side. The right sitting bone tends to fall behind you, which collapses your right groin and puts tension in your outer right hip. Press the outer right hip forward until your right sitting bone is directly above your right heel. Simultaneously, lift your right outer ankle and outer leg toward your hip.

To add a more rigorous element of truth to the alignment of your legs, practice this pose with a wall behind you, placing the little toe of your right foot next to the wall and your right heel approximately a half-inch away from the wall. This makes the pose more difficult because your standing leg is now prevented from dropping backward. In this position, you must squeeze your outer right leg inward and lift your left pelvis straight up in order to do the pose.

Energize the muscles throughout both your legs, creating a sense of compactness, as if all the flesh of your legs is being drawn into your bones. This will create a feeling that your right leg has become a pillar supporting your body; it will also make your left leg feel much lighter.

Ardha Chandrasana not only strengthens the legs but also uses the standing leg to bring energy up from the earth. This upward drawing of energy is a foundational principle in yoga and in many martial arts; it is why you contract your quadriceps in the standing poses. When your quadriceps are relaxed, energy does not lift up your inner legs; when you pull the quadriceps up, they become “pumps” that bring the energy from the earth into your pelvis, where your root chakra and second chakra reside. These chakras cannot function well without a flow of energy. Ardha Chandrasana gives you an opportunity to create this flow.

There are other actions that assist this process of lifting energy. I have found that only through combining the lift of the arches and the lift of the quadriceps can the energy of the earth be transmitted into the pelvis and transmuted into corporeal energy. Lift the arch of your standing leg, suck energy up your inner leg through your groin, and feed the energy into the pelvis via a slight lift of your perineum (Mula Bandha). To accomplish these actions, begin by pressing down the mound of your big toe and the inner heel of your standing leg. To create stability, the outer edge of your standing foot also has to be pressed down strongly.

Thus, you will create arches both lengthwise and widthwise, between your big toe and heel as well as between the inner edge and outer edge of your foot.

Now turn your attention to the left leg. As you continue to rotate the right hip externally (so your knee points directly toward the middle of your foot), externally rotate your left leg so that your left kneecap faces front. Once your left kneecap is facing front, do not rotate your left hip any further.

The next action in your left leg should be to press the top of your thigh back toward your hamstrings; then lengthen the back of your leg into your heel. Simultaneously, draw the left side of the pit of your abdomen—the region of your belly just above your pubic bone—toward your head, creating a stretch across your left groin. This will prevent your left thighbone from falling forward and your left buttock from over-contracting.

To prevent fatigue in the left leg, press it down as if you were resting it on a big balloon. Instead of hanging the upper leg from the outer hip muscles, contract your inner thigh muscles toward your outer thigh. This will take the tension out of your outer hip muscles and strengthen your inner leg, including your adductors.

Two primary actions that are involved in Ardha Chandrasana are the “stacking” of the pelvis and the lifting of the pit of the abdomen. The stacking of your pelvis on your right hip joint not only ensures your safety but also aligns your pelvis to receive energy from your right leg. When the left side of your pelvis moves away from the right foot in Ardha Chandrasana, you will get the sense of your pelvis as an ever-widening bowl. This widening makes the pelvis available for the energy that rises from the earth through your standing leg.

Similarly, the lift of the pit of your abdomen aligns your pelvis with your rib cage, making the floor of your pelvis and your diaphragm parallel. This alignment charges the energy of your abdomen and nourishes your kidneys. As you draw the pit of your abdomen toward your head, your tailbone will move toward your perineum and your sitting bones will tuck toward your top leg heel. Do not tighten or flatten your stomach. Instead, lengthen from your pubis to your chest. This action realigns your pelvis and extends your lower back, preventing strain and cramping around the lumbar spine.

If you have stiff hamstrings or are perhaps new to Ardha Chandrasana, place a block underneath your right hand. This will increase your stability in the pose and take stress off your right leg, thereby allowing you to lift your left pelvis and pull the pit of your abdomen upward without distorting your spine.

As you continue to work in the pose, attempt to make your left kneecap, belly button, and sternum face front by spinning the left side of your chest and abdomen back. This action prevents the abdominal organs from falling into the front of your belly (their state in most daily activities) and makes them instead fall toward your right side. This massages your abdominal organs and relieves stress in your lower digestive system.

In Ardha Chandrasana, once you have filled your pelvis with life force from the earth, draw this energy up into the heart center for inner reflection and inner work. This movement of energy is one of the foundational elements in the way I teach standing poses.

When you do Ardha Chandrasana to your right, your tendency will be to make the right side of your torso shorter than your left side. Instead, work to keep both sides of the waist equally long. To lengthen your right side, press your right armpit forward, opening the right side of your chest by working your right kidney toward the front of your body. Drawing your outer right hip toward your left heel will also help balance the two sides of your waist and your spine.

In addition, press both shoulder blades toward the buttocks and away from each other. These actions release the congested sensation and cramping that can occur in the upper back behind the heart center. The shoulder blade actions also free your shoulders and neck so that your head can turn without tension.

Try to bring both arms in one straight line perpendicular to the floor. To do this, press your left shoulder blade away from your head more strongly than the right. Also, you should counteract the tendency of the upper arm to drop behind you as you open and turn your chest to face forward. Restrict this tendency by lifting the back of your arm up through the nails of your fingers. The upper arm should now be perpendicular to the floor as viewed from the front and side of the room. Lifting your back arm will stabilize it and prevent it from falling backward. The more stable your upper arm, the more stable your pose.

Your bottom arm, like your bottom leg, lifts energy from the earth into your heart. Placing the pads of your fingertips on the floor, form a cup with the right hand. Suck energy up from the earth through this cup into your chest.

All through out your practice of Ardha Chandrasana, always keep your upper-arm palm wide and facing forward, with your fingertips and thumb tip pointing straight up toward the ceiling and with your fingers and thumb pressing together. These actions align your hand energy and develop concentration. You should pull equally into your thumb and little finger to keep both sides of your wrist even.

Do not let your body fall into a backbend; doing a backbend in this pose dissipates the energy from your kidneys through your belly and chest. In contrast, moving the body into one plane aligns the internal flows of spinal energy from your perineum to the crown of your head. When carefully combined, the following three actions will prevent your body from doing a backbend: Stretch from your left sacrum and right sitting bone into your left heel, from the pit of your abdomen into your diaphragm, and from your kidneys into your front upper chest. These stretches will additionally help move your spine toward your head, while pulling your coccyx and left leg toward your left heel.

Once you have incorporated all of these details into Ardha Chandrasana I (see Figure 4), your brain will have given out all the instructions necessary to create alignment in your physical body. After you reach and hold the alignment, your brain’s job is over. Next, you will have to separate your consciousness from your brain, moving it out of your head and into your heart while you perform the internal actions of the pose. To facilitate this separation of consciousness from your brain, relax the muscles of your face, jaw, and tongue.

As you inhale, bring vitality from your lungs into your whole body; as you exhale, make any necessary adjustments to your alignment. You will find that inhalations draw life force into your body, whereas exhalations channel that force through your body. Keep your breath soft and long, breathing only through your nose with the softness of Ujjayi Pranayama (Victorious Breath): Drawing your breath audibly across the back of your throat, inhale with a slight “s” sound and exhale with an “h.” All these actions will help your breath connect your brain to your heart and the world outside you with the world within.

#8835. The 10 Best Trail Running Shoes for Trails, Gravel, and More

Impeccable traction and responsive rides await. These are the shoes we lace up before hitting the trailhead.

When I lace up for a day on the dirt, I know my trail running shoes are the only thing separating me from the rocks, roots, and miles of pure, unadulterated trail shenanigans. Trail runners, simply put, are just built different. We rack up mud and rocks with our mileage, and that means we expect more from our gear than road runners while simultaneously abusing the hell out of it. Thanks to my location on the East Coast, I get to run on a huge variety of trails, from packed singletrack to rocky technical trails, to muddy backwoods fire roads, to sandy marsh basins. Basically, I hit all the surfaces, so when I’m testing my trail shoes, I’m really digging in, and so is our legion of shoe testers.

This year has been an interesting year for trail running shoes. Thanks to the growing popularity of trail running, there are more coming out than ever before, but because they are so specialized, reviews are generally all over the place. That’s why on this list you will see very specific workouts for every trail running shoe that we recommend. It’s also why I plan on updating it pretty often, and hopefully expanding the list as new shoes come out and we get our wear testers running in them. The major brands we all expect to see on this list are on here: Saucony, Altra, Salomon, and the like, but choosing trail shoes is complicated and personal, so make sure you read through these reviews to determine which are the best trail running shoes for how and where you run.

For over half a century, Runner’s World has been putting shoes through their paces with staff members and our diverse group of wear testers. These are everyday runners who hit the trailhead and make their shoes work. Every shoe I ran in was put through miles of testing based on its specificity—trail, gravel, technical shoes, et cetera. We evaluate for fit, grip, comfort, responsiveness, weather adaptability, and temperature regulation.

The Hoka Speedgoat 7 makes you forget the issues of the 5 and 6. They’ve nailed the fit this time with updated uppers, new midsole foams, and a smarter construction that finally fixes those nagging complaints about the fit and feel. This model is seriously dialed-in now, making it the perfect shoe for flying over dusty, sandy trails where you need reliable grip without the gunk.

Stack height bumps to 36mm heel, 29mm forefoot using supercritical EVA foam for softer landings and snappier energy return, contrasting to the 6’s firmer feel. A winged heel counter and refined jacquard mesh upper with the addition of a gaiter mean these hug securely without hot spots or blisters, ditching the predecessor’s issues.

Vibram Megagrip outsole upgrades to 5mm lugs with deeper siping and wider spacing; they shed sandy dust and rail trail grit effortlessly while biting hardpack and mild roots. No rock plate keeps it light and easy.

Testers hail the 7’s plush stability on dusty rails—lugs channel sand away for consistent traction; new foam eats vibration from chatter without mush. Uppers breathe during hot days and lock miles better than the 6 ever did.

Wear-tester Diane Grim did note they run a bit smaller, so sizing up is recommended for many, especially those hitting long distances, but she loved the improved fit over the 6, and says that “the lug pattern placement was awesome in gripping (trails were snow-covered and snowmobile groomed),” and she “loved how the lugs continue under the toes for pushing off grip.”

“The Speedgoat 7 engulfs your foot, giving you the security and confidence to get the job done,” she says.

The shoe is a great upgrade for singletrack/rail trail runners craving reliability on flowing, gritty paths from our breakdown. It’s less for pure rock slams, but dusty cruisers never felt this good.

The SensiFit upper with Quicklace locks your foot into the shoe—heel to toe—while breathable mesh keeps swamp feet at bay. The All Terrain Contagrip outsole features 4mm lugs for solid grip on dry dirt, gravel, and roots; it sheds mud decently but slips more on wet rocks.

No rock plate keeps weight low at 9.8 ounces, ideal for non-technical runs.

Wear-tester Rebecca Heflin praises the shoe’s comfort, stability, and versatility, wearing it from road to trail.

Shop Men’s at nordarun.com | Shop Women’s at nordarun.com

Trail shoes consist of four main parts: uppers, midsoles, outsoles, and rock plates. These components work together for protection, cushioning, traction, and durability on everything from gravel to gnarly singletrack.

Uppers form the breathable shell around your foot. They feature tough mesh with rubber overlays at the toes and heels to fend off rocks, roots, and trail debris while staying ventilated.

Midsoles provide the cushioning core, typically using EVA foam or advanced compounds like TPU or supercritical foams. They absorb shock from uneven ground and return energy to keep your legs fresh over long miles.

Outsoles are the grippy foundation with lugs made from sticky rubber compounds such as Vibram Megagrip. Lug depth and pattern vary by terrain: multidirectional for mud, clustered for rocks, all designed to shed debris and last through abrasion.

Rock plates sit between midsole and outsole as thin shields of plastic, aluminum, or carbon fiber. They protect against sharp stones and roots without adding much weight or stifling flexibility. With max cushioned trail shoes, they’re not necessarily a must-have anymore, though many runners still prefer them. They don’t exist in every trail shoe, and in the case where a trail shoe may have a carbon plate, it can add protection and stability.

Trail shoes specialize by terrain to optimize weight, grip, and protection. Choosing the right type means less slip, less fatigue, and more fun no matter the surface.

Drop refers to the heel-to-toe height difference, ranging from 0mm (zero drop for natural foot positioning) to 15mm (higher for calf relief on roads or long efforts). Low drops (0 to 4mm) build foot strength but demand adaptation; 8 to 12mm suits most runners.

Stack height measures total midsole thickness underfoot, outsole, and footbed—usually 20 to 35mm at the heel and slightly less at the forefoot. Max stack (30mm+) offers plush protection for heavy runners or rocky miles; low stack (under 25mm) delivers precise ground feel for agile, technical runs.

Gore-Tex and similar membranes laminate into uppers to block liquid water and wind while venting sweat vapor for a little bit of breathability. They shine in rain, snow, or mud, often paired with mesh drainage ports and quick-lace systems to handle stream crossings without sogginess.

I’ve scrubbed enough mud from lugs to write a whole damn article on it, because nothing tanks your trail high like dried clumps firing off mid-stride. Hit them with the hose right after runs to loosen crud and clean them off. Use an old natural bristle brush and mild soap to excavate lug crevices, then stuff with newspaper or paper towels to speed drying. Never toss in the washer; it wrecks glue and mesh. Insider hack: let the muddiest shoes that you can’t get to right away dry out and then bang off the mud. It works, I promise.

#8833. Unlock Your Full Potential by Fixing These Common Triathlon Body Imbalances

Triathletes can face muscle imbalances. These off-season exercises help build proper strength to prepare for next season. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete)

Triathlon training is all about repetition, with hours upon hours spent catching and pulling in the pool, turning the pedals on the bike, and turning the legs over on the run. With that repetition comes natural imbalance, with some muscle groups getting overworked while others get neglected (or even weaken with age).

Over time, these imbalances can impact performance directly or indirectly by contributing to injury development. That’s why taking time to identify and address these imbalances now will help keep you healthy in the long run.

By pinpointing areas of weakness or asymmetry early on, athletes can target the stabilizing muscles, improve biomechanical efficiency across all three disciplines, and significantly reduce the risk of overuse injuries that often arise from repetitive strain. Here’s how.

While swimming is generally thought of as the “safest” discipline in triathlon, issues can and do occur, often manifesting as “swimmer’s shoulder.” Swimmer’s shoulder is a bit of a catch-all term for pain in the front of the shoulder that encompasses several pathologies, including rotator cuff issues.

Typically, underlying laxity and instability exist. One factor that can contribute to shoulder problems is a strength imbalance between the shoulder internal and external rotators, with the internal rotators becoming disproportionately strong in comparison to the external rotators. This makes sense, as the shoulder internal rotators are active throughout the catch and pull, working to rotate the arm in and push against water.

But the external rotators still play an important role, as they help to stabilize the shoulder joint, keeping the ball of the joint centered in the socket to help prevent impingement and pain with overhead use and shoulder abnormalities. To decrease injury risk, external rotators should have about two-thirds of the strength of the internal rotators.

The most reliable, valid ways to check this involve specialized dynamometry equipment that measures force. But if you’re just looking to get a general idea, check how many reps of each of the below motions you can do until fatigue.

In this case, the test (lying prone, rotating the back of the arm up) can also be used as an effective strengthening exercise for external rotation. Start with higher reps, lower weights to learn the motion (3 sets of 10-12), then work up to higher weights, lower reps (4 sets of 6-8) to build more strength.

If this position causes pain or is too difficult at first, a side-lying shoulder external rotation is also a good option.

While the incidence of overuse injuries attributed to cycling is generally lower than those attributed to running, they can and do occur, most commonly impacting the knee and lower back. Although singling out contributing factors is difficult, the prolonged posture and muscle activations associated with cycling predispose athletes to overdeveloped quadriceps and an undeveloped posterior chain (glutes, hamstrings, back extensors) and lateral hip muscles.

Cyclists need strong quads – these are the predominant muscle used to power the pedal stroke. But the glutes and hamstrings do assist, so neglecting those leaves some power on the table. Plus, that injury-prone lower back needs adequate strength and endurance to withstand hours spent in a forward-flexed position.

Also, because muscle weakness and tightness often go hand-in-hand, related limitations in mobility throughout the posterior chain limit a cyclist’s ability to comfortably hold more aggressive aero positions. Those quads of steel will only help so much if you’re sitting up to ease back and glute discomfort by the end of a long ride!

The strength and endurance of the posterior chain (and also the lateral hip, which can play a role when it comes to knee pain on the bike) can be checked using a single-leg bridge hold.

The single-leg RDL is a good choice for eliciting both high force and stretch in the hamstrings and strengthening the gluteal muscles, back extensors, and lateral hips. Isolating each leg can also help with side-to-side imbalances.

When it comes to muscle strength and running, the glutes have been frequently implicated as the cause of (and solution to) many issues. But, while the glutes do play an important stability-related role in the run gait and deficits have been linked with injury, the true workhorse of the run gait – the calves – often gets overlooked and under-strengthened.

The soleus (one of the calf muscles) experiences forces of up to eight times body weight and produces up to 50% of forward propulsive power while running. Because the calves insert onto the heel via the Achilles tendon (which acts as a spring during running), the two are linked, with decreased calf strength seen in athletes with Achilles issues compared to healthy controls.

Strong calves can also help to protect against tibial bone stress injuries. Masters athletes lose calf strength (and Achilles tendon stiffness) disproportionately to other muscle groups with age, leading to both a reduction in propulsion and step length and an increased risk of lower leg soft tissue injuries such as strains and tendinopathies. So, when it comes to both performance and helping to guard against many common lower leg injuries, first check the powerhouse muscles below the knee!

Calf strength can be tested with a single-leg calf raise test.

The test here can again be used as the exercise – just load it up!

So, while the different disciplines and repeated motions of triathlon might lend athletes to certain imbalances, not all is lost! Triathletes can make themselves stronger, more resilient, and faster with some awareness and work – so don’t neglect those details.

#8832. No Medal, No Aid Stations, No Crowd: What a Solo Ironman Through a National Park Taught Me

He swam 2.4 miles, biked 112 miles, and ran a marathon—all by himself, through one of America’s most spectacular national parks.

Late last year, a friend in Seattle suggested we train for an Ironman 70.3 from opposite coasts. He did the runs, swims, and bike rides along the Pacific Ocean, and I followed suit along the Chesapeake Bay. We weren’t sure whether we’d meet in the middle for an organized event in Nebraska, or save on travel costs with an unofficial “Do-It-Yourself” approach in our backyards.

About halfway through training, he dropped out because of a knee injury. I soldiered on. After 16 weeks of prep, I felt ready, so I set out on my own—no aid stations or medals waiting at the finish line—and accomplished the trek to Annapolis, Maryland, and back in the middle of a snowstorm, with 84 laps in the community pool counting as my 1.2-mile swim.

Later on, I moved to Jackson, Wyoming, where my runs, swims, and bike rides would take place in the shadow of the Tetons. I decided to increase my training workload to try for a full-distance Ironman, also DIY, in Grand Teton National Park. I doubled everything from the 70.3 training block except for the weekend long runs. The schedule as written would have quickly had me running marathons the day after punishing bike rides that took half a day and marked my longest-ever distances in the saddle.

It wasn’t easy. Trail runs and lake swims easily eclipsed the distances I’d done for my high school cross country and swim teams, respectively. And the time was hard to schedule around my 9-to-5. I found a few encouraging partners to swim, ride, and bike with, but I did the majority of the sessions on my own.

The joy of training in pristine wilderness, as spring turned to summer, turned out to be solid motivation. After missing only a handful of workouts over 16 weeks, I felt ready.

I had done another solo half-Ironman to get a feel for the course, my gear, and my fitness level. The week before my target DIY attempt on August 8, I raced a short gravel triathlon with some friends in Steamboat Springs, Colorado, placing second in the first-timers category.

The week of my taper, I relaxed with virtually no workouts. On the day of my attempt, unfortunately, a thick smoke from a West Coast wildfire filled the valley. The swim felt fine, and the bike ride was issue-free, but I could feel my lungs working overtime. By the time I started the run, I couldn’t fathom the marathon ahead of me. Temperatures crested at 80°F, and I was dipping my face and hands in every available stream.

Seven miles in, I started walking and, from there, it was all over. Doing an Ironman without any of the pressure of an organized event means it’s much easier to quit at any point. And the moment I FaceTimed my parents to fill them in, I knew I could just as easily come back and try again the following weekend. No pricey entrance fee or travel to make up. This is my backyard.

So I waited for the smoke to clear, made sure to do a more reasonable taper, and tried again the following weekend, with some of the nerves already shaken out.

Sure, these are luxuries I wouldn’t have had if I’d done a “real” Ironman. But it’s certainly in line with the ethos of these mountains: Sometimes it’s not your summit day. Buoyed by a friend’s words of encouragement (“You have the fitness; you just need a better day”), I packed up the car again and set off for Jenny Lake.

This time, I had my nutrition more dialed: instead of 20-gram protein bars, I packed apple slices and an egg sandwich. The smoke was gone and overcast skies kept temperatures cool. Halfway through the bike ride, a light rain helped chill me even more.

One hundred miles in, disaster struck. My bike’s rear wheel went flat. Rookie road cyclist that I am, I had failed to heed the advice of a more experienced friend to invest in a patch kit. But the trail gods were smiling on me. I pulled right into the Jackson Lake Lodge, where, to my great luck, a pair of bikepackers on their way down the Continental Divide were happy to share some basic supplies.

In 30 minutes, I was back on the way to Jenny Lake, and made it into the parking lot—just as the tire went flat again. I nervously glanced at the odometer: 112.05 miles. Phew!

I felt I owed it to my trail fairy Don to complete the challenge at this point. In a break from official Ironman rules, I allowed myself headphones and music, figuring they were replacing some of the hype of fellow competitors and spectators on a real course.

After 26.2 medium-speed miles, I clicked stop on my watch and collapsed into the cool waters of Jenny Lake as the pink hues of sunset framed the mountains that had been my guide.

“I will forever be a changed man,” I thought to myself. I slept in late the next day, and returned to work on Monday, proud but mostly unchanged. What followed might surprise you.

As the days became shorter and the water colder, a next goal failed to materialize. I fell off my tri-sport routine and started to tick off a few longer hikes instead. I don’t know if I’ll ever do an actual, sanctioned Ironman.

I admire the YouTubers who inspired me to keep up with my training. I understand the appeal of qualifying for the championships in Hawaii. For me, I was simply curious if my body could string together the distances. It was enough that my friend in Seattle called me a beast.

Oddly, I didn’t feel stronger, or more disciplined, or more motivated than when I had started. It was great to have a distraction from work and the chance to push myself in another realm. But, absent others doing the exact same things at the same time, the distances felt arbitrary.

One blessing of living so close to a national park is there are countless adventures and challenges nearby. A few years ago, I tried my hand at the Teton Triathlon. Also known as The Picnic, this unsanctioned endeavor starts with a 20-mile bike ride to Jenny Lake, which you swim across before climbing Grand Teton, the tallest mountain in the range (its summit is 13,775 feet, about 7,000 feet above the Jackson valley), before descending and doing it all in reverse, swimming back across the lake (about 1.2 miles) and biking back to town. It took me 22 hours, and I’d do it again in a heartbeat.

There’s nowhere else in the country you can do anything quite like it. And, to me, the point is to test yourself, rather than beat a field of neoprene-clad athletes. The joy of completing even an unsanctioned Ironman in Grand Teton National Park paled in comparison to the deep satisfaction I felt after completing The Picnic.

A few friends told me it was more impressive to do the Ironman without competitors and fans urging me on. I understand how the public nature of competition helps some people push through hard training days and the race itself. I don’t know that it would have made a difference for me.

When I ran the Chicago Marathon a few years ago, the mandatory fundraising gave that race meaning. I wasn’t bummed that I didn’t qualify for Boston because I’d still hit my dollar goal.

A few weeks after this summer’s Ironman, I accompanied a man running a 50K route in every state in 50 days to raise $1 million for charity. He said that, after a few years of ultramarathons, he wanted to give his time and effort a greater purpose, and doing it for the Make-A-Wish Foundation did that.

That single slow, conversational 50K holds as much meaning for me as all the work I did for my own Ironman. Maybe because it’s a fraction less selfish. Or maybe because it was shared.

That experience, and that man, have stayed with me. I think both of us are chasing something similar in our non-running lives.

My friend Sean Mullaney, the FI Tax Guy, recently published an interesting article about the potential downsides of annuities. One of his observations is so simple that I think it's easy to overlook:

Most Americans already have an annuity. It's called Social Security.

Think about what an annuity is trying to accomplish. You give up some control over a pool of money in exchange for a predictable stream of income, often for the rest of your life. Social Security already provides lifetime income, with the added benefit of inflation adjustments.

#8830. Training on Fatigued Legs Builds Durability—as Long as You Do It Right. Experts Explain How.

These expert-backed strategies help you use fatigue to build speed endurance without risking injury.

Most runners know the feeling: dragging yourself out for a jog when your legs feel like lead.

Your calendar says it’s supposed to be an easy day, but your quads seem to have missed the memo. You settle into a shuffle, wondering how a pace that felt effortless last week could demand so much today.

“Running on tired legs means that your body is in a state of recovery following an effort or stimulus,” says Brad Whitley, DPT, a doctor of physical therapy and clinic director at Bespoke Treatments in San Diego. That effort might come from a hard run or strength session, but emotional and work stress can also contribute, he says.

A run in that state isn’t necessarily a bad idea. Practicing on tired legs can help prepare you for the later miles of a race, when you no longer feel fresh. The trick is knowing when pushing through fatigue is useful to performance—and when a rest day will do you more good.

Simply put, running through some fatigue makes you stronger, both physically and psychologically.

“Running on tired legs helps build resilience in the muscular system,” explains Victoria Sekely, DPT, CSCS, a doctor of physical therapy and certified run coach based in New York City. A more resilient muscular system means your muscles can not only recover faster, but also carry you longer and at a quicker clip.

“When your legs are tired, your muscles are undergoing a biophysiological change,” Sekely explains, which includes building stronger muscle fibers. “If you keep going past that fatigue, that will end in a positive adaptation—meaning you can start to run longer without the fatigue setting in.”

Whitley agrees and highlights the mental benefits: “One of the benefits of running on tired legs can be psychological—that is, teaching your central and peripheral nervous systems [the brain, spinal cord, and all nerves that extend to the rest of the body] that you are able to operate with higher levels of fatigue,” says Whitley. “This is helpful for longer races like a half marathon, marathon, ultramarathon, Ironman, and more.”

While it has its benefits, this training tactic requires thoughtful execution to avoid overtraining or injury.

Whatever you do, if you’re running on tired legs, keep the effort easy. “As a rule of thumb, runners shouldn’t complete high-intensity sprints or long threshold sessions when fatigued, as these types of workouts are when muscle strains can happen,” advises Whitley.

Here are a few strategies for how to practice running on tired legs.

“Initially, the best way to introduce training on fatigued legs would be to complete a run in the morning and a whole-body and/or lower-extremity strength session in the afternoon,” says Whitley. “This allows time for some recovery to occur and then would stress a different physiological system in the afternoon.”

It can feel difficult, but your body will become more resilient as the muscle and tendon capacity increases.

The easiest strategy to try running on tired legs is simply to schedule an easy run right after a long training run or speed workout.

“Running on tired legs is mainly for runners who run more than four days a week, and it will naturally happen if you’re following something along the lines of the 80/20 guideline, where 80 percent of your runs are easy and 20 percent are hard,” says Sekely. “On the days that are hard and followed up with an easy day, your legs will most likely feel fatigued. You are certainly at an increased risk of injury on that day, which is why it’s imperative to keep that easy day easy.”

If you’re increasing mileage or prepping for a long-distance race, consider running twice in one day. “Make the morning run a priority, and the p.m. run can be done at an aerobic pace—think zone 1 to 2—to make up for volume needed for the day,” says Whitley.

There’s a fine line between training smart and overtraining. If you’re not fueling properly or skimping on rest, pushing through fatigue is going to backfire, says Sekely.

“It’s important to recognize if you need a rest day—all athletes I work with implement at least one or two rest days every seven to 10 days,” she says. “Every runner benefits from rest days as much as they do easy days.”

Plus, adds Whitley, too much training when you’re feeling tired can mean you’re chronically overtrained—and leave you burned out or with an overuse injury.

So before you head out with heavy legs, check in on a few variables:

Check in with your emotional state before you head out for your run. “If you’re noticing it is incredibly hard to get motivated and you’re having difficulty getting out the door, this might be a sign of chronic fatigue, and you should modify your training schedule,” says Whitley.

Don’t be afraid to take a day or two off, so you feel ready to get back out there.

This is a good guideline to gauge whether you’d benefit more from a run or rest on any given day, says Whitley: If you start your run with moderately fatigued legs and find that you’re not feeling better after moving for 10 minutes, modify the run by making it lower effort (slowing the pace or eliminating hills), or cut it short if you’re seriously struggling.

Heart rate variability measures your individual readiness compared to yourself, and many smartwatches have features to help you easily track yours. If your HRV is way off from your average, Whitley advises opting for a rest day.

When you do call it a day and kick your legs up instead of lacing up to log some miles, remember that you’re not slacking; rest is when the real gains happen.

To get the biggest boost from your time off, Whitley recommends thinking about how you can reduce the root cause of your fatigue—whether that’s doing gentle yoga or getting a massage for sore muscles or meditating to clear a mind that’s been overwhelmed with work stress.

At the end of the day, running on tired legs isn’t about pushing through at all costs—it’s about knowing when to lean into discomfort for growth and when to pull back to avoid burnout.

From the Ghost to the Glycerin, Brooks is our go-to brand for comfiest trainers.

In 1977, the Vantage was the first Brooks shoe to top our charts. The running renaissance began several years prior, when Frank Shorter won the 1972 Olympic marathon in Munich. Two years later, the shoe industry would be changed forever with the introduction of ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA) foam, which was lighter, softer, and had more rebound than the rubbers used in midsoles around that time. Our editors knew Brooks had a winner when we tested the Vantage.

Almost half a century later, the brand is still dazzling us with its innovations and earning prizes in the 2026 Runner’s World Shoe Awards. And to think the company started out more than a hundred years ago manufacturing ballet slippers and bath shoes.

Since the 1970s, Brooks has solely focused on upping the ante in shoe tech. The Vantage also introduced the varus wedge, which was basically a medial post used to help with instability caused by overpronation. Now the varus wedge is dated and has been replaced with Brooks’s “GuideRails” system. EVA is also being phased out with improved foams that are bouncier and even softer.

Brooks has categorized its shoes to help runners choose the best pair that fits their running style and preferred experience. I’ve been a Brooks die-hard since my high school days. For the past 20 years, I’ve been keeping tabs on product updates and saying goodbye to discontinued lineups (taps for the PureProject minimalist list). Here’s a breakdown of everything you need to know—foams, stability tech—about Brooks’s footwear.

One helpful way to choose Brooks shoes is by knowing Brooks’s foams. The kind of foam determines the type of running experience the shoe is meant for.

Through the decades, Brooks revved up its EVA foam, developing MoGo foam in 2006, and then DNA foam in 2013. Known for its adaptive midsole cushioning, DNA has undergone an evolution of its own, breaking into its own subcategories in types of shoes.

Runners looking for a more cushioned shoe will want to try trainers with DNA Loft midsoles. DNA Loft v3, for example, which is featured in the Ghost 18 and the Adrenaline GTS 25, is nitrogen-infused EVA and rubber. It has large cells of air to pack in cushioning without adding extra weight.

At the beginning of 2025, Brooks released the Glycerin Max which showcased DNA Tuned. In developing DNA Tuned, the brand’s team found they could manipulate the cells creating larger cells in the heel and smaller cells in the forefoot. In an interview with Runner’s World, Brooks Chief Product Officer Carson Caprara explained how this dual-cell cushioning softens landings and becomes a springboard for responsive toe-off.

For runners looking for shoes for speedwork or racing, they should look for shoes with DNA Flash or DNA Gold; the latter is a pure PEBA midsole. DNA Hype is a combination of EVA and PEBA. We found in our testing its good for speedwork.

Before the Adrenaline GTS launched in 1999, Brooks had set out to build off of the success of the Addiction. Runners wanted a more flexible version of the stability shoe, and so, the Adrenaline GTS—Go-to-Shoe—was born.

In 2018, Brooks adapted a more holistic approach with stability, implementing a guide rails system into its shoes. The guide rails system has two dense foam pieces in the midsole, one on the medial side and one on the lateral side. These foam pieces reduce your foot from rolling outward and inward when your form becomes erratic due to overpronation or late onset overpronation.

Now redefined as Go-to-Support, GTS Brooks shoes are the stability counterpart of their neutral models. In this way, you can easily find your favorite Brooks trainer with just a little extra support in the midsole and not much else changed with the shoe.

Guide rails offer unobtrusive support for both overpronators and neutral runners.

Our lab tests show that DNA Loft remains Brooks’s softest midsole material.

Screen-printed mesh provides lightweight structure with more airflow and flexibility.

This sticky outsole compound aids grip and wet-surface traction on trail shoes.

The most responsive expression of Brooks’s DNA foam debuted on the Hyperion Tempo.

What’s the best Brooks shoe for beginning runners?

We always recommend the Ghost because it provides plenty of supportive cushioning without being too bulky. It’s an ideal daily trainer for beginners to start with as an offshoot.

How does the Hyperion Elite 6 compare to other carbon shoes?

According to testers, the Hyperion Elite 6 feels less softer and more accommodating compared to other super shoes they’ve tested. The new DNA Gold midsole adds more edge compared to the Hyperion Elite’s DNA Flash foams, with testers saying the rebound is comparable to the Adidas Adizero Adios Pro 4 or Saucony Endorphin Pro 5.

Does Brooks have bargain-priced shoes and how do they stack up to more expensive models?

The Launch 12, included on this list, has a fit and feel almost on par with more expensive models. It’s not as responsive compared to $140 to $160 trainers due to its EVA cushioning, but it delivers a smooth ride.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#8828. How Triathlon and Incurable Cancer Have Given Me a Way to Live Despite My Diagnosis

Age-group triathlete Rebecca Jaussi shares her personal story with Triathlete of how receiving a cancer diagnosis drove her to signing up for and racing an Ironman 70.3.

I have spent most of my life making plans.

Endless lists of goals. Race calendars. Career milestones. Bucket-list adventures. I have always believed that if I worked hard enough and planned carefully enough, I might chart the course of my life.

Running and occasional triathlons are at the top of my goal-making lists.

I was a late starter professionally, choosing to stay home with my children when they were young. When I eventually returned to school, I didn’t ease my way back in. I was accepted into an accelerated doctoral nursing program, completing an intense year of coursework and clinicals before becoming a registered nurse, followed by three years of doctoral study. In 2020, I earned my doctorate in nursing practice and became a family nurse practitioner.

I have always been willing to push myself, physically and mentally, and my tenacity has benefited me.

I never imagined I would need it to fight cancer.

This story began with a fall. It was another beautiful morning on the North Shore of Oahu (where I was living at the time) in February 2023, and I was running a technical trail when I went down on a rocky section. I experienced a pop in my right hamstring and some pain. But I did what I always do and just kept going.

I finished the run. I experienced some pain afterward, but not enough, in my mind, to stop running for good. I took a few days off and then returned to the trails.

As a healthcare provider, I knew better. But as a runner, I convinced myself otherwise.

I continued running through an increasingly persistent, insidious pain. Eventually, my pace deteriorated from slow to a limping shuffle. Finally, I went to my colleague who practiced sports medicine, and was referred to physical therapy.

I started PT in May. My physical therapist told me I needed to stop running, and I thought that was an unreasonable course of action. There have been very few occasions in my life when I stopped running, including childbirth and surgery, and they were brief periods of time.

Running wasn’t simply exercise for me; it was where I found my flow state and truly part of my identity.

I didn’t feel ready or willing to give up running due to the pain but trusted my physical therapist, whom I considered a friend and a respected colleague, that this was the best course of action.

For three months, I walked on flat trails. I continued my physical therapy exercises and cross-trained but abstained from running or hiking.

When I returned for another assessment, my physical therapist was puzzled. I wasn’t improving. He suggested imaging, and that push changed everything.

I went in for an MRI of my right leg. The imaging was ordered for my mid-thigh, which was not where I had originally injured my hamstring. When I discussed this with the technician, I pointed out that it was in my hip region, so he modified the imaging order.

The MRI showed enlarged lymph nodes in my right groin, hip, and possibly behind my knee, which was an abnormal finding.

I had no recent infection or other obvious explanation for the swollen lymph nodes. I asked colleagues and peers for their opinions, and most believed this was a benign finding.

My mind vacillated between thinking that it was probably fine and the worst-case scenario of malignancy. It felt unsettling to me, and I decided to push for a biopsy rather than wait a few months for an ultrasound to see if the lymph nodes were still enlarged.

After the biopsy, I waited eight grueling days for the results. The physician, who was also my colleague and friend, told me the findings indicated that I had a form of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

This was not easy to ingest, but I didn’t want to burden her with the heaviness of this diagnosis and began joking around. I was blasé and asked her, “How are we going to fix my leg so that I can run?” refusing to fall apart on the phone.

Then I hung up and broke down in front of my husband. Suddenly, all the plans I had spent my life making seemed irrelevant. Questions revolved in my head. What would happen to my family? My future? My career?

The next step I took was to do what I knew how to do, which was research my diagnosis to find out everything that I could about it. I wanted to know the prognosis, treatment options, statistics, anything to help me wrap my head around this.

What I discovered in this process was much more difficult to accept. There were things that I could not control.

I was driven to face the possibility that I may not live as long as I had expected. I had to accept that I would be living with the uncertainty of my health status and that fighting incurable cancer might become a permanent fixture in my life.

For someone who had devoted decades to building goals and marking off boxes, this was terrifying. There were no checklists for this.

I took time to process what I was facing and came to the recognition that I had a choice – not about living with cancer, but about living my life.

I was not going to allow this diagnosis to define me; I had a strong desire to live my life to the fullest with purpose and direction. I still wanted to work as a nurse practitioner for as long as I could. I still wanted to pursue medical humanitarian work. I still wanted to travel. I still wanted to be active.

In January, I was accepted into a clinical trial for immunotherapy.

Before treatment began, I did something that probably sounded slightly unreasonable to the people around me.

I signed up for Ironman 70.3 Hawaii on June 1, 2024.

I asked my oncologist and the lead investigator of my clinical trial whether I could participate. They told me that I was the first patient they knew of to ask about competing in a half Ironman while undergoing treatment.

They gave me their blessing with one caveat: It would be essential to listen to my body. This was going to be physically taxing on my body due to the cancer already exhausting my body and undergoing treatment in addition to the rigors of training for a 70.3.

I understood the risks. I also understood something else: Training gave me a goal and purpose to keep moving.

Although cancer had taken away my perception of control, it hadn’t taken away my ability to choose a direction.

I arrived in Kona on May 30, 2024. I was nervous and exhausted. I had received treatment the week before and was still recovering from it.

My younger brother, who had agreed to race with me when I asked, and I gathered our swag and attended the informational session. As we were walking out, I saw the iconic walls of all the participants, their bib numbers, and the “why” wall. Seeing my “why” story on the wall solidified my resolve in what I was doing.

The day before the race, I started receiving text messages with their pictures attached, early in the morning, from friends, family, and my whole care team from Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, wearing a T-shirt that had my cancer ribbon with the words “Fight Cancer Like a Girl” on the front and “Team Rebecca 01” on the back. My amazing husband made nearly 100 shirts and sent them out, asking them to send me a picture and words of encouragement the day before the race. I felt so much love and support from the people in my life.

On June 1, 2024, I stood on the beach waiting for my wave to start at Ironman 70.3 Hawaii. I remember feeling incredibly grateful to be there and have the ability to push my body to the limits.

The race was hard; the winds were cranking so hard that several cyclists were blown into the lava rocks along the highway. It took some serious grit to keep going, but with my husband and kids driving by with my favorite songs blasting on the stereo, cheering me on, I was able to finish the bike.

By the time I started the run, it was midday, and the sun was searing, with temperatures climbing above 90 degrees. My body was fatigued, and every part of me wanted the race to be done. I dug deep. My mantra was “I can do hard things” on repeat. I kept moving.

During those final miles, rolling thoughts in my head surfaced: If I can fight cancer, I can finish this race.

There was an alteration in my thinking and in the purpose of that day; this was no longer about the race but rather an understanding that I was capable of moving forward.

I crossed the finish line with my brother beside me and my family waiting and cheering. I was overwhelmed by my emotions as I crossed the line.

My body was spent; however, there was something strangely beautiful about that exhaustion. I would rather be exhausted from swimming, cycling, and running than exhausted from lying still, consumed by the knowledge that I have incurable cancer.

My training looks different than it used to. Some days are hard, and my body needs downtime.

I’ve learned that listening to my body isn’t a weakness, or even optional at times, but rather a way for me to keep up the fight.

With every step I take, every mile I cycle, every lap that I swim, it is more than just training; it serves as a reminder that my body is still mine and truly a gift to be cherished.

My cancer diagnosis has altered my relationship with time. I functioned at a faster pace and was always thinking ahead about what was next: the next race, the next degree, the next goal, the next item to add to my list.

I am more focused on the mile that I am in right now. I have not stopped making plans; I just hold them differently.

My desires to work, travel, race, and serve others remain, but their priority and intensity are more flexible, as my health and energy can be fluid.

This diagnosis has shifted my perspective – I no longer believe that my worth or value depends on completing every goal I write down.

Some days a win is simply to get out the door. Sometimes it is a slow swim, and the distance may be shorter than planned. Sometimes it is walking instead of running. Sometimes it is resting.

And sometimes, it is standing at a finish line I wasn’t sure I would ever reach.

The trajectory of my life feels unsure and more constrained. However, I know that running, swimming, and cycling are things I can do at the moment, and they make me feel alive.

Honestly, for me, that’s what endurance sport has become. This is not a means of escape from cancer but rather my way of living despite it.

One step, one mile, one breath, I will keep going.

#8826. Salomon Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX Review: Built for Wet, Gritty Miles

The waterproof Gore-Tex upper and grippy lugs handle sloppy gravel—and slick floors during long shifts.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The Salomon Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX is technically a gravel running shoe, and it excels in that arena. It’s also becoming an absolute cult favorite among nurses, techs, and other healthcare workers who spend 12 hours on slick floors and want something wipeable, grippy, and weather/other substances-tough. Personally, I tested it on the one surface it was born for: wet, gritty, cursed early-morning gravel that always tries to murder me. Tough luck, gravel gods. I’m still alive.

The Gore-Tex of the Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX is the cold, wet, ugly-conditions sibling in Salomon’s trail running gravel lineup. It’s a boss of a gravel trainer that shares its midsole, outsole, drop, and stack with the standard Grvl running shoe; the difference is that Gore-Tex upper, which trades some airflow and a little weight for weather and moisture blocking power. If you train through damp autumns and slushy winters, like I do, the GTX is 100 percent what you want. If you run mostly in dry, warm conditions, save the $20 and some sweat and take the regular version.

When it comes to the Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX, the lugs make the shoe. At 2.5 mm, the lugs aren’t the aggressive, mud-clawing teeth you’ll get on a mountain shoe. They’re short, chevron-shaped, and made of Contagrip rubber that gives you enough hold without digging, and they’re short enough that road-to-trail is totally doable.

I ran them at Shirley Chisholm Park in Brooklyn, which is a landfill-turned-park full of gravel hills. The conditions were damp, slippery, and gloomy. I took them out in the early morning, with loose stone over wet packed base. It’s weather that makes you wonder why you’re there and not at the TJ Maxx across the highway. But, even as a Maxxinista, I settled in fast and happy because the lugs gripped like they were made of sticky tack. My uphills weren’t tripping me up and pulling my toes under my knees, and the downhills didn't turn into a gravel slide. They have just enough give and flex in that rock-protected sole to keep my wobbly body upright, in spite of what gravity would want me to do.

Short lugs also mean less trapped debris and more contact area, which is why the grip carries over to hard, wet surfaces. That’s a big part of the healthcare-worker love: it’s a grippy sole that doesn't feel like a clunky work clog or like you’re rounding in cleats.

The optiFoam² midsole sits in the moderate-cushion zone. It’s soft enough to take the edge off a long shift or a long run, and firm enough that it doesn't feel mushy on uneven stone. It’s not quite a Goldilocks for all situations, but where it works it sings. The 8mm drop is traditional and calf-friendly, so it suits people who are on their feet all day.

It’s not terribly responsive overall, but somehow, in spite of that, it feels fast on gravel, especially on the trickier uphills, where you lose a lot of oomph in most hybrid shoes. It has a nice “settle into your stride” ride feel that gives you a lot of pep for the price. It’s not a racer, but I could see myself racing in them.

The weather in the mornings was, for a period of time, frankly, unholy. My feet stayed dry and comfortable the entire time. My body: not so much. The Gore-Tex membrane handles puddle splash, wet grass, and gravel dust (read: concrete) without seepage, and the upper is easy to wipe down, which is the second reason it’s popular in hospitals and clinics: spills, splashes, and grime aren’t likely to be permanent.

The trade-off is the standard Gore-Tex trade-off: it’s just less dang breathable than a mesh upper, so it runs warmer. Fit-wise, it’s a standard width suitable for most runners—save for those with a really wide midfoot—with a secure, wraparound lockdown.

There’s a quirk to gravel nobody chats about, but I obsess over—the aforementioned concrete situation. The quickLace neo bungee system is great for quick, adjustable fit, but wet gravel dust can dry on the bungee and basically cement it in place. The laces get stuck.

The fix: wet them down a little. A bit of water de-cements the dust and the system moves freely again. Rinse your shoes after dusty runs and you’ll never notice.

Here’s where I must be honest about the limits. This is not the shoe for flat, slabby rock or highly technical trails. The lugs are too shallow to bite into loose, steep, or rooty terrain, and the sole isn’t quite flexible enough to conform around rock features. If your trails look like a scramble, look at a deeper-lugged trail shoe instead.

And it looks good doing it. The number of these I see on chic New Yorkers in my office is wild. But, the important bits, like the abrasion-resistant upper, hold up to gritty, scuffy use, and the reflective details are aces for dark early-morning starts.

Is the Salomon Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX waterproof? Yes. It uses a Gore-Tex membrane, so it’s waterproof and wind-resistant.

Is it a trail shoe or a road shoe? It’s a hybrid gravel shoe. It’s at home on gravel, fire roads, and mixed paths, but it isn’t designed for technical, rocky trails.

Are Salomon Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX shoes good for nurses? Many healthcare workers swear by the third version and are grabbing the fourth for the grip. It’s easy to clean and moisture-resistant.

GTX or standard Grvl? Pick the GTX for wet, cold conditions. Pick the standard version for dry, warm weather and better airflow.

The Aero Blaze 4 Grvl GTX is a stylish, abrasion-resistant, grippy gravel shoe that doubles as a great on-your-feet-all-day option. It’s not a technical trail mistress, or a trail racer, and it isn’t trying to be. For gritty gravel, fire roads, and messy mixed terrain in lousy weather, it’s one of the best new choices around.

#8824. A Frightening Encounter on a Dark Road Nearly Took Night Running From Me. This Year, I’m Taking It Back.

I N THE DARK, the headlights cast a distorted version of my silhouette on the industrial building to my left as the vehicle makes its way past me. I’m running along an otherwise desolate road, not far from my house. The car comes to a halt at the stop sign about 300 feet in front of me—and idles. My legs instinctively slow down, my body reacting before my mind has a chance to catch up. I quickly calculate what to do next. There are no side streets I can turn into—I either have to run past the car or turn around, which would add a few miles to my run that I’m not ready for. Maybe the driver is just checking his phone, I tell myself.

But the broad-shouldered man with a long graying beard at the wheel is waiting for me with the window rolled down, his arm resting in its frame. He starts shouting before I can make sense of the situation: What do I think I am doing, running in the dark? Am I trying to get killed? My body tenses, anticipating the man’s possible next move. He has daughters my age, he continues, and he’d kill them if they did that. Could I at least carry this with me, he roars, throwing a key-chain alarm to my feet, then driving off before I have a chance to react.

I sprint the last half a mile home, propelled by anxious energy. My inability to focus only fuels my confusion; so does the blue egg-shaped alarm in my trembling hand that I don’t have a clear memory of picking up but am holding nevertheless. I try to replay in my head how it got there—and why. I have reflective bands on both my arms and my ankles, so drivers can spot me. I use my phone’s light to illuminate the ground in front of me whenever I need to.

The next day, I don’t run outside in the dark. Too cold, I convince myself when I step on the treadmill I hate so much in my apartment complex gym. Too rattled, is what I am unwilling to admit. Because do I have any right to feel that way when technically nothing happened to me? The stranger, in the end, didn’t hurt me.

Still, something changed on the road in the dark.

With every rhythmic thump the belt makes, I am less determined to keep going. My mind can’t handle the monotony. I start skipping days when I cannot make it out for a daytime run. At some point over the next few weeks, the key to the gym falls behind the shoe rack, and I don’t even notice.

THE LIKELY DIAGNOSIS is seasonal affective disorder. It could also be winter blues, but that one is milder and more temporary. My somber mood and low energy seem constant. For most people, it passes by spring, my therapist says. What helps? For one, exercise! But at that point, my couch’s cushions have resigned to accepting my body’s indentation as their new shape.

By the time spring comes, my fitness is at odds with my enthusiasm for the prolonged daylight, and I end up with shin splints. I spend the rest of the year trying to heal and return to form.

I don’t forget about the gray-bearded man. In fact, I share the story, framing it as a silly encounter. “Would you believe that?” I say with a forced smile.

“That’s not okay,” my friends and coworkers answer with their words as much as their faces.

My feelings start morphing from self-blame into anger. What should have been clear to me from the beginning dawns on me slowly: Vigilance is important, but the solution to a stranger’s concerns about my safety is not to instill more fear in the name of “protection.” Women running at night are not the problem. We’ve long ago dismantled the patriarchal notion that men should be our protectors when, in fact, they often pose the danger.

And so when the clock falls back an hour at the start of November, I’m determined not to fall back into a cycle of seasonal depression and injury.

BY MID-DECEMBER, it’s dark by 4:30 p.m. I wrap my torso in color-changing LED tubes. Today I pick emerald. As I descend the trail that clings to the bank of the Delaware River, the historic cantilever bridge that crosses the water comes into view, itself wrapped in green color-changing lights. I smile for no other reason but that we match.

I run up a semicircle road where, for a moment, the world is reduced to cones of warm yellow glowing from vintage streetlights. My chest lamp illuminates just enough ground in front of me to fit my next two steps. Beyond that, I trust that my feet remember what my eyes cannot see.

The darkness has a way of taming my unruly mind. The stillness mutes my whirling thoughts, a nearly impossible achievement among the hectic noise of daylight. It’s the closest I come to meditating, to understanding what it means to be present. It doesn’t matter where the road leads or how long is left of my run; it’s only here and now. The quiet is mostly disrupted by my own two feet. They take turns striking the ground, but their thuds meet in the echo that reverberates off building walls before getting swallowed up by the endless nightfall blue encircling me.

How did I ever allow this to be taken away from me?

Someone lingers at the end of the sidewalk in front of me, and I instinctively switch to the opposite side, picking up speed.

The person pays me no mind, looking in the direction of a leash they’re holding, the end of which I cannot make out. The black road becomes deserted again, and I slow my pace. What was born out of necessity has grown into my favorite part of the day. I love this. I need this. This is the world I want to live in.

This article originally appeared in the Spring 2026 issue of Runner’s World.

Pavlína Černá, an RRCA-certified run coach and cycling enthusiast, has been with Runner’s World, Bicycling, and Popular Mechanics since August 2021. When she doesn’t edit, she writes; when she doesn’t write, she reads or translates. In whatever time she has left, you can find her outside running, riding, or roller-skating to the beat of one of the many audiobooks on her TBL list.
