#8823. After Training for My First Marathon, I Felt Like My Body Didn’t Look Like the Runner I Thought I’d Become. Experts Helped Me See Otherwise.

Marathon training changed how I saw my body—even when it didn’t change how I looked.

Two weeks out from my first marathon, I looked in the mirror and didn’t see the version of myself I thought I would. There was no six-pack, not even a hint of ab definition. My glutes weren’t particularly sculpted, and I wouldn’t exactly describe myself as lean like many runners I see.

At 5-foot-10, I’ve never been the smallest girl in the room. And while my long legs certainly help me cover more distance, I expected months of marathon training to leave me looking more visibly athletic, with more muscle definition and a physique that reflected just how hard I’d been working. I thought that after months of early alarms, added protein, and steadily increasing mileage, I’d look in the mirror and see a different body type.

Somewhere along the way, I absorbed the idea that a runner’s body should look a certain way. When mine didn’t match that image, I started wondering if I wasn’t training hard enough, if I was doing something wrong, or if my body simply wasn’t responding the way it was supposed to.

As I approached race day, I thought about why I was holding myself to that standard in the first place, especially because I was running the New York City Marathon on behalf of Planned Parenthood of Greater New York, an organization whose work centers on bodily autonomy and compassionate care.

Why was I putting so much pressure on my body to look different when it was already doing something incredible? I realized training for a marathon isn’t just about building endurance; it can also mean confronting the expectations you place on yourself.

So many people have an idea of what a “runner’s body” is supposed to look like, particularly fed by what we see online. When you see the same body type represented over and over, it’s easy to start associating that appearance with athleticism. But running a marathon is an enormous physical undertaking, and there’s no single body type that proves you’re capable of doing it.

Clinical sport psychologist Hillary Cauthen, PsyD, explains that the concept of “a runner’s body” is “largely a socially constructed ideal influenced by media representation, sport culture, and the tendency to associate certain physical characteristics with athletic success.” She adds that distance running has historically been represented by a lean body type, particularly smaller-framed athletes, which can leave some recreational runners questioning whether they fit the mold.

Comparison is a large part of this problem, too, says Cindra Kamphoff, PhD, mental performance coach and founder of the Mentally Strong Institute. “We see elite runners and start believing that’s what we should look like,” she explains.

Marathon training is practically a master class in comparison, making it hard to avoid. You’re tracking your pace, watching your mileage climb, sharing runs on Strava, and seeing what everyone else is doing. It can feel like your body should be changing right alongside your stats.

There’s also a particularly frustrating point of tension for women, who can feel caught between the cultural expectation to be smaller and the athletic ideal of looking lean and strong. Carinthia Bank, LCSW, a social worker who works with runners on body image, describes this as the “female athlete paradox,” in which women are judged against both ideals.

For example, a woman might recognize that building strength and fueling adequately are essential to marathon training, yet still feel pressure to maintain a smaller frame or worry that eating more to support her mileage will change her body in ways she doesn’t want. These competing expectations can shape how women judge their bodies, even as they get stronger and more capable, Bank explains.

Marathon training can also increase the time we spend thinking about our bodies, particularly when we’re experiencing physical or emotional discomfort, Bank adds. Many runners tend to think they’d feel better if their bodies were different, which can lead to judgment and blame toward the body they have.

That’s the trap I found myself in. While I was training for 26.2 miles, part of me was still measuring my progress against an imaginary finish line where I’d emerge with a completely different-looking body. I would accomplish something I’d never done before, like running my farthest distance, yet I was using my appearance to dictate my progress.

Cauthen offers a simple definition to keep in mind: “A runner’s body is not a specific shape or size. It is a body that runs.”

Here’s the thing about marathon training: Your body adapts to the physical demands of running, but those changes don’t guarantee an aesthetic transformation. You might build muscle, experience weight fluctuations, or notice an increase in appetite as your body works to fuel and recover. “Improved fitness does not always result in weight loss or a smaller body,” Cauthen says.

There’s also a practical reason not to make getting smaller one of your goals in marathon training. Kamphoff encourages runners “to focus on fueling for performance rather than restricting for appearance,” reminding us that “you can’t expect your body to perform at its best if you’re constantly trying to make it take up less space.”

Marathon training requires substantial energy, and restricting food to change your appearance can leave you without enough fuel to support your workouts and recovery.

Plus, fixating on your size can affect more than physical performance. “Focusing on getting smaller can distract and discourage us from actions that are helpful to performance and mental health,” Bank says. When you’re preoccupied with changing your body, you can miss out on learning what helps you perform, enjoying the process, and appreciating everything your body allows you to do.

I had to confront the fact that I’d been treating my appearance as a report card for my training. If I was working hard enough, I assumed I’d eventually see visible proof in the mirror. But I realized I can become a stronger, more capable runner without looking the way I imagined I would.

For me, that meant recognizing that the body I’d been criticizing was the same one carrying me through early morning runs and increasingly long distances. My body wasn’t failing at becoming a runner’s body—I’d been expecting it to meet a standard that had very little to do with what I was asking it to do.

I wish I could say that learning all of this made me instantly love every inch of my body, but that wouldn’t be honest. I’m still working on it, and I still have moments when I catch my reflection and wonder why I don’t look the way I imagined I would after months of training. But I’m trying to shift my focus from what my body looks like to what it’s allowing me to do, with the help of these expert tips.

“One of the most important shifts runners can make is moving from body evaluation to body appreciation,” Cauthen says. Instead of asking whether I look like someone who runs marathons, I’m trying to ask myself what my body has helped me accomplish. And the answer is a lot more impressive than whether or not I have visible abs.

As I got closer to race day, I continued to remind myself that I don’t have to look a certain way to feel proud of what I accomplished. My body carried me through months of training, and that’s worth celebrating all on its own.

I’m also learning to give myself a little more grace when my expectations don’t match reality. Bank reminds runners that “human beings usually get uncomfortable when there’s a difference between what we wanted and what we get,” and encourages compassion rather than self-criticism.

I don’t have to ignore the fact that I expected marathon training to change my appearance, but I also don’t want those expectations to overshadow everything else I’ve gained, including running farther than I ever thought possible, learning how to fuel and maintain energy, and showing up for myself.

Cauthen recommends distinguishing between observing a physical change and assigning a negative meaning to it, which has really stuck with me. “Noticing that your legs have become more muscular, your weight has fluctuated, or your clothing fits differently is an observation,” she explains. “Deciding those changes mean you are too big, not fit enough, or don’t look like a runner is an interpretation.” This helped me realize how quickly I can turn a neutral observation into self-criticism.

Instead of jumping to conclusions, Cauthen says it’s helpful to ask yourself a few questions when those negative thoughts creep in. For example, “is this thought based on evidence or comparison?” and “am I evaluating my body based on appearance or how I feel and function?” These questions challenge the assumptions that we tend to make about our bodies.

Kamphoff encourages runners to develop what she calls an “inner coach” instead of listening to an inner critic. One strategy she recommends is to “capture your wins” by writing down three things you’re proud of after training. The idea is to shift your attention from perceived imperfections to the progress you’ve made.

I’m trying to practice this by celebrating the things that don’t show up in a mirror. For example, I’ve learned how to pace myself and keep going when a run gets uncomfortable. “Your body has been showing up for you mile after mile. Make sure your self-talk is showing up for your body, too,” says Kamphoff.

Ultimately, I’m learning that I don’t need to love how my body looks every single day to respect what it does for me. “Body acceptance does not require loving every part of your appearance every day,” Cauthen says. “Sometimes it starts with respecting your body’s needs and appreciating its efforts, even when your feelings about your appearance are complicated.”

I can have complicated feelings about the way I look and still be proud of the athlete I’ve become. And I can show up at the starting line without meeting some imaginary physical standard first.

That’s the mindset I carried with me to the marathon. I ran 26.2 miles for a cause I believe in, after months of training that challenged me physically and mentally. My body didn’t have to look a certain way to deserve that moment.

After all those early mornings and hours of preparation, I finally crossed the finish line, put the medal around my neck, and walked out of Central Park feeling something I hadn’t quite felt throughout training: pride. Not because my body looked different, but because of everything it had just done. I felt so grateful for my legs that kept moving, my strength that carried me through the tough miles, and a body that got me to the finish line without injury.

No, my body may not have looked like the “marathon body” I once imagined, but it was a marathon body. I didn’t need a mirror selfie to prove what I’d accomplished: I ran all 26.2 miles. Honestly, what could be more impressive than that?

Alyssa is a New York City–based runner and lifestyle writer covering the intersection of fitness, beauty, and everyday routines. Currently training for the NYC Marathon, she brings a firsthand perspective to stories on endurance, recovery, and the mental side of running—alongside the real-life habits that support it. Her work is rooted in what’s practical, personal, and worth incorporating into your own routine.

#8822. The Biomechanics of Speed: How Your Form Can Improve Your Pace

This “speedwork” is way more fun than sprint repeats.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Whether you’re lacing up your shoes for a 5K or gearing up for a longer endurance race, if you want to get faster, you have to do both longer runs and speedwork sessions to train your aerobic and anaerobic systems. But for the biggest speed gains, you should also look beyond your cardiovascular fitness and work your… posture?

“People often think of running as a lower body sport, but running is everything going on between your ears and everywhere below,” says Anh Bui, D.P.T., C.S.C.S., a former collegiate runner, doctor of physical therapy, and biomechanics specialist in Oakland, California.

While you probably can’t (and shouldn’t) transform your running form into the stride of, say, Olympians on the podium, you can incorporate tweaks to make your mechanics more ideal for you. And that can help you improve performance, get faster, and lower your risk of getting hurt.

“There’s high variability between everyone’s biomechanics based on how you’re structurally and genetically built,” says Bui. “The key is to optimize movement, not force idealism, and to run efficiently to maximize speed and minimize injury risk.”

Read on for more about how each part of your biomechanics, from head to toe, contributes to your speed—plus a handful of moves to add to your routine that’ll help you pick up the pace.

It’s easier to maintain good posture on a short jog versus a long training run when your body starts to drag. But focusing on staying tall and keeping your shoulders from slumping is an important part of efficient running form—not to mention makes it easier to breathe.

Standing up straight as you run with a slight forward lean helps pull you forward, says Ellen Foster, D.P.T., a doctor of physical therapy, movement quality expert, and running coach in Cincinnati. “I like to encourage runners to sort of ‘fall’ forward from the ankles so that their hips are slightly in front of their feet,” she says. “Just make sure you don’t lean forward by bending at the hips or waist, as that would lead to pushing your hips back and losing valuable hip extension.”

Your arms play a surprisingly big role in picking up your pace. Just try pumping your arms harder next time you’re huffing up a hill and see how much it helps. Here’s why: The motion of your arms and legs are linked. “And our arms act as pendulums to help balance our trunk, as forces travel up our body from our legs,” says Foster. “So, when we swing our arms in a more efficient way, our legs often follow their lead.”

While research on just how crucial the arm swing is to running mechanics is limited (most studies focus more on the lower half of the body), and results offer mixed information, most researchers agree that swinging the arms helps with vertical oscillation (or how much we move upward as we stride), side-to-side balance, and minimizing rotation.

“Anecdotally, I find that arm swing drills can be a good starting place when working on increasing cadence, especially if someone is struggling to increase cadence due to poor coordination,” Foster says. Cadence, or the number of steps you take per minute, often changes depending on the speed you’re running, but experts suggest a quicker cadence can limit overstriding and help with forward momentum.

Sprinters tend to drive their knees up aggressively, about 90 degrees from the ground. That’s not sustainable over longer distances, says Bui, who says distance runners should ideally maintain more like 45 degrees of knee drive.

Why does the position of your knees matter? “Picking up your speed without appropriate knee drive will increase likelihood of overstriding, or landing with the foot far in front of your body,” Bui explains. That can slow you down and increases ground reaction forces—or forces exerted by the ground onto the body, Bui says—and ups your chances of injury.

When considering how your feet play into your form and your pace, a lot of it is about those ground reaction forces. If you reduce the time your feet come in contact with the ground, you can potentially lower the force on your body—and lessen your risk of injuries like shin splints, says Foster.

“When we look at vertical ground reaction forces (vGRF) across time, midfoot striking has a lower rate of vGRF with one smooth peak,” Bui explains. By contrast, heel striking has a longer ground contact time, leading to a higher peak force and greater load on the body. This is because your ankle dorsiflexors (when you pull toes toward shins) can’t efficiently absorb the impact of your foot strike, and therefore, your knee joint takes on extra force, she adds.

Try to pick up your cadence and adjust so you’re striking the ground with your foot underneath your body (rather than out too far in front) to help reduce those forces up the leg. Typically, heel striking accompanies overstriding—which can increase risk of injury from the added load—and upping your cadence can help you avoid it.

Keep in mind that your body needs time to adjust to any changes you make in your form. Also, while your body may take on more force with a heel strike, it doesn’t always lead to more injuries or slower speeds. It’s one piece of the biomechanical puzzle. “Heel striking isn’t inherently dangerous by itself,” Foster says.

To improve your biomechanics, working with a run-form coach or physical therapist with advanced training in motor learning or neuromuscular re-education is hugely beneficial, says Foster. “It’s easy to understand the correct biomechanics, but it’s much more challenging to implement them,” she says.

Although working with one of these pros is ideal, a few exercises you can practice on your own can help you get a jumpstart on improving biomechanics.

Here are five biomechanical drills that focus on different aspects of your form. Do them often (for a few minutes as part of your warmup before every run, for example) to make the movements feel like second nature. Then, when you’re working to incorporate tweaks to your form into your run, don’t try to make several changes all at once; try sprinkling them into your runs slowly, thinking about a single form tweak for 30 seconds once per mile.

Just make sure not to jump in too quickly. All tweaks to your body’s biomechanics should be gradual or you risk the chance of injury, says Foster.

Why it works: This super-quick drill emphasizes balance and stability while firing up your posterior chain, which helps develop a more powerful push-off.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Raise right knee to hip height. In a quick, explosive movement, lower right foot to floor and raise left knee high, then lower left knee and raise right knee to hip height again. Do 5 reps. Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Why it works: Practicing this movement at a quick, consistent pace helps make your arm swing more efficient.

How to do it: Set a metronome app (like Metronome Beats) to a beats per minute that feels in sync with your running cadence; 180 bpm is ideal but dial it back if that feels too quick. Sitting on the edge of a chair or standing with feet hip-width apart, pump arms forward and back to the beat, starting with 10-15 seconds. Do 3-5 sets, resting for about 10-20 second between sets.

Why it works: The plyometric motion of this jump helps prep your tendons to store and release energy quickly. Start by doing the move with both legs, then progress to one leg at a time, recommends Bui.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Keeping legs straight, push off the floor from the ball of feet and swing arms up to jump as high as you can. As soon as you land, jump again. Do 5 reps, jumping as quickly as you can (and minimizing your feet’s contact with the floor). Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Why it works: This quick movement increases tendon capacity, trains your body to absorb load as you make contact with the ground, and decreases the time your feet stay in contact with the ground.

How to do it: Stand on the edge of a step or box about a foot tall. With right foot leading, step both feet down to floor. As soon as left foot hits floor, jump up explosively, pushing off floor with both feet. Repeat for 5 steps. Then repeat with left foot leading the step down. Do 2 sets.

Why it works: This move is really just running, with exaggerated motions that mimic ideal sprinting form—and helps develop speed, power, and explosiveness.

How to do it: On a track or long patch of ground, jog forward with as long a stride as possible. As you move, raise the front knee as high as possible while lifting the back foot (keeping leg straight) behind you. Continue for 10 reps total. Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Recommended Experience: No experience necessary! Anyone can accomplish this training plan.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: This plan is for a new runner who is just getting back into exercise.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a new runner who has been exercising regularly for at least a year, or someone who has completed a few 5Ks or 10Ks and can complete 6 miles in one workout. This plan peaks at 28 miles in a week with a 12-mile long run.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For runners comfortable exercising for at least an hour at a moderate effort. This plan peaks at 32 miles in a week with a 14-mile long run.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a consistent runner used to regularly working out four to five times a week. The plan starts with a 10-mile long run and peaks at 44 to 47 miles a week with a 22-mile long run, helping you average under a 9:10 per mile come race day.

#8821. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a 5K & 10K

Learn how to tackle the approachable distances with the power of walk breaks.

You’ve completed your Magic Mile time trials, dialed in your pacing, and tracked your progress with your run/walk workouts. Now, it’s time to hit the starting line!

The 5K and 10K make for perfect race distances for beginner and veteran run/walkers alike. Whether you’re shooting to cross your first finish line or earn that big PR, you can train for and race toward your goals with the run/walk method powering every step.

The Runner’s World guide, How to Master the Run/Walk Method, helps you get to the finish line and cover two of the most popular and approachable distances. Pair our chapter with one of our dedicated training plans to prepare for your first or fastest 5K or 10K yet.

For beginners, a 5K or 10K serves as a great introduction to using the run/walk training strategy for race day. It’s an opportunity to get accustomed to pacing, structure your intervals, and follow a dedicated run/walk training plan. Once you’ve nailed your 5K/10K training block, you may find it easier to bump up to longer distances and chase after new race goals.

But even if you’re not a racing newcomer, a shorter, approachable distance can be an ideal place to start with run/walk. You might even race faster with the run/walk method than you did previously when running the entire distance.

The shorter the distance, the shorter the walk break will likely be, especially if you’re shooting for a PR. Use your data from your Magic Mile test to determine your goal pace for race day.

Some crucial benefits of using run/walk for a 5K/10K include:

With one of Runner’s World’s dedicated 5K and 10K run/walk training plans, you can build your endurance and speed for tackling your race. Spanning anywhere from six to eight weeks, our plans include three run/walk days, two to three rest or cross-train days, and even additional easy walk and strength training days, depending on the plan. Whether you’re a beginner looking to dip your toes in run/walk or an experienced run/walker chasing after a personal best, we have a plan tailored to your goals.

#8820. Dragon Pose Is the Essential Recovery Stretch For Tight Hips and Back

The yin yoga pose we love to hate, Dragon Pose, is a smart recovery tool for cyclists to improve hip extension. Because cycling involves repetitive hip flexion at the top of the pedal stroke, the primary hip flexor muscle (psoas major) can tighten and become compressed over time, making it harder to access a powerful position off the bike.

The low torso angle on a tri-specific bike provides aerodynamic benefits, but also requires greater hip flexion. In the aero position, the hip flexors, which not only flex the hip but also stabilize the pelvis and lower back, repeatedly contract without fully extending, shortening the muscles and potentially leading to low back pain and stiffness.

Dragon Pose is useful for triathletes who spend a lot of time folded over the handlebars during indoor training through the winter. It can also help you during the warmer months by restoring hip extension and preparing you for the longer stride that running off the bike demands. On the run, you repeatedly load one leg as the hip extends behind the body. Dragon Pose simulates that position, so you step off the bike feeling ready to hit your running stride.

Add Dragon Pose to your recovery routine. Practice this pose after a training ride or race to stretch the hip flexors and improve hip mobility.

Keep in mind that multiple bike fit factors affect hip angle and comfort. This guide provides five elements of a proper bike fit for smoother pedaling and to keep your position within your comfortable hip flexion range.

Improving hip extension can help you feel less compressed on the bike, move more easily through transitions, and ease low-back discomfort.

#8819. Tracksmith Created the Blueprint for Indie Running Brands. Can It Survive Without Its Architect?

The Boston-born apparel company enters a new era following the sudden departure of founder Matt Taylor.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The running journalist Mario Fraioli still remembers the shorts Matt Taylor sent him in 2014, when Taylor was launching a new apparel brand.

Dubbed the Longfellow short, the prototype pair had a button at the waist, they were longer than typical running shorts, and they didn’t have a liner. The idea was, in Fraioli’s telling, that you could go straight from an easy run to a coffee shop and still look presentable. Taylor wanted to know what Fraioli thought.

Fraioli’s reaction? He didn’t love them. The sizing was off for him.

He was, however, intrigued by Taylor’s passion for the apparel and the nascent brand.

“He was super excited,” Fraioli told Runner’s World.

With $35,000 of his savings from a previous endeavor and seed round capital, Taylor launched Tracksmith later in 2014. The initial product line was four men’s items, including those Longfellow shorts and a “Grayboy” T-shirt that mimicked the standard-issue shirt of college athletic departments, plus a spike bag and Meter magazine. Women’s clothing followed about nine months later.

The idea of Tracksmith? Top-quality running apparel for people who were not professional athletes, but trained hard and loved their sport. The names and designs of the products reflected the roots of the sport and Taylor’s reverence for its history.

Frugal runners initially had sticker shock. Tracksmith manufactured its clothing in the U.S., using quality materials, which cost more. But the company was one of the earliest independent running brands selling apparel for serious runners outside of the major shoe companies. Women’s running apparel brand Oiselle had hatched earlier, in 2007.

Tracksmith quickly grew. It added retail locations in Boston and New York, and hundreds of items for sale—including four shoe styles, which were added in 2022.

Now, Taylor has been abruptly pushed out of the company he founded, and industry observers are left wondering if the brand can keep growing without him.

Fraioli, who is now a coach and writer of the Morning Shakeout newsletter, announced the news of Taylor’s departure in his October 13 email, writing that the newsletter would no longer have Tracksmith as a sponsor.

“A big part of my belief in Tracksmith was tied to my belief in Matt’s character, authenticity, and creative vision, and with him gone, I’ve lost confidence in where the brand is headed,” he wrote.

It’s unclear what precipitated the split. Taylor declined to speak to Runner’s World, and former employees were in the dark about the details of his ouster.

Taylor had hired a CEO in January, Jared Carver, a veteran of Converse, to handle the day-to-day operations so he could get back to focusing on the “brand’s vision and creative expression,” according to a company LinkedIn post eight months ago.

In a concurrent post, Taylor wrote: “I didn’t start Tracksmith to be a CEO—I started it to change the way running is presented with the hope of changing how it is perceived. My goals were to build distinct products, tell compelling stories and create a sense of camaraderie, the same you might feel on your cross country team.”

Insiders and one analyst painted a picture of a brand that opened a lane for rival independent retailers to follow suit—and perhaps surpass—Tracksmith. Bandit and Satisfy are two of the brands frequently cited as competitors, especially as the sport has seen enormous growth coming out of COVID.

“Other people have, I think, drafted on their success and made the marketplace more competitive,” said Matt Powell, an industry analyst who is a senior advisor with BCE Consulting. “For any brand, I think it’s hard to stay ahead of the trends, and you never have an unassailable position. Somebody’s always trying to copy you, or do what you do better. That's a big challenge for a small brand.”

It is not known if Tracksmith was profitable, as the company is privately held, and those who were close to Taylor in the company’s early days wondered whether investors and board members were growing impatient. Tracksmith would not talk about the company’s financials or name the members of its board. A Tracksmith representative confirmed Taylor’s exit and that of Matt Pauk, the head of product, who left in August, and offered a statement:

“Matt Taylor, Tracksmith’s founder, has transitioned out of his role with the company and departed Tracksmith. Matt’s unique vision created the Tracksmith we know today, and undoubtedly shaped the culture and business of running. At its core, Tracksmith has always been about people—our team, our partners, the people who push the sport forward, and the runners we serve. These values remain unchanged, and we are confident in our ability to continue building upon the strong foundation established in Tracksmith's 12 years.”

As early employees try to process what happened, they expressed appreciation for what Taylor brought to the industry.

Taylor, they said, was the animating force of the brand. He named the various products after runners in history, and arranged artful photo shoots with athletes in the mist and the mud. His love of the sport was obvious. (He’s still a serious runner. In 2024, Taylor ran the Boston Marathon, at age 47, in 2:43:18.)

Lou Serafini was one of the first employees. Like Fraioli, he didn’t immediately get what the brand was about. At the time, he was working at Heartbreak Hill Running Company before Taylor recruited him to work for Tracksmith.

“I remember being kind of confused,” Serafini said, “not really understanding what they were trying to do. I think most visionary brands have a little bit of that, where it has to be different enough where it makes people kind of scratch their head a little bit.”

Serafini went to Tracksmith’s first Boston Marathon pop-up in 2015, in an empty storefront at 285 Newbury Street, which in 2017 became its permanent home, just blocks from the marathon finish line. (Now pop-ups are a standard part of major marathons with cutting-edge brands; expos are in dreary convention centers, a necessary stop for runners to make to pick up their bibs.)

Serafini’s first job was managing the shop and building a running community there. “That was the first time where I really realized the ethos of the brand,” he said.

When he first started at Tracksmith in 2017, if Serafini saw any runners wearing Tracksmith clothing along the Charles River paths, it was an exciting moment. By the end of his tenure, in 2024, he remembered spotting runners in the brand all over the world.

The best days at Tracksmith always have been Boston Marathon Monday and the Tuesday after. Runners would crowd the shop, pick up a free poster, and get it stamped with their finishing time. “The focus of those days was to sit in the track house and stamp posters and have a 30-second conversation with somebody about how their race went,” Serafini said. In 2018, the year Boston went off in a nor’easter, the Tracksmith headquarters on Newbury became a hospital of sorts for runners trying to get warm.

Two other former employees, in conversations with Runner’s World, echoed Serafini’s assessment of Taylor as a visionary.

One former employee, who asked not to be named, said the committed runner didn’t have much to choose from before Tracksmith, describing the industry’s 2014 offerings as “neon, boring, and not high performance.” Tracksmith took the better products the pros were getting and gave them to amateurs. (And though the price point was initially surprising, these days, in the era of $300 super shoes, it seems reasonable.)

But getting eyeballs on a new business is cash intensive, and Taylor had big, expensive operations, which included stipends for unsponsored Olympic Marathon Trials qualifiers and hosting twilight 5Ks for the fast amateurs looking to run PRs. Real estate on Newbury Street and in Brooklyn does not come cheap, either. A London location that opened in 2023 closed in August.

Without Taylor, does the brand have legs? The fear is that it becomes “performance J.Crew,” preppy running apparel without the investment in the sport.

In response to a question about bolstering the sport, the Tracksmith spokesperson confirmed the company would be continuing with its programming and support of amateur runners through clubs and meets like Tracksmith Stamata, the Twilight series, Hare AC, and the Amateur Support Program. “Nothing has changed or will change there,” the spokesperson said.

But with Taylor’s departure, some see Tracksmith being at a crossroads, caught between funders seeking a return on their investment and fast-growing competition.

“I think a lot of investors, private equity investors, they revere founders and understand that the business that they’re in, particularly one like this, it’s as much of a cultural business as anything else,” said Ryan Eckel, who worked for Tracksmith as the brand president for five years, from 2019 to 2024. “And when you start treating it like it’s making widgets, I think you lose sight [of the culture] and ultimately I think it hurts their investments long term.”

Powell, though, still sees a lane for Tracksmith, especially with consumers who are willing to pay premium prices.

“On one level, I would tell you there's never been a better time to be a small brand, because I think the consumer is looking for unique products,” he said. “But because the consumer is always demanding new and next, that part is really hard for a small brand to execute.”

Sarah Lorge Butler is a writer and editor living in Eugene, Oregon, and her stories about the sport, its trends, and fascinating individuals have appeared in Runner’s World since 2005. She is the author of two popular fitness books, Run Your Butt Off! and Walk Your Butt Off!

#8818. What the New Moon in Scorpio Means for You

The new Moon is a time of new beginnings. And the new Moon in Scorpio brings intensity, magic, and the opportunity to turn your shadows into light. It is one of the most powerful new Moons of the year for manifestation. And it is one of the most powerful of your life for remembering something you were not taught, which is that you are the creator of your life. Not a passenger in it. Not a person waiting for the right conditions, the right timing, or the right permission. The creator.

The Moon starts its cycle on Sunday, November 8, 2026, at 11:03 pm PST.

On the new Moon, the Sun and Moon meet in the sky in the same zodiac sign. They rise and set together, syncing their energy and their vibration. Because the Moon sits between us and the Sun, no sunlight reaches the side of it that we can see, and the Moon seemingly disappears. On the night of a new Moon, only stars light the sky, and we are left with the darkest point of the lunar cycle.

We tend to think of darkness as negative, but it is neither positive nor negative. Darkness is the void that all life and all energy spring from, and it is the seat of creativity. When we close our eyes or enter a dark space, the imagination opens and we gain access to our inner world. Darkness also calms the nervous system. The mind quiets, and in that quiet intuition gets louder. We stop searching for answers and start receiving them. We can see our blocks and our shadows, and we can also see our dreams and our true desires. Darkness gives us a more expansive view of who we are and what we want.

Each new Moon is an invitation to align with that darkness and travel to the center of yourself. Every month you get a chance to learn something new about your own hopes, fears, and patterns, to hear your intuition more clearly, and to fine-tune the energy you need to manifest your intentions.

The zodiac sign the Sun and Moon are traveling through gives each new Moon its theme. This month they meet in Scorpio, and the theme is transformation. The intuitive guidance you receive tonight point toward the same work, turning your shadows into your strengths.

Scorpio is the alchemist of the zodiac, and alchemy is not a metaphor here. It is a description of what you are actually able to do. An alchemist takes one substance and turns it into another. That is what you do with energy every single day, whether or not you know you are doing it. Every emotion moving through you is raw material. Every feeling you have ever called too much, too dark, or too dangerous is power in an unrefined form. Scorpio hands you the ability to take any energy and make something out of it.

That is why this new Moon is such a potent point of creation. It does not just help you set an intention. It reminds you who is doing the setting.

The new Moon in Scorpio has a particular quality this year. It arrives after weeks of retrograde in Mercury as well as Venus and five days before they each station direct. You are not walking into this new Moon guessing. You have been exploring. You have already reread the journals, replayed the conversations, and finally felt the things you had been avoiding. Whatever you were unsure of a month ago, you are closer to sure about now. That honesty is not a side project. It is the raw material of your creation.

Most of us were handed a story about how life works. Something out there decides. Luck decides, or the economy, or your family, or the person who did not choose you, or the version of yourself you were told you would always be. It is a quiet story and it runs underneath almost everything.

You are an energetic being living in an energetic universe, and everything around you responds to the frequency you hold. Your thoughts, your beliefs, and your emotions are not commentary on your life. They are the instructions. What you carry, you call in. What you believe is possible sets the outer edge of what shows up. This is not wishful thinking. It is how energy works, and it is working right now whether you are directing it or not.

The only real question is whether you are creating on purpose.

That is what this new Moon is intended to remind you. Scorpio takes you underneath your conscious mind, where the actual instructions are stored. Your conscious intentions are only half the transmission. Underneath them sit the beliefs you absorbed before you could evaluate them, the conditioning society handed you about what you are allowed to want, the shadows carrying the messages that you are too much, not enough, or not the kind of person things work out for. Those run quietly, and they are broadcasting too.

You can write the most beautiful intention, yet if some part of you believes you are not allowed to have it, that part will keep creating the life you already have. This is not a flaw inherent in you. This is simply information you did not have access to until now.

The new Moon in Scorpio gives you access. It opens the doorway to your subconscious and lets you see what is normally hidden. When you look at them honestly, you learn exactly where your creation has been blocked. You also feel your true desires, including the ones you have never been comfortable admitting. The new Moon is the night to own them without shame.

Owning your power is not a feeling that arrives one day. It is a decision you make, usually before you feel ready. It means you stop waiting for someone to confirm that you are allowed. It means you stop handing your authorship to your circumstances, your history, or your fear. It means you accept that the life in front of you is one you have participated in creating, which sounds like blame for about ten seconds and then becomes the most freeing sentence you will ever say. Because if you participated in creating this, you can participate in creating something else.

Scorpio does not let you own your power through positive thinking. It makes you earn it. The price of admission is honesty. You have to be willing to face your emotions instead of manage them. You have to confront your shadows instead of outsource them to the people who trigger you. You have to look beneath the layers of conditioning that society placed on you, the rules about who you should be, what a woman is allowed to want, how much success is too much, and what it costs to be seen so you can find the truth of who you actually are underneath all of it.

What you find is a creator. One who has been there the whole time. It is through honest self inquiry that we change our lives. That look at ourselves is not always comfortable. And it is the doorway to everything.

This new Moon in Scorpio carries an unusual amount of support and an unusual amount of heat. Here is what is shaping it.

Mercury is still moving backward in Scorpio, five days from stationing direct. It has already passed through its cazimi, so the the new mental cycle is underway. This is why tonight feels clearer than the rest of the retrograde. The excavating is nearly done. Write what you know now, and understand that some of it might want a final edit after November 13th. That is not a problem. Intentions are living things.

On the West Coast, the new Moon in Scorpio chart places retrograde Mercury opposite the Midheaven by 1°29. The Midheaven is the highest point of a chart, the most public part of a life, and directly across from it sits the most private, the root. Mercury is sitting down there in the dark, and it is pointed straight up.

That is the entire season of Scorpio in one image. The truth that you have been finding in private is being aimed at your public life. Something you have understood quietly is preparing to be said out loud. Angles shift with location and time of day, so this placement is exact for those of us on Pacific Time, yet the message reaches all of us. What you uncover in the roots does not stay in the roots.

The fire is coming. A week after the new Moon in Scorpio, Mars, the traditional ruler of Scorpio, meets Jupiter in Leo, and the Sun squares them both right afterward. Mars is at 22°41 Leo and Jupiter is at 25°15 Leo, and they are closing in on each other, which will be exact on November 15th. This is the aspect that defines the second half of Scorpio season.

Mars is the traditional ruler of Scorpio. It is the planet of courage, drive, heat, and the willingness to go first. Jupiter expands whatever it touches, makes it larger, louder, and more generous. When the ruler of this season meets the planet of expansion in the sign of the heart, the message is direct. It is time to expand by walking through the fire. Not around it. Through it.

Scorpio has spent three weeks showing you the truth underneath your life, and some of that truth is uncomfortable. Mars conjunct Jupiter says the discomfort is not a stop sign. It is the doorway. The conversation you have been avoiding, the work you have been circling, the desire you have been embarrassed by, the boundary you have not set. Whatever you are willing to move toward grows faster than it would at any other point this year, because Jupiter is standing right there making everything bigger.

Fire is the element of courage and Leo is the sign of the heart. Put those together and this is not reckless action. It is heart-led action. Ask yourself tonight what you would do if you were not afraid of being seen doing it, and let that shape at least one of your intentions.

Venus at 23°19 Libra makes a sextile to Mars at 22°41 Leo, with an orb of only 0°38. That makes it the tightest aspect of the entire new Moon in Scorpio chart, which gives it unusual weight.

Venus is still retrograde, meaning it is still reviewing what you love and what you are worth. Mars is fire, forward motion, courage. A sextile is an open door. It is an opportunity that asks you to reach for it rather than handing it over. So the heart, in the middle of its honest review, is being offered courage. The two energies are cooperating.

This is the aspect that lets you act on what you have discovered about love. It softens Mars so its action comes with grace, and it gives Venus boldness so its honesty comes with follow through. If there is something you need to say to a person you love, this aspect is the one supporting you.

Venus also sextiles Jupiter at 25°15 Leo, within 1°56. The same open door, this time to expansion.

Venus retrograde in Libra is asking whether your relationships are balanced and whether you value yourself the way you deserve. Jupiter says whatever you decide about that is going to grow. This is a generous, warm aspect that expands the heart. It supports generosity, forgiveness where forgiveness is true, and a genuine enlargement of what you believe you are allowed to want.

Notice that both of these sextiles involve Venus retrograde. The heart is in review and the universe is handing it two supportive angles at once. That is a strong signal. Whatever you have learned since October 3rd about love, worth, and value, this new Moon wants you to live it.

Through the lens of Scorpio, emotions are simply energy. Scorpio does not teach us to get rid of intense feeling. It teaches us to transmute it. Emotions carry raw potential. They are powerful. And they change our lives once we learn to direct them.

The first step is acceptance. As you work with the new Moon in Scorpio, ask yourself whether you are hiding from any emotion. What is it you do not want to face? Suppressed feelings still affect you. It is better to acknowledge it. When you hold an emotion consciously, it loses its power to run your life from the shadows and becomes fuel you can actually use. Feel your courage as you move through your feelings.

Then ask what the energy could become. Anger accepted often becomes motivation and clarity. Fear becomes surrender and trust anchored in the present moment. Anxiety points you toward the shadow you are running from and can turn into calm or even excitement. Sadness becomes creativity and self-acceptance. Attachment becomes gratitude and the ability to move forward. Grief, given space, can become some of the most creative energy a human being can hold.

Feel the fluidity of your emotions tonight, and notice how easily they shift from one state into another when you stop resisting them. Nothing in you is wasted. Nothing in you is disqualifying. It is all material. And you are the artist.

So write intentions you are actually willing to walk toward. Not the safe version. Not the one that sounds reasonable to the part of you that learned to want less. Write from the truth Scorpio has been uncovering, and write from the knowledge that you are capable of manifesting anything you truly believe is possible for you.

That last part is the work. Not the wanting. The believing. Scorpio is here to help you clear everything standing between you and that belief.

You hold your destiny in your hands. You always have. Tonight the universe is inviting you to stop setting it down.

Learn more about the new Moon in Scorpio, including additional astrological insights and journaling prompts, in the Scorpio Season + New Moon Workbook, from which the above is excerpted.

The gold standard business class redemption using British Airways Avios

Picture this: you're seated in a private suite at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, your door clicked shut behind you, a glass of Dom Pérignon on the side table, and a fully flat bed dressed in Westin Heavenly bedding waiting for you. Your partner is in the suite next to yours — and when you lower the center dividing panel, you're sharing a meal in what Qatar Airways calls the "Double Bed" configuration. This is QSuites, and it is, without exaggeration, the single most celebrated business class product in the world. Now here's the number that stops the ChooseFI community cold: a cash ticket in QSuites from New York JFK to Doha DOH typically runs **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's a mortgage payment. That's a family vacation budget. That's real money that compounds in an index fund. With Qatar Avios through the Privilege Club program, that same seat costs **75,000 Avios**. When you do the math against even the conservative cash price of $5,000, you're extracting **6.7 cents per point**. Against the top-end cash price of $10,000, that's **13.3 cents per point** — in a world where most loyalty currencies are "worth" 1 cent each. This is a 6x to 13x multiplier on every point you've earned. Here's what makes this a genuine pricing inefficiency rather than just marketing: Qatar's award chart is fixed and partner-friendly, meaning the number of points required doesn't scale dynamically with cash prices the way most airline programs now do. When demand spikes and cash fares hit $10,000, your award price stays exactly 75,000 Avios. The loyalty program hasn't caught up to the revenue management engine, and that gap is your opportunity. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is the travel rewards philosophy in its purest form: redirect real spending you're already doing onto the right cards, accumulate points as a byproduct, and convert those points into experiences that would otherwise require liquidating investments. The QSuites redemption is the pinnacle of that system — a **nearly free** business class experience that delivers more luxury per point than almost anything else in the world of travel rewards.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegant once you see it, and once you see it, you'll start recognizing similar patterns everywhere in the loyalty space.

Qatar prices its own flights in its own currency — and that currency is cheap to acquire.

Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios are the program's native points currency. When Qatar sets award prices for its own operated flights, including QSuites, it prices them in a way that's competitive and fixed — not subject to the dynamic pricing algorithms that have made programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles increasingly unpredictable. Seventy-five thousand Avios for a transatlantic or transoceanic business class seat is a published, stable price. Qatar isn't trying to extract maximum value from every award booking; they want to keep the program attractive to drive loyalty.

The critical insight is this: you don't need to earn Qatar Avios through Qatar flights. You can transfer them directly from credit card programs you're probably already using.

Citi ThankYou Points → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — This is the fastest and cleanest route. Transfers from Citi to Qatar are instant, meaning you can search for availability, confirm the seat is bookable, and transfer in the same session without risk. For anyone holding a Citi Premier or Citi Prestige card, this is a direct pipeline to QSuites.

Capital One Miles → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — A strong secondary option. Capital One's transfer to Qatar takes 2–5 days, so you'll want to confirm availability first and ideally put the seat on a 24-hour hold if possible before initiating the transfer. Venture X and Venture card holders have access to this path.

Marriott Bonvoy Points → Qatar Avios at 3:1 — This is the least efficient path. The 3:1 ratio means you're effectively diluting your Bonvoy points, and transfers take 1–5 days. Use this only as a top-off strategy if you're a few thousand Avios short and have Bonvoy points sitting idle.

This is a huge deal that deserves its own callout. Qatar charges zero fuel surcharges on Qatar-operated award flights. This is not universal — British Airways Avios, for example, can pile on $700+ in carrier-imposed surcharges on longhaul awards. With Qatar Privilege Club, what you see is what you pay: 75,000 Avios plus the government taxes, which are typically modest.

Qatar allows stopovers in Doha and open-jaw routing on award tickets. This means you can build a trip that stops in Doha — giving you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, one of the world's premier airport lounges — before continuing to a final destination. The stopover rule turns a single award redemption into a multi-destination experience, a classic FI travel rewards optimization move.

This is the cardinal rule of all transfer-based award bookings: never transfer points until you've confirmed the seat exists. Go to qatarairways.com and run a search using the "Privilege Club" award booking tool. Select Business Class, enter your route (e.g., JFK to DOH), and look for QSuites availability specifically — you'll see the aircraft type and cabin configuration in the search results. QSuites is typically available on Boeing 777-300ER and A380 flights, not all Qatar aircraft, so confirm the product before you get excited.

Qatar Privilege Club opens its award booking window at 361 days in advance. QSuites availability is genuinely limited — this is a Difficulty 2/5 on the availability scale — and the best seats disappear quickly, especially for peak travel periods and popular routes like JFK–DOH. Set a calendar reminder now for exactly 361 days before your target departure date and be ready to book the moment the window opens. This single habit separates people who get QSuites awards from people who watch them disappear.

You'll need 75,000 Qatar Avios per person. Check your current balances across:

Decide your primary transfer source before you need the points. If you're using Capital One, initiate the transfer 5–7 days before you want to book to give yourself buffer time.

If you don't have a Privilege Club account, create one at qatarairways.com/privilege-club — it's free and takes minutes. Once you have your account number, you can link it as a transfer destination in your Citi, Capital One, or Marriott account.

Once you've confirmed availability and are ready to book, log into your credit card rewards portal and initiate the transfer to your Qatar Privilege Club account number. For Citi, this will post instantly. For Capital One, monitor your Avios balance over the next 2–5 days.

Return to qatarairways.com, log into your Privilege Club account, and book the award using your Avios balance. Have your passport and payment method ready for the taxes and fees. Confirm the aircraft type one final time at booking to ensure you're on a QSuites-equipped aircraft.

If you can't find two seats together, try splitting the booking into two single-seat reservations, then request to link them. Also try ±3 days on either side of your target dates — availability patterns are uneven. Calling Qatar's Privilege Club phone line (rather than booking online) occasionally surfaces inventory not shown on the website.

British Airways Avios uses a distance-based award chart rather than a flat-rate chart, which creates a pricing inefficiency on long-haul routes operated by Qatar Airways. While BA prices short-haul flights competitively, flights over 4,000 miles to Qatar and beyond land in a pricing band that dramatically undervalues the QSuites product. Qatar Airways is a oneworld alliance member, which means BA Avios can book any Qatar-operated award flight. The key insight is that you are booking through BA's system using BA's pricing, but flying on Qatar's hardware — and Qatar's business class product is in a completely different league than BA's Club World. This mismatch between the booking partner's award chart and the operating airline's product quality is exactly what makes this a sweet spot.

Let's build a real booking so the numbers stop being abstract.

The Route: New York JFK → Doha DOH on Qatar Airways, Boeing 777-300ER, QSuites Business Class.

Cash Price: A one-way QSuites ticket on this route runs roughly $5,000–$8,000 depending on timing and booking window. For a couple, you're looking at $10,000–$16,000 in cash — a number that probably makes the FI-minded reader physically uncomfortable.

Award Price: 75,000 Qatar Avios per person, one-way. Taxes and fees on Qatar-operated awards are minimal — typically under $100 — because Qatar charges no fuel surcharges. A couple flies QSuites for 150,000 Avios plus roughly $150 in taxes total.

The CPP: At the midpoint cash value of $6,500, you're getting 8.7 cents per Avios — nearly nine times what most people assume a loyalty point is worth. At $10,000, you're at 13.3 cents per point. Even at the conservative end, 6.7 cents per point makes this one of the top redemptions in the entire travel rewards ecosystem.

You arrive at JFK and access Qatar's partner lounge before departure — a preview of what's to come. Once aboard, you're shown to a fully enclosed private suite with a sliding door, direct aisle access from every seat, a large personal screen, and a seat that converts to a lie-flat bed stretching over 6 feet. The bedding is genuine Westin Heavenly quality. You and your travel companion request the Double Bed configuration — the center divider lowers, and you're sharing a full-width sleeping surface mid-flight.

Dining is a la carte, on-demand — no set meal times. The wine list is legitimate. The service is attentive without being intrusive.

If you've added a Doha stopover to your ticket, you deplane into Al Mourjan Business Lounge — a cavernous, beautifully designed space with dedicated dining, shower suites, and quiet zones. It is, consistently, one of the top-rated airport lounges on earth.

This is the experience your 75,000 points buy. No amount of economy class upgrades gets you here.

Prioritize earning Citi ThankYou Points if this redemption is a goal.

Do this: Add a Doha stopover. Qatar allows stopovers in Doha on award tickets. If your ultimate destination is beyond Doha — whether that's Asia, Africa, or the Indian subcontinent — building in a Doha layover costs nothing extra in points and gives you access to the Al Mourjan Business Lounge, which is worth experiencing on its own terms.

Avoid this: Using Marriott Bonvoy as your primary transfer path. The 3:1 ratio means you need 225,000 Bonvoy points to get 75,000 Avios. Marriott points are valuable for hotel redemptions — burning them at a 3:1 ratio for airline miles is rarely optimal unless you have a massive surplus.

Avoid this: Waiting for a sale or hoping for better availability. Qatar doesn't run award sales. The award chart is fixed, and availability only decreases over time on popular routes. The readers who say "I'll book when something comes up" are the ones sharing their story about the year they almost flew QSuites.

Remember: Miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Keep your Privilege Club account active with at least one earning or redemption activity every 36 months. A single small transaction resets the clock.

This redemption is purpose-built for the ChooseFI couple or family who has spent a year or two being intentional about travel rewards and is ready to cash in on the premium cabin experience they've been building toward. If you and a partner each hold a Citi Premier or Capital One Venture X and have been putting real spend on those cards, 150,000 combined points for two QSuites seats is a realistic 12–18 month accumulation target.

Minimum points required: 75,000 Qatar Avios per person. For a couple, plan on 150,000 Avios. Have this balance confirmed before you begin the booking process.

This redemption earns a **Moderate** difficulty rating, and that's honest. The value is a 5/5 — there is almost no better use of transferable points in the entire loyalty ecosystem. But you'll earn that value. **What makes it hard:** First, **availability is legitimately limited.** QSuites seats don't sit open for weeks. Qatar releases a constrained number of award seats, and on popular routes, they go fast. This isn't a system you can approach casually. You need to search early and book decisively. Second, **the booking process has multiple steps.** Unlike a straightforward Chase Ultimate Rewards hotel redemption, this requires confirming availability on one platform, identifying points across potentially multiple credit card programs, executing a transfer, and booking on a separate airline's website. Each step has its own timing consideration. Third, **aircraft confirmation requires attention.** Not every Qatar flight is a QSuites flight, and the average traveler can easily book Business Class on a non-QSuites aircraft without realizing the difference. **Three tips to overcome the challenge:** 1. **Build your Citi ThankYou balance specifically for this redemption.** Instant transfers eliminate the timing risk that makes other transfer paths stressful. 2. **Set your 361-day calendar alert today**, even if your travel date is hypothetical. Practice the search so you know exactly what to look for. 3. **Use Qatar's own website for searching**, not third-party tools — Qatar award inventory is most accurately displayed on qatarairways.com. If you've successfully booked a domestic partner award before, you can absolutely do this. The moderate difficulty reflects the preparation required, not insurmountable complexity.

Log into your Qatar Privilege Club account and search for business class award space on your desired route. Look for flights showing QSuites availability — check the aircraft type (A350-1000 or 777-300ER with QSuites). This confirms what BA Avios can book since both programs are in oneworld.

Not all Qatar 777s have QSuites. Check SeatGuru or Qatar's fleet page to confirm the specific aircraft configuration. Routes to major US gateways (JFK, IAD, ORD, IAH, LAX, DFW) typically operate QSuites-equipped aircraft.

Once you confirm availability, transfer the required Avios from Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant), Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days), Capital One (1-2 days), Citi ThankYou (instant), or Bilt (1-2 days). Transfer only after confirming space.

Search for the same Qatar-operated flight on ba.com using your Avios. If the flight appears, book online. If you cannot find it online, call BA Executive Club to book partner award flights — agents can see availability that may not display on the website.

British Airways charges approximately 70,000 Avios one-way for business class from the US to Doha on Qatar Airways-operated flights, plus taxes and fees typically between $30 and $80. Return flights are priced the same, making a round trip roughly 140,000 Avios total.

Yes, but finding 4 business class award seats on the same flight is challenging. Your best strategy is to search 330 days in advance when availability first opens, or check within 2-3 weeks of departure for last-minute releases. Consider splitting across two flights departing the same day if needed.

QSuites features a fully enclosed suite with a closing door, a lie-flat bed, Bric's amenity kit with Diptyque products, and the option to create a Buddy Suite by lowering the partition between center seats. Standard Qatar business class uses a reverse herringbone or staggered layout without doors — still a solid product but a significant step below QSuites.

No. When you book Qatar Airways-operated flights using British Airways Avios, there are no fuel surcharges. You will pay the Avios cost plus minimal taxes and airport fees, typically $30 to $80 depending on the route. This is one of the key reasons the Avios route is preferred over booking through some other programs that impose carrier-imposed surcharges.

Qatar QSuites via British Airways Avios is the single best business class redemption available to ChooseFI community members. At roughly 70,000 transferable points for a $6,000 or more experience, the value per point is exceptional. The product itself — a fully enclosed suite with a door, lie-flat bed, and world-class service — redefines what business class can be. Whether you are heading to Doha, the Maldives, or Southeast Asia, routing through Qatar's hub gives you access to a global network at sweet spot pricing. Start searching 330 days out, have your transfer partners ready, and book the moment you find availability. This is the redemption that converts skeptics into travel rewards enthusiasts.

#8816. The Top 9 Running Shorts That Prevent Chafing, Store All the Snacks, and Keep You Cool at Every Pace

Our editors tested several bottoms to determine the top shorts for runners.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

As a year-round shorts runner, I’m an expert in the good, the bad, and the miserable when it comes to running shorts. Comfort, potential for chafing, and storage are front-of-mind when I’m shopping for a pair. When runners look for their next pair, there are all kinds of questions to consider: What’s the right inseam to prevent friction? Are the pockets big enough to store my phone, sunscreen, and gels?

For all my hot summer runners and year-round leg barers, this guide is for you. We go over the best shorts that’ll have drawer life well beyond the first fall leaf, plenty of race-day storage for all the gels and gummies, and other features to look out for when shopping for bottoms.

Runner’s World has been testing products since 1966, vetting the best gear for runners so they can train hard, race their best, and enjoy all the other runs throughout their lifetime. Over the course of three weeks, we had our staff test several shorts to narrow down the best men’s and women’s bottoms during their workouts, from trail running to marathon training, from speed to recovery.

The RW team includes runners of varying levels (not all of us have run a 26.2!), ages, body types, heights, and running goals. We considered well-known shoe brands’ offerings, activewear-centric apparel, and lesser-known brands to give you a range of shorts styles and pricing. Our input lends a well-rounded collection of feedback so we can find shorts for every type of runner.

We awarded Tracksmith’s Session Shorts in our annual Gear of the Year, because they have all the essential features, including comfort, storage, and adjustability. The older version had a zippered side pocket that positioned the girth to the front, causing whatever you stored inside to hit your thigh as you ran.

The newest Session remedies that issue, with the girth set to the back. The waistband is also updated; it’s more flexible and has an internal drawstring, unlike the previous Session. The “Session 3.0” is great for training and racing; three rear drop-in gel pockets make fueling easy when you’re hours on the road, and the silky material provides plenty of airflow.

Shop Men’s at tracksmith.com | Shop Women’s at tracksmith.com

The RC Essential 3” is a short made for racing—at a Best Value price. The amount of storage alone makes the RC Essential a winner; individual compartments along the waistband make separating your gels easier (no more caf or no-caf surprises midrun). The four drop-in compartments are complete with a zippered rear pocket for storing discards (though the pocket is large enough to store a phone, doing so results in jostling).

I tested the short and loved the short inseam and split-leg design. The lightweight, quick-drying fabric alone makes these shorts not a distraction, but I can’t help thinking the lack of fabric on my thighs makes me stride better—and faster.

Shop Men’s at newbalance.com | Shop Women’s at newbalance.com

Runners flock to the cheap Amazon brand Baleaf because its threads are comfy and check all the boxes when it comes to affordable, functional activewear. Take the men’s Running Athletic Shorts: these bottoms are adjustable, breathable, have inclusive sizing, lots of storage, and just feel dang comfy.

“The shorts performed very well,” said a tester. “My first time wearing these was at a local 5K in August, and the shorts did not hold me back in any way. The drawstring made the shorts nice and secure. I carried only my keys in the zipper pocket on the back, and there were no issues there either. I continued running in them on various types of runs following the race and it was more of the same. Great performance and very comfortable.”

Sweat-wicking mesh briefs provide support, while an internal drawcord allows you to adjust the waistband to ensure a secure, nonslip fit. You may need to tighten that drawcord too, since these shorts run large. They also run quite long; if you usually wear a 30-inch inseam or shorter in pants, these are not the shorts for you.

There are two side pockets and one lower back zipper pocket; all are sizable for a phone, in case you’re a thigh phone pocket runner or the more advanced lower back pocket runner.

These Old Navy shorts are at a jaw-dropping price—and our testers were impressed with how they performed on their runs. Even though the inseam is only 3 inches, Assistant Commerce Photo Editor Saba Ahmed reported no thigh chafing on her runs. “These are definitely the shortest inseam running shorts I own and I surprisingly really enjoyed running in these, especially on an almost 80-degree sunny day!” she said.

The elastic waistband has a drawstring for adjustability. The poly-spandex material felt especially breathable, even on very hot days. They also dry extremely quickly. These are Senior Gear Editor Cat Bowen’s shorts of choice to wear on rainy summer days. The only downside with the shorts was the one side pocket. “I was pretty confused about why there was only one pocket on one side,” said Ahmed. “I appreciated that it had a zip, but I found myself trying to find a pocket on the left side as well and then remembering there was none.”

The 2-in-1 short is a divisive topic (like wearing underwear under your shorts), but tester and RW Editor Matt Rudisill said these shorts by Janji felt like running in half tights.

“The tights portion fit very well,” he said. “Not constricting and not loose. They found that perfect middle ground where they’re snug but they didn’t cause any issues (no chafing, sliding around, etc.). The pocket situation was fantastic.”

The Multi Short could very well be our Best for Storage short, as well. The waistband has five compartments for all the gels, gummies, and Sour Patch Kids you crave on your runs. The legs have snug side pockets to store your phone.

Rudisill was delighted to find one of the waistband pockets had an attached S-Biner MicroLock carabiner inside to stash your keys.

For Your Consideration: Ladies, if you want a 2-in-1 yourselves, we also tested the Ciele DLYShort 4” Long Brief 2, which changed Editor Ashley Tysiac’s mind about 2-in-1 shorts.

“Not only were they comfortable for any workout duration or speed, but I never had to worry about discomfort or chafing,” she said. “In a way, they gave me peace of mind. I could throw them on, and knew that they would feel great and perform well, no matter the workout, distance, or pace.”

Have you fallen victim to the dreaded crotch sweat mark postrun? Enter the Bandit Vanisher collection, which promises threads that don’t show sweat.

Both the men’s and women’s shorts have seven waterproof pockets so your phone won’t become sweat-logged, because even though these shorts don’t show marks, they still retain moisture. The cuffs also have silicone grippers so the legs won’t slide up.

“The apparel does exactly as it promises: it makes sweat vanish,” Features Senior Editor Pavlína Černá wrote in her review. “I ran 9 miles in 80-degree heat one weekend and 10 miles the weekend after, and while my skin was glistening, there was not a single sweat mark on my outfit.”

Shop Men’s at bandit.com | Shop Women’s at bandit.com

The Hotty Hot High-Rise is a classic flow short that we love for all kinds of workouts—especially fast ones. The cut is so flattering with mesh panels on the sides and reflective detail in case you’re an early riser or dusk dancer.

We wish there was more room for storage, but the liner stash pocket and zippered pocket on the side provide just enough room to stash keys and a card.

The flat, high waistband has an interior infinity cord for adjusting.

For men, we like the Pace Breaker Lined Short, which comes in five-, seven-, and nine-inch inseams. The short is updated for a comfier fit around the waist and low-bounce hand pockets.

The airy Smartwool Active Lined achieves a miracle you rarely see in short-seamed, flowy shorts: it doesn’t cause chafing. Senior Gear Editor Cat Bowen praised the shorts for their ample storage room, breathable liner, and ability to stay put as she runs.

Bowen reported no bunching or riding up of the leg openings. An added bonus: the shorts launder well without falling apart. And even though you should wash your shorts after a sweaty session (read: bacteria), the liner is efficient at wicking moisture and not gathering odor—so only you know you’re late on laundry day.

Shop Men’s at smartwool.com | Shop Women’s at smartwool.com

While testing the Twilight Short Tights, I honestly couldn’t stop brushing the palms of my hands against my thighs. The textured fabric, a nylon/elastane blend, is ultrasoft.

I wore the shorts during my marathon training and appreciated the storage they provided for fuel and my phone.

Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough was surprised at the Twilight’s generous storage space despite having only three pockets when he tested the men’s version, the Twilight Half Tights.

“Though it may not seem like it at first glance, the Tracksmith Half Tights have great storage capacity,” he said. “Their three pockets (two drop-in side pockets and a rear zippered pocket) look skinny—very skinny. The side pockets are just over 2.5 inches wide, and the rear pocket runs just over 3.5 inches at its max depth. But the secret to the pockets is their stretch. My phone is more than three inches wide, but it was still able to fit in the side pocket.”

Shop Men’s at tracksmith.com | Shop Women’s at tracksmith.com

It’s about comfort and intention. Some runners prefer a bike short (compression or half-tight, as these shorts are also called) to ensure the legs don’t ride up. Many brands add grip tape on the inside of the cuffs to make the legs stay secure.

On the other hand, a flowy short (or loose or relaxed fit) provides more airflow and can come in a split-leg style, which some runners prefer for racing to enhance mobility.

Inseams can be as little as 1.25 inches or as long as 10 inches for maximum coverage. Some runners prefer a longer inseam to prevent the dreaded thigh chafing, while others want as little leg coverage as possible for racing.

To run with underwear or commando is a question RW staff heatedly discusses every so often. The right liner wicks away moisture and doesn’t cause a wedgie or camel toe midrun. If you prefer to run with underwear, who’s to know? But there are some shorts out there sans liner.

Another hot topic besides running with or without underwear: Storing your phone in the thigh or back waistband pocket? If you run with a phone, location is one thing to consider as well as security. After all, no one wants to feel their phone constantly hitting their leg as they run.

Brands are also finally understanding that both men and women need pockets. Some shorts come with 360 waistband storage; others have deep side pockets. Lastly, if you carry small valuables like keys or an ID, you’ll want to consider zippered or envelope pockets over drop-ins.

We included some options for runners on a budget, but we understand our top picks are up there in cost. These shorts are made of durable, sweat-wicking materials that should last you for races and years to come. But we understand not every runner can afford such an investment.

Some ways to make your shorts last longer are washing without fabric softener (you should do this with all workout clothes so it doesn’t degrade sweat-wicking capabilities) and air drying.

How do I prevent my inner thighs from chafing?

If your runs tend to end with chafed thighs, my first recommendation is to try some shorts with a longer inseam. I find that a 7-inch, or half-tight length, usually provides enough coverage to prevent thigh rubbing. Bike shorts with interior strips on the cuffs also help by keeping the legs from riding up.

If you don't like a long inseam, you can also apply Vaseline or BodyGlide to trouble spots, which will minimize friction where you usually chafe.

Is running in shorts in the winter bad for your knees?

As a runner who resists wearing leggings for as long as I can before hypothermia sets in, I spoke with Shane M. Davis, MD, when I noticed how my knees ached on winter runs. Davis, who is a physiatrist of non-operative medicine at Tufts University School of Medicine in Boston, told me that the cold affects the elasticity of your tissues. You may also experience arthritic joint pain as the weather changes due to decreased blood flow.

If, like me, you're adamant about training in shorts when there’s snow on the ground, one way to prevent joint pain is doing dynamic stretches, like high knees and toe-and-heel walking, before your run.

Should I go commando or wear underwear when wearing running shorts?

This is a hot topic at RW HQ: Some shorts have built-in support, but you should definitely try them on before making a commitment. If you're already getting a wedgie before you start to run, they’re going to be a nuisance during a workout.

Some brands make no-liner shorts, so you can wear underwear instead of an attached liner. Alternatively, 2-in-1 shorts offer more coverage like a bike short with a flowy outer layer for added protection.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.
