#8775. Ilona Maher Now Looking to Take Rugby—and Girls’ Fitness—to the Next Level

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

During the 2024 Paris Olympics, USA women’s team rugby player Ilona Maher suddenly became a household name.

“I think for some people when they get famous, maybe it changes who they are and who they believe themselves to be,” Maher tells Muscle & Fitness. “I just never found that to be me.I think I’m kind of a similar person I was before the Paris Olympics.”

The bronze-medal winner posed on the cover of Sports Illustrated shortly after the games wrapped. From there, Maher went on to compete on Dancing with the Stars, launch a successful podcast, and secure major partnerships with brands like Maybelline New York, Adidas and Burn Boot Camp.

Although it seems like all eyes are on Maher, very few of her fans are watching her while she’s on the field that made her a celebrity.

“Honestly, it doesn’t frustrate me because we don’t have enough places for them to watch rugby,” Maher says. “So I would tell you to watch rugby. I could tell you there’s games on this weekend, but it’s not like you tune into one game, then I’ll keep watching that team.”

Despite the lack of eyeballs on the game, much like Caitlin Clark in the WNBA, Maher is credited for helping put the game back on the map and even boosting ticket sales.

“That’s where it’s hard for me is that there’s really not a lot of opportunities to watch the game,” Maher explains. “And when they want to watch me play—a lot of people would love to watch me play, but I play in places like South Africa and then I go to Perth. So if you want to wake up at 4 in the morning to watch me play the first two minutes of a game…”

Although Maher admits it’s a hard pill to swallow, she doesn’t let it discourage her and remains hopeful for the future of the sport.

“It’s a very tough thing in that I want to get more people in. I think more people should be in, but there we need more opportunities or need more things for [fans], games and in terms for them to be able to watch that are on home soil, too.”

The San Diego resident currently has her sights set on the 2028 L.A. summer games so all of her other projects get planned around her training for Team USA.

“We have meetings throughout the day and rehab and stretching to ramp the body up and whatnot,” explains Maher. “I have to do whatever timing my team says. I’m not an individual athlete that can build my life around my podcast. I have to build the podcast and everything else around my training life, I have to be in the gym at 8 a.m. with all the girls. It’s not worth it to miss a day of training when maybe something else will come up, because I do think I’m a team athlete through and through.”

Despite knowing her obligations to her teammates come first, Maher understands there’s a balance, especially to keep people intrigued in the sport for the upcoming olympic games.

“If my girls are grinding, I want to be out there grinding with them and not just taking the easy road,” Maher says. “But it is important for me to also focus on things like the podcasts or speaking, because that’s how I financially live the life I do.”

Maher admits she’s become so popular that she’s had to pass on some things to prioritize her love of the game.

“I have to say no to a lot of opportunities,” Maher says. “I will get invited to this cool event and I just have to pick my battles.”

Maher admits her newfound fame has created a “pretty hefty schedule,” her physical training remains her top priority. Her training schedule includes two daily on-field sessions along with a gym workout that can include speed and skills work, and up to about 20,000 steps of running. She also adds four days fo weightroom work, focusing explosive movements. The days she’s out of the gym, Maher is recovering and prepping to repeat the same schedule the following week.

The athlete says she thrives on pushing her limits in the weight room, especially with squats and bench presses.

“I like the ones where you really get to like to test yourself and see how much more you can do,” Maher says.

Despite being a professional athlete, Maher admits she still has her own personal wins in the gym.

“I do love dumb bell incline bench press,” explains Maher. “Where you do a weight and then you’re like, ‘I think I can do a little bit more weight!’ and you put a little more weight and you did and you’re like, ‘OK, I can do a little more weight. Those are the moments where I really love being in the gym”.

Off the field, Maher knows girls everywhere are looking up to her for guidance and empowerment, which is why she partnered with Burn Boot Camp to spread the message about their 45-minute high-intensity fitness classes.

“I just watched it and the energy and the way that these women came to this class, so excited to be there,” says Maher. They were high-fiving each other and they were getting stronger and it was the sort of community that I’m trying to foster and I think create, and that’s why I decided to work with this brand. Because I have so many girls who message me saying, ‘I wanna get strong. I wanna be strong like you. I just don’t know where to start and I’m intimidated by the gym.’

#8774. The Best Power Racks of 2025: Our Top Picks for Strength Training

Our expert shares his experience, and an Olympic lifting titleholder shares advice on choosing the best option so you get stronger with this home gym staple.

Written by Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Stephen Sheehan, CPT Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

A power rack allows you to safely perform weightlifting exercises like barbell squats and bench presses, without a spotter, in your home gym. Add-on accessories like pull-up bars, dip stations, and resistance bands can help you get the most out of your power rack, giving you the tools for a versatile full-body workout.

Whether you have limited space or are looking for a budget-friendly power rack, there are options that may work for you. We compiled a list of the best power racks for your home gym with all the details you need to find the right equipment to take your fitness routine to the next level in 2024. Shane Sevcik—a USAW-1 (USA Weightlifting) certified coach, current USA Weightlifting Foundation board member, state record holder, and Masters Pan American and World title holder—also shares his insights into what to look for in power racks.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

The REP Fitness PR-1000 Power Rack has a four-post frame made from 14-gauge steel with laser-cut holes spaced two inches apart. There are two pull-up bars—one is 1.25 inches thick, and the other is two inches thick—so you can do accessory work such as pull-ups and grip exercises without using additional space or buying a separate piece of equipment. The pull-up bars are strategically placed on the rack, spanning the front and back posts, contributing to the overall stability. There are built-in weight storage pegs on the back base for additional sturdiness. You can customize the rack using multiple accessory options such as safety straps, a dip station, and more.

Tester Brandon Lunsford, C.P.T., CF-L1, used this rack to do exercises like squats, bench press, strict press, pull-ups, and more for almost two years. He describes it as an intermediate or beginner rack and noticed movement while un-racking 350 pounds. “The rack held the weight just fine, but there was some swaying after I removed the bar. I’d recommend it to a beginner or someone who doesn’t lift to that capacity because I was happy with it otherwise.”

We like that the PR-1000 comes with chrome-coated safeties extending past the rack, offering an additional place for a barbell. The numbered uprights allow you to adjust the safeties or J-hooks quickly and never have to worry about your bar being crooked. “The J-hooks were easy to move, and the hole spacing of one inch is adequate to get the bar lined up where you need it,” Lunsford says. “I can attest to the functionality of the safeties; they worked great for me when I failed a heavy bench over 250 pounds.”

The Titan Fitness T-3 Series Power Rack is a wall-mounted power rack that folds to a closed position, which only sticks out five inches from the wall. The bolt-down uprights and side bracings keep it stable, so you feel comfortable lifting weights to 1,100 pounds. Those who want to use the dual pull-up bars for dynamic movements such as kipping pull-ups or toes-to-bar benefit from the added stability the floor attachment provides. The rear pull-up bar is two inches thick, and the front pull-up bar is the industry standard of 1.25 inches thick.

This rack is made from 11-gauge steel and features two-inch by three-inch tubing. Typically, newer racks have three-inch by three-inch steel tubing, so attachments from other brands may not work. Lunsford says, “A rack is an essential piece of fitness equipment. What sets them apart is the build, value, and accessories. A full power rack of this style with a weight capacity of 1,100 pounds for around $400 is an excellent bang for the buck.”

Lunsford says the brand uses manufacturing processes to elevate the overall quality. “The holes are laser cut instead of punched, and the brand uses robot welders instead of guides operated by humans.” This technique allows for more efficiency, precision, and consistency in enhanced craftsmanship. The laser-cut holes are two inches apart, and the bench and clean pull zone have Westside hole spacing—holes in the upright that are closer together for more precise positioning.

Free shipping is available on all Titan products, and a one-year warranty covers manufacturing defects and issues that may arise while using the product. One callout we have is the rack does not come with safety arms, which range in price from $90 to $190, depending on which type you get. The rackable weight capacity is 1,100 pounds, but the included J-cups are rated up to 1,000 pounds, so if you want to move heavier weights, you’ll need to upgrade the J-cups.

Titan offers several accessories for purchase separately, including safety bars or straps, stabilizer feet, spotter arms, pin and pipe safety set, or an extension kit to upgrade to six uprights. Other customization options include choosing from a black, red, or blue rack color, two rack depths and heights, or adding a four-pack of weight plate holders.

At only 72 inches tall (six feet), the REP PR-1050 Short Power Rack is a solution for home gyms with low ceilings, such as garages or basements. This equipment has a sturdy yet compact footprint of 58 by 48 inches and supports up to 700 pounds.

While this power rack is short, it provides a solid range of features. It comes with dual pull-up bars (supporting up to 400 pounds), numbered upright holes spaced two inches apart, rear base weight horns, chrome-coated safeties, and plastic-lined J-cups. It’s also compatible with various add-on attachments, including cannonball grips for grip strength exercises and landmine attachments for exercises including landmine presses and rows.

The Fringe Sport Retractable Power Rack is an excellent option if your garage or home gym is tight on space because it is compact and easily stored. This convenient home power rack can be retracted and folded inward or outward for storage. When retracted, it only sticks out five inches from the wall. It has a compact base and can support up to 800 pounds.

The uprights are two-by-three-inch 11-gauge steel and feature Westside spacing in the bench zone. You can set the rack’s 1.25-inch diameter pull-up bar to multiple heights. It’s 91 inches tall, which may not be ideal for low ceilings.

The unit comes with J-hooks coated with ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMW), a strong, abrasion-resistant material, to protect your barbell. Fringe Sport provides an installation video to help guide you through the installation of this power rack. It includes four mounting brackets and six detent pins to lock the rack in position.

The Sunny Health & Fitness Power Zone Strength Rack Power Cage Squat Rack has a pulley system attachment for lat pulldowns and adjustable resistance you can load with weight plates up to the 352-pound limit. You can use the lat pulldown attachment for exercises like upright rows and curls. When you aren’t using the attachment, built-in safety hook latches provide easy storage for the top long or short lever bar.

This power rack has features to help you get a well-rounded workout. The adjustable angled pull-up bar has four positions, including wide and narrow grips. The J-hooks have 18 vertical height settings, and the spotter bars with safety latches help you squat with heavier weights. There are six resistance band pins, for additional resistance against the bar.

The Rogue Fitness R-3 Power Rack is the most compact option in Rogue’s R-Series and is an excellent option for a home garage gym. This power rack comes in two height options—90.4 inches or 84.4 inches—so it works in garages and home gyms with low ceilings.

This rack is made of heavy-duty 11-gauge steel with Westside spacing (a type of spacing that allows for granular control of bar placement, such as barbells and safety bars) through the bench in a one-inch pattern and two-inch spacing above and below the bench. The unit is compatible with various Rogue Infinity Series add-on attachments, such as the Rogue Matador, fully adjustable dip handles, or a bar hanger for barbell weight storage.

The unit has a 43-inch pull-up bar, infinity J-cups, pin/pipe safeties, and four band pegs. You can customize this rack by adding a bar, bench, or plates to your purchase on the Rogue Fitness website. This unit is versatile enough for various exercises, including low rows, pull-ups, chin-ups, squats, bench presses, powerlifting, CrossFit, and Olympic lifting.

The Fitness Reality Squat Rack Power Cage has an official weight capacity of 800 pounds. This unit can help anyone hit their goals, from beginners to elite powerlifters.

Like all good squat racks, the Fitness Reality Squat Rack Power Cage has solid steel safety arms rather than hollow tubes. It features two rear stability bars. Thanks to 19 adjustable height levels, you can use the unit for various exercises besides squats, including pull-ups, chin-ups, bench presses, and overhead presses. And it’s $299, the most affordable option on our list.

It has a multi-grip pull-up bar and two 23-inch safety bars with chrome locks. While it doesn’t come with J-hooks, dip bars, or plate storage attachments, one-inch holes allow you to use this equipment with standard-sized attachments.

A power rack—or power cage—has four uprights designed to serve as a base for powerlifting, Olympic lifting, and other strength training. They are commonly used with a barbell but may have optional attachments for non-barbell exercises using cables or body weight. A full power rack allows athletes to lift inside or outside the cage. Half racks have two uprights, so athletes must lift outside the rack because there is less depth.

Research links strength training, including weightlifting, to long-term health benefits like reducing disease.

A power rack provides equipment, like safety bars, to help you lift heavy weights safely without a spotter. Some power racks come with add-on attachments, such as pull-up bars and dip bars, to help you get a well-rounded workout. Additionally, most power racks are compatible with accessories you can buy for an extra price to customize your workout for your needs.

Exercisers use a power rack for strength training, Olympic lifting, and powerlifting. Additional attachments, such as a dip station or pull-up bar, allow you to use it for bodyweight exercises. Some have pulley systems for other resistance exercises.

Correctly using a power rack can successfully enhance strength training. “It’s all about consistency,” Sevcik says. “Make sure you have some kind of progressive overload built into your programming.”

Power racks provide a safe lifting experience, which is of utmost importance, especially if you plan on training alone. The safety straps, pins, or arms—also called safeties—are a critical safety feature. “One of my biggest pet peeves is when I see people who don’t know how to set the safety arms the right way and have the pins set way too low,” Sevcik says. “The purpose of those safety arms is to give you a safe way to bail out of a lift. Otherwise, you’re just using a power rack as a big immobile squat stand.”

So, what is the correct way to set up the safety arms? “To set them up for squats, put the unloaded bar on your back and squat down to the deepest position you can get yourself into,” Sevcik says. “The safety bars should be about an inch and a half or one notch lower than your bottom position, so if you ever fail on a squat, all you do is sit your butt down to the very bottom.”

Many come with safety arms, pins, or nylon straps, but some budget options may require purchasing them separately. If you’re new to using a power rack, we recommend asking a fitness professional for guidance on different exercises and safety.

Before purchasing, measure your space and look at the rack’s total footprint. While measuring the floor and comparing it to the base is essential, ceiling height is another crucial factor. You may need a shorter option if you use your rack in a basement or a room with low ceilings.

You can retract and store a folding power rack if you’re limited in space or need room for other activities. It’s a good idea to consider your height and weight when looking at the dimensions, especially if you plan to use the pull-up bar or other attachments. You may want to leave space on each side for accessories so you can attach them on the sides if necessary. We recommend you keep the space around the rack clear of obstructions, particularly in front, so you can safely complete your lifts or bailout.

Power racks come in a variety of styles, colors, and materials. Some construction and style factors to consider include:

The power racks on this list have capacities ranging from 700 pounds to 1,100 pounds. The lower and middle weight range will likely work for you if you are a beginner or intermediate exerciser. If you are an advanced athlete, you may want to opt for a power rack with a high weight capacity and heavy-duty steel. Attachments such as safety arms, J-hooks, or pull-up bars have varying weight limits. Always stay within the recommended weight range for your safety.

How much you’re willing to spend depends on your budget and training style. Many racks on this list include a basic setup, with the option to add accessories as needed, which cuts the cost. Other racks come fully loaded with accessories, so they are incredibly versatile. However, these options cost more, so it is crucial to consider the features and whether or not they are helpful for your workout style and goals. The racks on this list range from around $299 to $965, and many brands offer free shipping.

Power racks come in various styles and features. The following sections break down Sevcik’s power rack must-haves.

Sevcik says to look for thick, heavy-duty steel such as 11-gauge. “A rack made out of thicker steel creates more leverage on the uprights. Especially when you add those attachments.”

“I think a big must-have a lot of people overlook is to make sure your J-cups, or J-hooks, have some coating on them to preserve the knurling on your bar,” Sevcik says. “If you’re doing a bench press or deadlift, [knurling] is no big deal, but if you’re an Olympic weightlifter, that’s where my snatch grip is holding onto, and I want it to be as sharp and aggressive as possible.”

“I would make sure you have enough hole patterns to make a lot of adjustments. Sometimes, they’re too spaced out, for example, in two-inch increments instead of one,” Sevcik says. “I like to have the added adjustability, especially for those heavier weights.”

Sevcik says having the option to do pull-ups is a good idea. “They’re one of the most basic, fundamental movements. Plus, if you dedicate the square footage to put the rack in there, you’ll want to get as much utility as possible because you are sacrificing some real estate.”

“It’s important to have the option to add accessories,” Sevcik says. “You might not want a dip bar right now, but down the road, you may decide to incorporate more dips in the training program, and it sure is nice to have your power rack as your one central piece of equipment.”

Many power racks come with attachments, though certain brands require you to purchase add-on attachments separately. Some of the power racks on this list come with pull-up bars (chin-up bar), safeties, and J-cups included, while others do not. It’s important to read the details of what comes with your unit to know what additional purchases you’ll need to make to achieve your desired power rack workout.

We considered the following while choosing each product on this list:

We chose budget-friendly and high-end options suitable for any fitness level and listed several compact and folding options for those with limited space. We also spoke to Shane Sevcik, a USAW-certified coach and competitive athlete, about essential add-ons and safety features.

Research suggests 30 to 60 minutes a week of muscle-strengthening exercises can benefit your health. With the help of a power rack, you can achieve a wide range of strength training fitness moves without needing a spotter. A power rack can add convenience to your workout by enabling you to get a safe weightlifting workout anytime from the comfort of your home gym.

A full power rack has four to six uprights attached by cross members, creating a cage to lift in. A squat rack—also called a squat stand—is typically two uprights and weighs less than a power rack, making it more portable. Power racks are more versatile, with the option to add accessories, while squat racks usually do not.

If you choose a freestanding power rack, anchor it following the manufacturer’s instructions to ensure it’s safe and secure.

Generally, a freestanding power rack should be a few feet from the wall so you can perform exercises comfortably and safely. Always refer to the manufacturer’s guidelines and recommendations when setting up your rack.

Common gauges are 11-gauge and 12-gauge, with lower numbers providing thicker and stronger steel; however, these tend to be more pricey options. A thinner 14-gauge steel is slightly less sturdy but likely works well for a general home gym setup. We chose racks ranging from 11-gauge to 16-gauge to suit various budgets and fitness levels.

Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC, is a writer and editor in the fitness and nutrition industries. She has contributed to PowerliftingTechnique, FeastGood, Garage Gym Reviews, BarBend, and Fitbod. When she's not working, you can find her training in her garage gym; cuddling with her dog, Charlie; trying to keep her two cats, Raven and Riley, from destroying her house; or hanging out with her family - all with a cup of coffee close by.

#8773. The Best Elliptical Machines for a Low-Impact Cardio Workout at Home

Looking for a low-impact but high-intensity workout? Snag one of the best elliptical machines for an effective, joint-friendly workout.

Written by Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Stephen Sheehan, CPT Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

Elliptical machines have come a long way, with major developments in specs and technology. Their ergonomic design maximizes the quality and intensity of your workout, incorporating both upper and lower body muscles. This provides you with a full-body workout to enhance your cardio fitness while maintaining the structural integrity of your joints. We consider that an all-around win.

If you are on the hunt for the best elliptical of 2025 but aren’t sure where to start, you’ve come to the right place. Below, you’ll find our top picks for the best elliptical machines and a comprehensive guide on what to consider before you make your purchase.

The NordicTrack FS10i isn’t your average elliptical—it combines a treadmill, elliptical, and stair stepper all into one machine designed to give you the flexibility to switch up your cardio. The 32-inch adjustable stride adjusts based on your leg movements. In other words, if you use the FS10i as a stair stepper, your legs move up and down, but your stride goes back and forth in elliptical mode.

You can follow an iFIT class (with a $39/month subscription) on the 10-inch HD touchscreen, which tracks key stats such as time elapsed, speed, distance, and calories burned. Trainers can digitally adjust your incline up to 10 percent or tap into the 24 resistance levels based on the workout. If you’re working out manually, you can make these adjustments yourself via one-touch buttons next to the touchscreen.

If you’re on a fitness journey, a weight-loss diet and exercise are essential to achieving your goals. If you already have a favorite weight-loss program or weight-loss app, an elliptical can help you knock out your daily sweat session. While any elliptical will help you work toward your goal, the E95 stands out thanks to its free fitness app and integrated streaming services, perfect for when you need more motivation to get moving. Unlike some of the other ellipticals on our list, the E95’s companion app, Sole+, is free with your new machine. Sole+ includes more than 3,000 trainer-led workouts and classes for on and off your elliptical. For even more entertainment while you work out, the E95 is integrated with several streaming services, including Netflix, Amazon Prime, Hulu, and more.

The Sole E95’s cushioned foot pedals are designed to keep your knees and ankles from feeling the brunt of an extended workout. The pedals adjust to fit your gait, but default to a two-degree inward angle. The Sole E95’s 20 resistance levels let you challenge yourself and can be easily switched via buttons on the handles. Sole’s drive system is engineered to stay quiet, but if you want to listen to your class or music on its built-in speakers, simply plug in your smart device and prop it up in the inserted tablet holder.

The Sole E35 Elliptical is a great choice for anyone looking for a reliable, simple elliptical with a smooth ride for joint comfort. It’s easy to set up and use and has everything you need to start working out in the comfort of your own home—no gym membership required.

The Sole E35’s ramp-like design allows users to simply step on and start moving. With this elliptical, you can get a full-body workout without having to worry about straining your back or joints. It is equipped with 20 different levels of resistance so users can adjust their workouts according to their fitness levels and goals. With 10 preloaded workout programs plus free access to the Sole+ fitness app, even beginners can start their training immediately. Even though it’s not as heavy-duty as other ellipticals, the  Sole E35 works for users up to 300 pounds.

And while it comes with all the features you’d expect from an elliptical, it also has some great extras that we love: built-in fans keep you cool during workouts, and a user-friendly, fully adjustable console ensures a comfortable workout.

If you’re short on space but looking to up your cardio workout with an elliptical, take a look at the Bowflex Max Trainer M6. Bringing together form and function, the M6 stamps out a footprint measuring just 46 inches long, 26 inches wide, and 64.2 inches high—quite a bit smaller than your average treadmill or other cardio machine. Its 15-inch stride length may not be a great fit for taller individuals, but it still supports a user weight of up to 300 pounds.

The M6 offers a great workout with 16 levels of resistance, a USB charging port, a water bottle holder, Bluetooth heart rate compatibility, and multi-grip moving handles with pulse contact grips to measure heart rate. It’s also equipped with a unique burn rate display to track how many calories you burn per minute and allows you to set activity level targets throughout the workout.

If interactive programming is your jam, you’re in luck. The JRNY digital fitness platform for Bowflex products houses tailored workouts, on-demand classes, real-time coaching, and personalized programming. Purchasing the M6 gives you a free membership to JRNY. Download the workout app, place your device in the magnetic media, and get pedaling.

Bowflex offers in-home assembly for an additional fee, which we recommend because assembly takes a few hours (according to reviewers). The warranty is a bit disappointing, offering only two years on the frame and parts. Most competitors cover the frame with a 10-year warranty, so you’ll want to make sure your Bowflex is assembled correctly.

The little elliptical that could, the Cubii Go provides an elliptical experience for a fraction of the space and price. This portable elliptical fits seamlessly underneath your desk and can be taken on the go with its built-in wheels and retractable handle.

Unlike under-desk treadmills, you don’t have to stand to work out with the Cubii Go. Instead, you can stay seated and pedal during a meeting or while watching TV. Its large flywheel lets you go up to ten resistance levels while an illuminated display projects your stats back to you. Use the Cubii app to keep track of the details of your workout plus. The Cubii Go is also easy to take with you, thanks to built-in wheels and a double telescoping handle.

This compact elliptical currently has an average rating of 4.8 out of 5 stars on the Cubii website. Out of 238 reviews, only five give the Cubii Go one star. Negative ratings include criticism of the machine’s stability and design. Four-star reviews praise the Cubii Go as effective and easy to use.

If you’re a first-time elliptical buyer who’s feeling a little intimidated by the whole process, you might find the Niceday Smart Elliptical CT11 a comfortable option. Equipped with large pedals and constructed with steel, the Niceday Elliptical trainer can support users up to 400 pounds. It’s also designed to fit users between 4’9″ and 6’4″ tall, although it’s worth noting that the 15.5-inch stride length may feel restrictive to people on the taller end of that range. This elliptical also comes 90 percent pre-assembled, a feature sure to appeal to those less mechanically inclined. If you find quiet workouts comfortable, you’ll appreciate the Smart Elliptical CT11’s magnetic drive system. It’s designed to reduce noise and keep the sound of the machine below 20 decibels—about the same amount of noise as rustling leaves.

This elliptical trainer offers 16 levels of resistance, so you can use it for anything from light workouts to more intense leg and glute exercises. It’s also compatible with Kinomap and digitally records stats including speed, distance, calories, and heart rate.

The Niceday Smart Elliptical CT11 has an average rating of 4.4 out of 5 stars on Amazon with nearly 3,000 reviews. While most Amazon feedback is complimentary about the machine’s performance, criticisms include noise level and suitability for taller users.

Elliptical machines are an excellent choice for people looking for a low-impact, total-body cardio workout of any intensity. “You’re using both your arms and your legs to propel yourself, and you can adjust the resistance based on what works for you,” says Samantha April, P.T., D.P.T., U.S.A.-W. They’re also great for people with balance issues. “Someone may use an elliptical over a treadmill if they’re looking for something that’s a little more controlled and they want to move with the machine and keep their feet stationary versus a treadmill where they’re required to move,” says April.

However, elliptical machines are not ideal for people with small home gym spaces. “If space is a concern inside of your home gym, ellipticals take up a pretty fair amount of space, so it’s important that you’ll actually have the space to accommodate that,” April says.

Users can do a variety of workouts on an elliptical trainer, from slow, easy walks to fast and intense interval sessions.

Don’t forget to warm up with some deep breaths and stretching. When you’re ready, place your feet on the pedals and grab the handles. Begin moving your feet forward in a general walking motion.

Although you’re free to go at your own pace, a good baseline for elliptical workouts is 15-20 minutes. As you get more comfortable and build your endurance, you can increase your speed, resistance, and incline (if your machine has variable incline settings).

We asked Matt Petrillo, C.S.C.S., director of adult fitness at The Annex Sports Performance in Passaic, N.J., how to get a great workout on the elliptical.

“My clients utilize ellipticals through low-intensity interval training. To do this, choose a work interval ranging from 30-90 seconds and a rest interval between 30-60 seconds, making sure your work period is longer than your rest,” Petrillo says.

He says when you are in your work period, you want to begin each round with your heart rate as close to 120 beats per minute as possible. By the end of your work period, you want your heart rate to be between 150-160 beats per minute.

“During your rest period, the goal is to drop your heart rate to as close to 120 beats per minute as possible,” says Petrillo. Don’t have a heart rate monitor? That’s OK, too. “Simply go at the fastest sustainable pace you can while only breathing through your nose during your work periods,” Petrillo says.

Depending on fitness level and time constraints, go through the work/rest process for 15-30 rounds. “This type of workout helps build our aerobic system, which can greatly improve our cardiovascular and overall health,” Petrillo says.

To help you choose the best elliptical for your needs and goals, we evaluated dozens of machines and looked at several factors, including:

The flywheel is the heavy, rotating wheel inside your machine. It provides stability and momentum while you pedal. A heavier flywheel offers a better, smoother ride and is generally more expensive.

A range of resistance levels is important for workout intensity variability and training progression. Ellipticals function on a fixed track, so increasing speed is limited.

You’ll want an elliptical with enough resistance options for challenging workouts as your physical fitness improves.

Incline ranges on an elliptical are more of an added bonus than a must-have. They can add a level of variability to training. By increasing or decreasing the slope, you activate different muscle groups and change the intensity of the workout without necessarily changing speed or resistance. As the slope increases, more output is required from the user to generate speed, which will increase heart rate. It’s similar to walking up a hill versus walking on flat ground.

Stride length refers to how far apart the pedals move from one another when in use. The stride length most affects how comfortable and natural the stride feels for you. A short stride length will feel cramped to anyone with longer legs or particularly long strides. Conversely, a large stride length may feel awkward and clunky to someone with short legs. There is no universal best stride length since it’s highly dependent on your leg length and overall height. Most ellipticals feature a 20-inch stride length, which works for the vast majority of users.

If you live in a small apartment or are equipping a tiny home gym space, you’ll want a compact elliptical that occupies minimal real estate. Measure out the space where you plan to use your elliptical before you start your search.

If you’re a sucker for technology and place a premium on programming with top-of-the-line features and conveniences, make sure you find an elliptical that checks off all your boxes. Write out a list of your must-have technology specifications and features before you begin your search. This will help you narrow down your focus and streamline the process.

This may seem like a no-brainer, but knowing your budget is imperative when buying any type of home exercise equipment. Ellipticals come at a variety of price points, from a few hundred dollars to several thousand.

Elliptical cross trainers are a great way to improve your cardio fitness and strength. The combination of the resistance from the pedals and handlebars provides you with a full-body workout.

Treadmills and elliptical trainers are great ways to get aerobic exercise. Choosing between them primarily depends on your fitness goals, your current fitness level, and whether you have an existing injury or condition that affects your joints or muscles. Consider these factors:-A full-size elliptical provides a full-body workout that targets your arms and shoulders in addition to your legs, calves, and glutes.-Ellipticals are not as high-impact since your feet remain in contact with the pedals rather than repeatedly striking the running deck of a treadmill. If you have joint pain or a lower-body injury, an elliptical will probably put less stress on those areas.-A treadmill makes more sense if you’re focused on building endurance and leg strength. It’s the better choice for runners and walkers.-The learning curve with an elliptical machine could be more difficult since it involves more complex movements than simply running or walking.Other factors besides workouts could also affect your decision. For example, treadmills tend to be more expensive than ellipticals. A high-quality elliptical trainer will almost certainly be less noisy than a treadmill, an important consideration for home workouts.

How many calories you burn depends on your body size, fitness level, and the intensity and duration of your workout. However, according to Harvard Health Publishing, users can expect to burn between 270–370 calories for 30 minutes of exercise on an elliptical machine.

Yes, but not specifically. While it’s impossible to target fat burning in specific areas of your body, exercising on an elliptical machine, when paired with a weight-loss diet, can help users maintain a calorie deficit, contributing to all-over fat loss.

Consistency and accountability are crucial when it comes to weight loss. The best elliptical for weight loss is the machine you use regularly. Look for an elliptical with features to keep you motivated and focused. However, proper nutrition is just as important as having a consistent workout schedule.

Yes. The elliptical works both the upper body and lower body, targeting your glutes, quadriceps, hamstrings, calves, arms, and core.

Walking and the elliptical are cardio workouts. Typically, ellipticals enable you to burn more calories with varied intensities, resistance, and preset workout options. Ellipticals are easier on your joints than walking, offering a solid alternative to the impact of walking on pavement or a treadmill.

Seeing results from any form of exercise depends on your goals and the effort you put into your workouts.

#8772. Science Has Zeroed in on Why Lifters Need Cardio for Heart Health

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Every gym (real gym) has a dude like this—we used to call them “fire plugs” (if you’re not from New York, that means fire hydrant). He has arms like sewer pipes, a chest like a gun safe, zero degrees of V-taper, and he’d probably be proud of the fact that he has a squat rack in his living room in case he needs some extra sets—your basic Midwestern corn-fed Jethro type. The exact guy you would never imagine seeing on a treadmill.

Cardio? That’s what people do when they don’t have huge muscles to worry about. Besides, he can see his abs (ab, actually, but it’s like a rock). What more evidence of health could anybody possibly need?

That depends on how long Jethro wants to live. A study recently published in Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise looked at 562,234 adults who had undergone clinical treadmill testing. Researchers wanted to know whether measuring cardiorespiratory fitness improved predictions of who would die over the following decade, beyond the usual suspects: age, sex, high blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol problems, and smoking. The answer was yes. Not because the treadmill possesses magical cognitive powers, but because how much work your heart and lungs can support tells doctors something the other numbers don’t.

The researchers measured peak exercise capacity in Metabolic Equivalent of Task (MET). It’s a way of expressing how much energy a physical activity demands relative to rest. In the study, the bottom fifth of fitness fell below five METs. After adjusting for traditional risk factors, the estimated ten-year mortality risk in that least-fit group was 32.9 percent, compared with 13.4 percent among the fitter participants. That’s a considerable difference, even allowing for the fact that these were people referred for clinical exercise tests, not a random cross-section of every healthy person walking around America.

Another number worth understanding correctly is that each additional MET of measured fitness was associated with a 16 percent lower hazard of death over follow-up. Notice I said associated. Not caused. The researchers did not take half a million people, put some on treadmills, leave the others on the couch, and wait ten years to see who was still kicking. This was an observational analysis. Healthier people may be able to exercise harder because they’re healthier in the first place. The study accounted for several major risk factors, but it cannot eliminate every possible explanation.

Nor did adding fitness transform mortality prediction into a crystal ball. The model’s discrimination score improved from 0.662 to 0.682 when cardiorespiratory fitness was included. That’s statistically meaningful and potentially useful, but modest. The headline isn’t that doctors can now tell you the day you’ll die by watching you jog, but rather that a basic measure of physical capacity deserves a seat at the table alongside blood pressure and the rest of the measurable health markers.

What I find fascinating is the cultural blind spot this exposes. Bodybuilders understand that muscle matters, as do strength, bone loading, glucose regulation, mobility, and the ability to get yourself up off the toilet when you’re eighty—all excellent reasons to keep lifting. Somewhere along the line, a segment of the iron community decided that cardio was bad. It was either an inconvenience or an enemy that ate muscle, or both. A lot of old-school, Arnold-era bodybuilders didn’t do cardio. Then suddenly the Life Cycle was invented, and a lot of us felt good about adding endurance training to our mix, mainly because of the massive calves and quads we started to see on Olympic cyclists. So, maybe there’s something to this? Blasphemy!

Until you consider your heart and your potential lifespan, with or without cardio and with or without muscle.

Of course, if you’re a bodybuilder, you’re going to take an extremist position. But you don’t have to become a distance runner. In fact, if your knees, hips, or general disposition object to running, there are bicycles, rowing machines, swimming pools, incline walks, and any number of ways to get your breathing up without pounding pavement. The practical target isn’t to chase a laboratory number you saw in an article. It’s to build enough aerobic capacity that ordinary life doesn’t feel like a stress test. Start where you are, progress gradually, and if you have symptoms or known heart disease, get medical guidance before going all out.

I still think a man should be strong. But if he’s strong enough to deadlift a Buick and gets gassed carrying groceries up one flight of stairs, we might have overlooked something. For the slight handful of you who compete at a very high level, doing cardio is etched into your coach’s DNA at this point. You have no choice. Except to keep doing it after the show is over. The rest of you, do cardio! Times have changed, technology has changed, and research has accumulated. Adding these data to the mountain of evidence thus collected on the topic, the overall consensus, if your desire is longevity, is simple: the lighter, stronger, leaner, and more cardiovascularly fit you are, the longer you get to bother everyone.

The best workaround for Delta dynamic pricing on premium cabins

Here's the insight that changes everything: Delta prices its own award seats dynamically, which means when you search Delta.com for a SkyMiles redemption, you're at the mercy of an algorithm that reads demand, load factors, and booking timing. A Delta One Suite that costs 50,000 SkyMiles one week might jump to 120,000 or even 250,000 SkyMiles the next. It's unpredictable, often punishing, and fundamentally unfair to the loyal customer who saved up miles expecting consistency.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club doesn't play by those rules.

Virgin Atlantic is a Delta SkyTeam partner, which means Flying Club members can book seats on Delta-operated flights using their Virgin Atlantic miles. But critically — and this is the entire mechanism — Virgin Atlantic prices Delta award seats on a fixed award chart, not Delta's dynamic pricing system. That chart currently prices Delta One (business class) on transcon routes like JFK–LAX at 50,000 miles one-way. No matter what Delta's algorithm is doing that day, your Virgin Atlantic redemption rate stays fixed.

This is a classic pricing inefficiency created by partner award charts lagging behind airline pricing strategies. Delta has every incentive to raise its own SkyMiles pricing — it captures more revenue from its own loyalty currency. But Delta has far less control over what a partner program charges to access its seats. Virgin Atlantic's award chart is, in effect, a door into Delta inventory that bypasses Delta's own toll booth.

The points you need to fund this redemption are almost certainly already sitting in currencies you have or can easily earn:

For a redemption this valuable, the 1:1 instant transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt are your primary path. You transfer exactly what you need, the miles appear in your Flying Club account immediately, and you book. No waiting, no uncertainty.

Virgin Atlantic has a reputation for imposing high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights — and that reputation is well-earned. But here's the critical nuance: surcharges do NOT apply to partner awards. When you book a Delta-operated flight through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, you pay only the standard carrier-imposed taxes and fees, which are minimal on domestic U.S. routes. On JFK–LAX, expect to pay roughly $5–$15 in taxes. That's it. The surcharge concern that makes some people avoid Virgin Atlantic entirely simply doesn't apply here.

Flying Club miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with at least one earning or redemption activity every three years, and your miles will remain intact indefinitely. This is a very traveler-friendly policy compared to programs with hard expiration dates.

Do NOT start at Virgin Atlantic's website — their search tool for partner awards is limited. Instead, go directly to delta.com and search for your desired route (e.g., JFK → LAX) in the date range you're targeting. Select "Use miles" as your payment method and filter by Business class. You're not booking here — you're prospecting.

What you're looking for: Delta One availability showing in the results. When you see it, note the exact flight number, date, and departure time. Delta.com will show you the SkyMiles price (which will be high under dynamic pricing), but ignore that number entirely. You just need to confirm the seat exists.

You need 50,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles per person. Before transferring anything, confirm which flexible points currency you're working with:

All transfer at 1:1 instantly. If you're using Marriott Bonvoy points, the ratio is 3:1 (so 150,000 Bonvoy points = 50,000 Flying Club miles), and transfers take 1–5 days.

Once you've confirmed availability on a specific flight, transfer your points. Use the transfer portal within your credit card program's website (Chase, Amex, Citi, or Bilt). You'll need your Flying Club membership number — create a free account at virginatlantic.com/us/en/flying-club if you don't have one.

For Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers: miles appear instantly in your Flying Club account. Confirm the balance before proceeding.

Critical warning: Do not transfer points until you've verbally confirmed availability with a Virgin Atlantic agent (Step 4). Points transfers are irreversible.

This is a phone booking, not an online booking. Call Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at 1-800-365-9500. Have your flight details ready:

Ask the agent to confirm that Delta One award availability exists on your chosen flight before you transfer points. If they confirm it, then transfer and call back — or ask to be placed on a brief hold while you complete the transfer (instant transfers make this possible).

Once your miles are transferred and the agent has confirmed availability, they'll complete the booking. You'll pay only standard carrier taxes and fees — expect roughly $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. route. You'll receive a Virgin Atlantic booking confirmation, but your ticket will show Delta as the operating carrier.

Virgin Atlantic can book Delta awards up to 331 days in advance. For the best seat selection and availability, aim to search within that window as early as possible.

Delta SkyMiles uses fully dynamic pricing with no published award chart, meaning business class awards can range from 80,000 to 500,000 SkyMiles for the same route depending on demand. Virgin Atlantic, as a Delta joint venture partner, maintains a fixed award chart for Delta-operated flights — creating a massive pricing arbitrage. A JFK-to-London Delta One Suite that Delta prices at 350,000 SkyMiles can often be booked through Virgin for 47,500 Flying Club miles. Both programs see the same award inventory, but Virgin prices it using their distance-based chart instead of Delta's demand-based algorithm. Since Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club accepts 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Capital One, Citi, and Bilt, you can earn these miles through credit card spending without ever flying Virgin Atlantic.

Let's walk through a real example so the numbers become concrete.

The Route: New York JFK → Los Angeles LAX The Aircraft: Airbus A350-900 The Cabin: Delta One Suites

Pull up Delta.com on a typical travel date and you'll find Delta One Suites on this route priced anywhere from $2,500 for a off-peak weekday to $5,000–$6,000 during peak summer weekends or holiday travel. Let's use a realistic midpoint of $3,500 — a completely standard price for business class on one of America's most competitive routes.

If you earned those 50,000 points via a Chase Sapphire Reserve welcome bonus (currently 60,000 points) and some organic spend, your real cost to acquire the points was a small fraction of the flight's retail value.

You check in at JFK's Terminal 4 with Delta status access or a Priority Pass card in hand, clearing into the Delta Sky Club or the premium Centurion Lounge (if you carry the Amex Platinum). Then you board the A350-900 and find your suite.

The five-hour flight from New York to Los Angeles becomes an experience rather than a commute. You arrive rested, full, and having spent roughly $11 out of pocket on a seat your fellow passengers paid $3,500 for. That gap — that's the ChooseFI travel rewards mindset in action.

Virgin Atlantic can book Delta awards up to 331 days in advance. Delta One availability on high-demand routes like JFK–LAX is not unlimited — it's released in waves and often fills quickly for peak dates. Set a calendar reminder to search exactly 331 days before your target travel date. This is especially important for holiday travel, summer weekends, and any dates where you have a hard deadline.

Since transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt are instant, you can do a same-call transfer — confirm availability with the agent, ask them to hold for a moment, transfer your points in a separate browser tab, and confirm with the agent that the miles have landed. This eliminates the risk of availability disappearing between your transfer and your booking attempt.

While this sweet spot is available year-round, Delta One availability is generally better on Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday departures when leisure demand is lower. If your travel dates are flexible, searching across a week of dates will often surface better availability on midweek flights.

Virgin Atlantic's award chart has high fuel surcharges on Virgin Atlantic-operated flights. This guide is specifically about Delta-operated flights. Never confuse the two. When you call to book, confirm the operating carrier is Delta. The surcharge-free benefit applies only to partner awards.

Points transfers are irreversible. A common and painful mistake is transferring points to Flying Club only to discover the specific flight you wanted has no award availability. Always confirm availability verbally with a Flying Club agent before initiating any transfer.

The most efficient path to 50,000 points is a single credit card welcome bonus. The Chase Sapphire Preferred or Chase Sapphire Reserve both offer welcome bonuses that can fully fund this redemption — and both transfer to Virgin Atlantic at 1:1 instantly. Alternatively, the Amex Gold Card or Platinum Card welcome bonuses work equally well via Amex's instant transfer path.

Flying Club miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. A simple fix: make a small earning transaction (even a hotel stay or car rental through their partners) at least once every three years.

This redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers who want a genuinely luxurious experience on one of America's premier transcontinental routes and are comfortable with a moderate amount of booking complexity — primarily a phone call to Virgin Atlantic.

Minimum points needed: 50,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles per person (100,000 for two). These are most efficiently sourced via a single credit card welcome bonus.

For the FI-minded traveler who has earned a moderate points balance and wants to experience premium cabin travel on a meaningful domestic route, this is a standout use of currency. The 5–12 CPP range makes it one of the most efficient domestic business class redemptions available.

This redemption is rated **moderate** — not because any individual step is technically complex, but because it requires coordinating two separate systems (Delta.com for availability searching and Virgin Atlantic by phone for booking) and making an irreversible transfer decision under some time pressure. **What makes it moderately challenging:** 1. **Availability is the main hurdle.** Delta One award inventory released to partners is limited, particularly on peak dates. You won't always find seats when you want them, and the 331-day booking window means planning further ahead than most travelers are accustomed to. 2. **The booking requires a phone call.** There's no self-service online booking for Virgin Atlantic partner awards. Some travelers find this intimidating; in practice, Flying Club agents are helpful and accustomed to partner award bookings. 3. **The transfer-before-booking sequence requires discipline.** The rule is: confirm first, transfer second. Getting that order wrong is an expensive mistake. **Three tips to make this easier:** - **Use Delta.com as your search engine.** It shows real-time award availability far more reliably than third-party tools for Delta-operated flights. - **Call Virgin Atlantic during off-peak hours** (early morning Eastern time tends to mean shorter hold times and more patient agents). - **Have your flight details written down** before you call — flight number, date, origin, destination, and Flying Club number. A prepared caller gets a faster, smoother booking. If you've ever transferred points to an airline program and called to book an award, this process will feel completely familiar. If this is your first partner award booking, treat it as a learning experience — the 5–12 CPP reward on the other side is well worth one phone call.

Log into your Delta SkyMiles account and search for one-way business class (Delta One) award flights. Filter for nonstop flights on the A350-900, which is the aircraft with Delta One Suites. Note the dates that show availability — this is the same inventory Virgin can book.

If you do not already have a Virgin Atlantic Flying Club account, create one at virginatlantic.com. You need an active account to receive transferred miles and to reference when calling to book.

Transfer the required miles from your preferred partner: Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant transfer), Amex Membership Rewards (typically 1-2 business days), Capital One (1-2 days), Citi ThankYou (instant to 24 hours), or Bilt (1-2 days). Always confirm availability before transferring.

Call Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at their US number. Provide the specific flight number, date, and route you found on delta.com. The agent will search for the same availability and quote the mileage cost from Virgin's fixed award chart. Confirm the booking and pay taxes and fees.

Virgin Atlantic's fixed award chart prices Delta One flights based on distance. Transatlantic routes (US to Europe) typically cost 47,500 to 60,000 Virgin miles one-way in business class. Transpacific routes cost more, around 60,000 to 80,000 miles. Compare this to Delta SkyMiles, which can charge 200,000 to 500,000 miles for the same seats.

No. As of 2026, Virgin Atlantic does not support online booking for Delta partner awards. You must call Virgin Atlantic's Flying Club phone line to book. Search for availability on delta.com first, then call with the specific flight details. The call typically takes 10-15 minutes.

Delta One is the business class cabin available on multiple aircraft types with lie-flat seats but no closing door. Delta One Suites are only on the A350-900 and feature a fully enclosed suite with a closing door, a wider seat, and a more private experience. When booking, verify the aircraft type is A350-900 to ensure you get the Suite product.

Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers to Virgin Atlantic are instant. Citi ThankYou points are also fast, typically completing within minutes to 24 hours. Amex Membership Rewards and Bilt usually take 1-2 business days. Capital One transfers take 1-2 days as well. If you find availability and need to book quickly, Chase is the best source.

Booking Delta One Suites through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club is the definitive workaround for Delta's punishing dynamic pricing. Paying 50,000 transferable points for a seat that Delta prices at 350,000 SkyMiles is one of the largest arbitrage opportunities in travel rewards. The fully enclosed suite with a closing door is the best international business class product any US carrier offers. Yes, you need to call to book — but that 15-minute phone call saves you 300,000 miles. Build your transferable points balances with Chase, Amex, or Bilt, search delta.com for A350 availability, and let Virgin Atlantic's fixed award chart do the rest.

#8769. 5 Mobility Moves to Improve Your Bulgarian Split Squats

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

The Bulgarian split squat is the exercise almost all lifters love to hate. Still, you cannot deny its benefits, including increased quad and glute strength and size and reduced strength imbalances, which can improve bilateral squats.

But it has a funny way of humbling those who perform it because it demands more than strength. It requires hip mobility, ankle dorsiflexion, pelvic control, and single-leg stability.

If one of those is off, let’s hope you’re not on camera.

Here, I’ll cover common BSS performance issues and five mobility exercises to help you get the most out of the most dreaded exercise in gym history.

Before blaming the Bulgarian split squat for all your woes, let’s test whether it’s a mobility issue.

The goal isn’t a perfect-looking rep but finding any performance limitations that are holding back your gains. But before adding mobility drills, let’s see if it’s a setup issue.

Not every Bulgarian split squat problem requires another corrective drill. Before blaming tight hips and reaching for the foam roller, a few small adjustments could make a big difference.

About to perform Bulgarian split squats? Here’s what your body needs to bring to that first set.

A well-performed Bulgarian split squat requires hip and ankle mobility and stability everywhere else. Mobility gets you into position, but strength and stability let you own it.

5 MOBILITY MOVES TO OWN THE BOTTOM POSITION OF YOUR BULGARIAN SPLIT SQUAT

If the adjustments above cleaned up your performance issues, great, you’re good to go. If not, the five mobility exercises below are exactly what you need.

The Bulgarian split squat may be an up-and-down exercise, but your hips must also control side-to-side movement to keep your pelvis and knees stable. That’s where the Lateral Lunge to Box earns its keep. It improves adductor mobility and builds hip strength and control, allowing you to reach the bottom without issues.

Why Lifters Need It: The lateral lunge to box trains the adductors through a lengthened position while developing the hip strength and mobility needed to resist excessive lateral shifting.

Programming Suggestions: You can perform this unloaded as a warm-up for 10 reps per side, or load it up as an accessory movement for your squats and deadlifts for 2-4 sets of 8-15 reps per side.

https://www.youtube.com/shorts/TML8Vqy-ACQ

If your rear hip flexors and quads are tight, it’s hard to get to the bottom without arching your lower back. The Couch Stretch targets the hip flexors and quads that can restrict the rear leg.

Why Lifters Need It: The rectus femoris is unique among the quadriceps because it crosses both the hip and knee joints. If it’s restricted, you may feel excessive pulling in the front of your thigh, arch your lower back, or shorten your range of motion to avoid discomfort. The Couch Stretch can restore length to the rectus femoris and the quads.

Programming Suggestions: Perform two sets of 30-60 seconds per side as part of your warmup.

If you struggle to get your knees over your toes, your heel may lift, your balance may suffer, and your knee may have difficulty moving forward. The Weighted Ankle Rocker helps you build that missing range without any mobility circus tricks.

Why Lifters Need It: During the Bulgarian split squat, your front ankle moves into dorsiflexion as your knee travels forward over it. Sufficient dorsiflexion lets you distribute pressure evenly across your foot as you lower to the bottom position.

Programming Suggestions: Perform two sets of 8 reps per side as part of your warm-up.

4. Front-Foot Elevated Split Squat With Pause

The front-foot-elevated split squat made the list because it promotes deeper hip and knee flexion. You might be able to get into a deep split squat, but if you bounce out of the bottom or lack the strength to hold it, this variation builds the mobility and strength needed for the BSS bottom position.

Why Lifters Need It: If you lack strength at the end of the range of motion, you may rush the eccentric or rely too much on the rear leg. Elevating the front foot lets you practice a deeper split squat position, while adding a pause builds strength there.

Programming Suggestions: Perform two sets of 6 reps per side with a three-second pause at the bottom as part of your warmup.

5. Half-Kneeling Hip Flexor Mobilization With Overhead Reach

There are other hip flexors besides the rectus femoris needed for the Bulgarian split squat. Your iliopsoas, the other hip flexor, also affects how your rear hip extends. This mobility drill strengthens hip extension while maintaining pelvic stability and improves iliopsoas length. The overhead reach and side bend add extra range and intensity.

Why Lifters Need It: When your trailing hip lacks full extension due to short hip flexors, you may compensate by arching your lower back or tipping your pelvis forward as you descend. A few sets of these will have your hips primed for the BSS, even if you are not.

Programming Suggestions: Perform two sets of 8 reaches per side, pausing for three seconds in the stretched position.

The Bulgarian split squat is tough enough without performance issues fighting you on every rep. The gains happen when you reach the bottom, when the muscles are under a loaded stretch. If getting there is a problem, fixing the setup and mobility issues will help.

Mobility gets you to the bottom, and strength and stability get you out. Master both, and this dreaded exercise becomes one of your best tools for building stronger legs.
